key_findings: Thick (35‑40 µm) FFPE sections retain ~70 % of cells intact versus <5 % in standard 5 µm sections, dramatically reducing lineage misidentification.
3D imaging revealed that ~40 % of CD8+ T cells in tumors exhibit LAG‑3 staining only in deeper z‑planes, explaining false‑negative checkpoint marker detection in 2D slides.
Morphological analysis showed average T cells make 5–10 functional contacts with neighbors; synapse distances contract from ~1 µm to ~30 nm during cytolytic engagement.

Serial reconstruction of ~470 tertiary lymphoid structures in lung adenocarcinoma and tuberculosis demonstrated heterogeneous developmental stages within a single follicle, which 2D sections misclassify.
Light‑sheet 3D imaging of a 2 mm‑thick colon specimen captured ~30 million cells, allowing tracing of nerve‑immune interactions and vascular‑associated immune niches.
Foundation models can embed H&E tiles into high‑dimensional vectors that predict patient outcomes and highlight prognostic regions such as venous invasion without additional training.
A GAN‑based pipeline converts quantitative phase images into realistic H&E, allowing existing H&E‑trained models to be applied to label‑free imaging.
Diffusion models successfully synthesize multiplex IHC (e.g., insulin/glucagon) from a single H&E slide, enabling retrospective multi‑omic analysis of archived specimens.
Optical‑flow algorithms reconstruct missing intermediate sections in CODA and Visium datasets, improving continuity for 3D reconstructions and spatial transcriptomics.
AI‑driven nucleus and tissue segmentation using models like Segment‑Anything achieve >90 % concordance with manual annotations across multiple organ systems.
readouts: synthetic multiplex IHC generated by diffusion models

key_findings: Clinical ALK FISH assay demonstrated 100% sensitivity, 99% specificity, and 100% PPV in validation against RNA‑Seq, setting a high bar for AI‑based predictors.
AI model trained on public colorectal cancer slides achieved AUROC ~0.9 for MSI prediction, the highest performance among mutation‑prediction tasks.
Predictive performance for EGFR, KRAS, PIK3CA, and other mutations ranged from AUROC 0.5‑0.7, indicating limited clinical utility at present.
Foundation models fine‑tuned on institution‑specific data (e.g., Campanella et al.) can raise EGFR prediction AUROC to ~0.9 and enable triage of lung cancer cases for rapid molecular testing.
ctDNA assay (Guardant360) identified ALK fusions in only ~50% of cases, illustrating that sub‑optimal sensitivity can still be useful for longitudinal monitoring.
Spatial multiplex IF and transcriptomics platforms (e.g., Singular Genomics 18‑plex IF + 500‑plex RNA) now achieve 10 samples per slide throughput, moving toward clinical feasibility.
open_questions: How can standardized pre‑analytical corrections be implemented to improve reproducibility of multiplex immunofluorescence across institutions?
What minimal performance metrics (AUROC, AUPRC, PPV) are required for AI‑based mutation predictors to be adopted in clinical decision support?
Can multimodal models that integrate radiology, H&E, IF, and spatial transcriptomics achieve clinically actionable predictive power for immunotherapy response?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Confounding variables such as biopsy size, sample type (resection vs. fluid cytology), and co‑occurring biomarkers (e.g., BRAF with MSI) can inflate AI performance.
Rare tumor entities (170 soft‑tissue sarcoma subtypes) are under‑represented in training data, limiting model generalizability.
AI models may learn non‑biological shortcuts (e.g., ruler presence in skin lesion images) that do not translate to robust clinical biomarkers.

key_findings: Intraprostatic inflammation measured in unbiased end‑of‑study biopsies is prospectively associated with increased prostate cancer risk (dose‑response with percent inflamed area).
CMV seropositivity is positively associated with greater intraprostatic inflammation in the PCPT cohort.
High variability of telomere length among cancer cells together with short stromal telomeres confers a 14‑fold higher risk of prostate cancer death, replicated at ~5‑fold in independent cohorts.
Long‑term statin use is linked to a ~50% reduction in metastatic prostate cancer and death, independent of cholesterol levels.
Long‑term digoxin use shows a similar inverse association with both organ‑confined and lethal prostate cancer.
Lower stromal telomere length correlates with reduced lamin B1 expression, supporting a senescent fibroblast hypothesis.
open_questions: What molecular mechanisms link statin‑induced cholesterol lowering to reduced prostate cancer aggressiveness?
Can the telomere variability biomarker be translated into a clinically feasible assay?
What is the causal pathway by which digoxin reduces prostate cancer risk—ion‑transport inhibition or off‑target effects?
readouts: fluorescence in situ telomere length assay

key_findings: Zoldonrasib achieved a 52% ORR and median PFS of 11 months in KRAS G12D mutant NSCLC (n=40) with only minimal grade 3 toxicities.
Deraxone rasib combined with gemcitabine/nab‑paclitaxel yielded a 59% ORR and 90% disease control in first‑line metastatic KRAS‑mutant pancreatic cancer, albeit with 73% grade 3+ adverse events.
Elacestrant produced a 32% partial response rate in KRAS G12C NSCLC patients who had progressed on prior G12C inhibitors.
VE‑1 plus PKMYT inhibition resulted in a 60% ORR in FBXW7‑mutant ovarian cancer harboring cyclin E1 amplification, demonstrating target‑driven efficacy.
Sequential combination of trastuzumab deruxtecan with olaparib achieved a 54% overall response rate, supporting schedule‑optimized ADC‑PARP synergy.
Claudin‑6 and folate receptor ADCs each generated >50% response rates across multiple tumor types, even in low‑expressing cohorts.
Cilta‑cel induced 100% MRD negativity and objective responses in high‑risk smoldering myeloma with no grade 3+ CRS, indicating curative potential in pre‑malignancy.
open_questions: What molecular features define the subset of KRAS G12D NSCLC patients who achieve durable ctDNA clearance?
How can the high grade 3+ toxicity of pan‑RAS PROTAC combos be mitigated while preserving efficacy?
What biomarkers predict response to VE‑1/PKMYT therapy beyond cyclin E1 amplification?
Can ADC payload diversification overcome the class‑wide resistance observed with topoisomerase‑based ADCs?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Mesothelin CAR‑T trials showed low response rates due to tumor microenvironment immunosuppression and T‑cell exhaustion.
CCR8‑targeting antibodies yielded single‑digit response rates, suggesting inadequate target engagement or compensatory pathways.

key_findings: In vivo BCMA CAR-T generation via TCR-targeted VLPs led to stringent complete or very good partial responses in 4 out of 5 multiple myeloma patients.
In vivo BCMA CAR-T therapy showed a bimodal toxicity profile: an initial infusion reaction followed by traditional cytokine release syndrome (CRS).
mRNA-LNP delivery of anti-CD19 CARs achieved transient B-cell aplasia and reduction in SLEDAI scores in refractory SLE patients.
Preclinical NHP data showed persistent B-cell aplasia following CD7-targeted VLP delivery of CAR20, though anti-CAR antibodies developed in 7-14 days.
Calculations suggest that only 0.05% to 2% transduction efficiency of total body T cells is required to reach the therapeutic dose of ~200 million CAR-positive cells.
open_questions: Whether tissue-resident immune effector cells in lymphoid organs are better suited for cancer immunotherapy than circulating blood T cells.
The exact cause of early inflammatory toxicity in in vivo VLP delivery (innate immune response vs. CD3 cross-linking).
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Immunogenicity of the CAR construct can lead to the development of anti-CAR antibodies, which may cause B-cells to return (observed in NHP models).

key_findings: Intracerebroventricular (ICV) delivery is 10-fold more potent than IV delivery in preclinical models.
Arm A (IV + ICV + lymphodepletion) showed significant tumor shrinkage and improved OS, but high-grade CRS occurred after IV infusion.
Arm B (ICV only, no lymphodepletion) resulted in transient responses (<3 months) due to rapid immune rejection of CAR T cells.
Anti-CAR responses include CD4+ (IL-2, IFN-gamma) and CD8+ (degranulating, 4-1BB+) T cells, as well as IgA antibodies produced by B cells within the CNS.
Arm C (ICV + lymphodepletion every 4 cycles) resulted in durable responses with median OS not reached and a plateau of >50% survival.
open_questions: Whether myeloid cells in the CNS contribute to a second axis of resistance.
Whether stealth platforms (used in allogeneic CARs) could prevent rejection in autologous CARs for solid tumors.
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Immunogenicity of the mouse-derived scFv and junctional domains (4-1BB/zeta) triggers robust host immune rejection.
IgA antibodies in the CNS suggest that the immune response is initiated within the CNS or peri-CNS tissues.

key_findings: NR4A2 is highly tumor-restricted and safe for driving high-toxicity transgenes like IL-12, whereas RGS16 is more potent but less restricted.
IL-12 driven by NR4A2 showed potent anti-tumor effects without the systemic weight loss seen with RGS16 or PD-1 promoters.
IL-2 driven by the RGS16 promoter showed the strongest anti-tumor effect and was well-tolerated.
A 'next-generation' knock-in strategy using a P2A linker to preserve endogenous RGS16 expression significantly reduced peripheral GFP expression while maintaining high tumor expression.
The one-step CRISPR knock-in of both the armoring gene and the CAR into the TRAC locus increased CAR expression without reducing transgene output.
open_questions: Whether this strategy can be used to deliver chemokines (CXCL9, CXCL10) to increase T cell trafficking to the tumor.
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Disruption of the RGS16 gene through standard CRISPR knock-in led to a loss of gene regulation and increased peripheral expression; this was corrected using a P2A linker strategy.

key_findings: Anti‑CTLA‑4 treatment expands ICOS‑positive CD4 T cells; absence of these cells predicts lack of response.
CTLA‑4 blockade induces novel spatial 'tetrad' structures (CD4 ICOS+, CD8, dendritic cell) that are enriched in responders and absent with PD‑1 blockade.
In CTLA‑4 knockout mice, CD4 cells co‑express multiple lineage transcription factors (BCL6, GATA3, RORγC), indicating deregulated differentiation.
Adding ICOS‑ligand to a tumor vaccine converts a non‑curative anti‑CTLA‑4 regimen into 100% tumor eradication in a resistant B16 model.
Combination of anti‑CTLA‑4 with anti‑PD‑1 shifts the exhausted CD8 population to a stem‑like TCF7+ phenotype and improves survival (>50% at 3 years in melanoma).
Long‑term follow‑up of ipilimumab trials shows ~20% of melanoma patients achieve 10‑year survival, whereas median pre‑trial survival was 6–7 months.
open_questions: What specific role do macrophages play in the formation and function of the CTLA‑4‑induced tetrads?
Can the tetrad architecture be leveraged as a predictive biomarker in human cancers beyond melanoma?
How can checkpoint strategies be adapted for pediatric fusion‑driven cancers that may lack immunogenic neoantigens?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: PD‑1 monotherapy expands terminally exhausted CD8 cells and shows higher relapse rates (25‑35% at 2 years) compared with CTLA‑4.
CTLA‑4 blockade rarely leads to disease recurrence, but efficacy depends on intact ICOS–ICOSL signaling.

key_findings: Identified ~80,000 circRNAs in 200 prostate cancers; average 7,000 per tumor; up to 400,000 circRNAs cataloged genome‑wide.
Functional screen of 10,000 circRNAs across seven cancer types revealed ~1,300 essential circRNAs, >90% previously uncharacterized and >95% act independently of linear host gene.
circRMST is >100‑fold enriched in neuroendocrine prostate cancer and small‑cell lung cancer versus adenocarcinoma, and is the dominant transcript from its locus.
CRISPR deletion of intronic MIR repeats reduces circRMST expression to ~30% and impairs tumor cell viability in vitro and xenograft growth in vivo.

circRMST knockdown shortens NKX2.1 protein half‑life from 17 h to ~5 h via loss of Hsp70‑binding site protection, leading to loss of ASL1 expression and blockade of neuroendocrine transdifferentiation.
circRMST is detectable in patient plasma with a >1,000‑fold higher circular/linear ratio than in tumor tissue, suggesting a liquid‑biopsy biomarker.
Circular RNA translation can generate novel peptides; immunopeptidomics identified 80 circRNA‑derived peptides, including 12 from reverse‑strand translation, providing new vaccine antigens.
open_questions: Does the circular‑to‑linear RNA ratio vary systematically across disease states and could it serve as a quantitative biomarker?
Can circular RNAs replicate or be amplified in cells, analogous to viroid mechanisms?
What are the functional consequences of the 700+ circRMST‑interacting RNAs identified in the interactome?

key_findings: Multiplex CRISPR editing of donor T cells to delete CD7 and TCRα enables universal CAR‑T cells that achieved an 82% complete remission rate in the first‑in‑human UCART7 Phase I trial for relapsed T‑ALL.

Deletion of CD2 in CAR‑T cells caused severe functional exhaustion in vitro and loss of antitumor activity in vivo, which was rescued by epitope‑masking of CD2 or by inserting the CD2 cytoplasmic domain into the CAR construct.

Long‑acting IL‑7 (NTi‑7) given between days 1‑7 after CAR‑T infusion expands CAR‑T cells 10,000‑ to 100,000‑fold and cures murine models of T‑cell lymphoma, B‑cell lymphoma, and AML, whereas later dosing is ineffective.

A high‑throughput screen of 700 kinase inhibitors identified PI3γδ inhibitor (Devolasib) and JAK1/2 inhibitor (Ruxolitinib) as synergistic suppressors of IL‑6 production without impairing CAR‑T cytotoxicity; combined prophylaxis eliminated grade ≥2 CRS in a randomized patient cohort.

CD4⁺ CAR‑T cells are the primary source of IL‑6 via membrane‑bound CD40L, while CD8⁺ cells mediate killing; CD40L knockout or blockade markedly reduces CRS, highlighting a mechanistic link between CD40L signaling and cytokine release.
open_questions: How can the profound immunodeficiency caused by CD7/CD2 depletion be mitigated while preserving antitumor activity?
What are the molecular mechanisms underlying CD7 downregulation in relapsed patients (e.g., splice variants vs. genomic loss)?
Can the optimal timing and dosing of IL‑7 be refined for different CAR‑T products and disease settings?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Relapse after UCART7 is frequently associated with loss of CD7 surface expression through biallelic deletion or splicing alterations.
CD2‑CAR‑T cells lose efficacy when CD2 is knocked out because CD2 provides essential costimulatory signaling; epitope‑masked CD2 restores function.
Targeting CD7 and CD2 depletes normal NK and T cells, leading to profound immunodeficiency and infection risk.

key_findings: Developed ~200 high‑quality chemical probes, including 50–70 epigenetic modulators, all freely available to the community.
Identified OICR-9429 as a potent, selective WDR5‑MLL interaction inhibitor that suppresses growth of MLL‑rearranged leukemia and p53‑gain‑of‑function breast cancer cells.
Discovered a PROTAC that recruits FBXO22 to degrade NSD2, eliminating H3K36me2 and selectively killing NSD2‑mutant ALL and multiple myeloma cells after 18–21 days.
NSD2 degradation restored dexamethasone sensitivity in mutant ALL cell lines, suggesting a combinatorial therapeutic strategy.
Machine‑learning‑guided DNA‑encoded library screens across 18 WDR proteins yielded low‑micromolar, ligand‑efficient hits for ~1/3 of the targets, expanding the druggable proteome.
Unsupervised clustering of ATAC‑seq data from 71 mCRPC samples defined four subgroups based on repetitive element chromatin variants (LINE1+, SETL, SINE1+, constant).
LINE1+ subgroup showed intrinsic resistance to androgen‑receptor selective inhibitors, with markedly shorter survival.
AR locus amplification (up to >150 copies) and ecDNA positivity were enriched in LINE1+ tumors.
Repetitive element‑derived accessible sites in LINE1+ tumors physically interact with the AR promoter (Hi‑C), recruiting AR, FOXA1, and OCTB13.
Chromatin variant classification did not align with gene‑expression‑based subtypes, highlighting orthogonal heterogeneity.
open_questions: Do repeat‑derived chromatin variants directly generate ecDNA, or are they a consequence of ecDNA formation?
What upstream mechanisms (e.g., p53 loss, metabolic stress) drive the emergence of LINE1+ chromatin variant profiles?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: LINE1+ tumors are intrinsically resistant to AR‑selective inhibitors due to extreme AR overexpression driven by repeat‑derived enhancers.

key_findings: 80% of dedifferentiated endometrial cancer (DDEC) cases show loss of SMARCA4 and/or ARID1B, components of the SWI/SNF complex.

CRISPR‑mediated SMARCA4 knockout in endometrial cancer cells reduces in‑vitro tumorigenicity but, after serial in‑vivo passaging, restores growth and yields mixed well‑ and poorly‑differentiated histology.
SMARCA4‑deficient tumors display global DNA hypomethylation and distinct chromatin accessibility patterns compared with wild‑type.
Single‑cell multi‑omics reveal that SMARCA4 loss increases cell‑state plasticity, generating an uncommitted transcriptional state without a stem‑cell or embryonic signature.
Patient DDEC samples retain heterogeneous E‑cadherin expression, supporting a model of cell‑state disorder rather than true dedifferentiation.
open_questions: What upstream signals (e.g., hypoxia, metabolic stress) trigger SMARCA4 loss‑induced chromatin variants?
Can epigenetic drugs restore chromatin stability and re‑sensitize SMARCA4‑deficient DDEC to chemotherapy?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: SMARCA4‑deficient tumors are resistant to carboplatin chemotherapy in vivo.

key_findings: LKB1 loss in KRAS‑mutant mouse models induces spontaneous adenocarcinoma‑to‑squamous transition (AST) that is enriched after targeted therapy.
High squamous transcriptional signature predicts shorter treatment duration in LKB1‑mutant lung cancer patients.
KLK6A expression serves as a predictive biomarker for poor response to aggressive therapy in LKB1‑deficient tumors.
ROS accumulation activates NF‑κB; NF‑κB inhibition accelerates p63⁺ squamous differentiation, while ROS scavenging (NAC) reduces RELA activation.
p63⁺ squamous cells secrete IL‑1α, reprogramming CAFs to IL‑1β‑producing leukocyte‑like CAFs that trigger neutrophil NET formation, promoting squamous tumor growth.
Combined KRAS‑G12C inhibitor (IMC‑6236) with IL‑1 receptor antagonist or NET inhibitor (GSK‑484) markedly reduces squamous tumor burden and improves overall tumor control.
open_questions: What determines the threshold of ROS/NF‑κB activation that switches from protective to pro‑AST signaling?
Can early detection of the double‑positive p63⁺/RELA⁺ state predict imminent squamous transition in patients?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: AST confers resistance to KRAS‑G12C inhibition; NF‑κB activation maintains adenocarcinoma lineage but its inhibition promotes squamous transition.

key_findings: Batf3‑/- mice lacking DC1s show tumor and viral responses as weak as Rag‑deficient mice, demonstrating DC1 necessity for classic cross‑presentation.
Targeted deletion of three IRF8 enhancers abolishes DC1 development, providing a refined genetic tool superior to Batf3 knockout.
WDFY4 is uniquely expressed in DC1s; Wdfy4‑/- mice fail to cross‑present cell‑associated antigens and cannot reject fibrosarcoma, confirming its essential role in vesicular cross‑presentation.
Rab43 co‑localizes with WDFY4 in DC1s and traffics with phagocytosed Listeria, supporting a vesicular, non‑cytosolic cross‑presentation pathway.
mRNA‑LNP vaccination induces CD8 tetramer responses that persist after DC1 or WDFY4 loss, indicating DC1‑independent priming.
Complete depletion of conventional DCs (CD11c‑DTR) abolishes the mRNA‑vaccine response, proving DC dependence but not subset specificity.
Class I MHC loss on DCs (CD11c‑Cre β2M flox) eliminates tumor‑induced cross‑presentation but only partially reduces mRNA‑vaccine responses, implicating cross‑dressing as a major mechanism.
Single‑cell RNA‑seq of tetramer+ CD8 T cells shows that DC1 priming yields fewer but more proliferative effectors, whereas DC2 priming yields broader effector populations.
open_questions: What cell types provide the peptide‑MHC complexes that cross‑dress DCs after mRNA vaccination?
Does DC2‑primed CD8 T‑cell memory differ qualitatively from DC1‑primed memory in durability or tumor control?
How do route, dose, and lipid composition of mRNA‑LNPs influence the balance between direct DC transfection and cross‑dressing?
Could cross‑dressing contribute to autoimmunity (e.g., myocarditis) by presenting self‑peptides?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: DC1‑specific cross‑presentation (WDFY4‑dependent) is not required for mRNA vaccine efficacy, suggesting potential resistance mechanisms if this pathway is impaired.
High doses of class II peptide can divert DC2s to present CD4 epitopes, suppressing tumor rejection, highlighting a dose‑dependent selectivity issue.

key_findings: CRISPR screens of SMARCB1‑deficient rhabdoid tumor lines identified DCAF5 as a highly selective dependency (Q‑value ~10⁻²²).
Mass‑spec revealed that DCAF5 knockdown increases abundance of nine SWI/SNF subunits, confirming DCAF5‑mediated degradation.
DiGly tagging showed direct ubiquitination of multiple SWI/SNF subunits by DCAF5.
DCAF5 loss restores 30‑70% of wild‑type enhancer‑driven transcription in SMARCB1‑null cells, reactivating developmental gene programs.
In vivo degradation of DCAF5 eradicated established SMARCB1‑deficient tumors; no regrowth observed after 100 days.
Germline DCAF5 knockout mice are viable with only mild growth phenotype, indicating a therapeutic window.
Initial small‑molecule binders of DCAF5 have been identified in collaboration with Gray and Fisher labs, enabling a drug‑discovery program.
open_questions: Can DCAF5 inhibition be combined with existing epigenetic therapies (e.g., EZH2 inhibitors) for synergistic tumor control?
What biomarkers predict sensitivity to DCAF5 targeting beyond SMARCB1 loss?
Will chronic DCAF5 inhibition affect normal tissue homeostasis given its mild phenotype in mice?
readouts: ChIP‑seq for SWI/SNF and histone marks
in vivo tumor growth assays with degrader
tumor_types: small cell carcinoma of the ovary

key_findings: BRCA1‑heterozygous mice develop basal‑like mammary tumors ~20 weeks earlier than WT mice after Cre‑mediated BRCA1 loss.
ATAC‑seq of normal alveolar cells shows a distinct subcluster with intermediate chromatin openness that aligns with tumor profiles.
AP1 (c‑Jun, JunD, FOSL2) motifs are enriched in these open regions; c‑Jun protein is up‑regulated in early lesions.
Dominant‑negative Jun expression delays tumor formation only in heterozygous mice, indicating AP1 dependency.
WNT10A locus exhibits increased accessibility and expression; WNT10A knockdown impairs organoid growth and in‑vivo tumorigenicity.
WNT10A overexpression accelerates tumor onset and raises tumor grade in mouse cohorts.
RUNX/CBFB transcription factors are up‑regulated in pre‑malignant and tumor cells; CBFB and RUNX2 knockdown reduces proliferation of derived cancer cell lines.
open_questions: What upstream stress signals trigger AP1 activation in BRCA1‑heterozygous alveolar cells?
Can pharmacologic AP1 or WNT10A inhibition prevent tumor onset in high‑risk BRCA1 carriers?
How do physiological stressors (pregnancy, obesity, aging) interact with chromatin priming to modulate risk?
What is the contribution of stromal/immune compartments to the early chromatin changes observed?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: AP1 inhibition selectively delays tumorigenesis in BRCA1‑heterozygous background but not in WT, suggesting a context‑specific dependency.

key_findings: PanIN lesions display DNA methylation patterns intermediate between acinar and ductal cells, indicating an epigenetically plastic transition zone.
UHRF1 knockdown abolishes soft‑agar growth of ALL cells, linking it to epigenetic entropy in leukemia.
CRISPR screen of metastatic PDAC PDX identified KLF5 as the top gene whose loss impairs metastatic growth but not primary tumor growth.
KLF5 knockdown restores heterochromatin (H3K9me2/3) in metastatic cells and reduces migration in Boyden assays.
KLF5 regulates NCAPD2 and MTHFD1; their knockdown also restores heterochromatin, placing them downstream of KLF5.
High KLF5 expression in human metastatic PDAC correlates with poor survival in TCGA data.
open_questions: What microenvironmental stress signals trigger KLF5 up‑regulation in primary tumors?
Can circulating nucleosome signatures reflect the epigenetic entropy state of emerging metastases?
Will pharmacologic KLF5 inhibitors be effective in adjuvant settings for PDAC?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: KLF5 inhibition selectively impairs metastatic but not primary tumor growth in PDX models, suggesting a metastasis‑specific vulnerability.

cited_papers: Pena‑Ruiz and Fernandez‑Epico 2024 Molecular Cancer editorial

key_findings: Discovery of cell‑free fetal DNA in maternal plasma enabled non‑invasive prenatal testing with >99% accuracy using digital PCR of chromosome‑specific targets.
A genome‑wide NIPT based on low‑coverage sequencing accurately detected trisomy 21 in 28 pregnancies (100% sensitivity and specificity).

Plasma EBV DNA serves as a highly specific biomarker for nasopharyngeal carcinoma, detecting 34 cancers in a 20,000‑person Hong Kong screen and shifting 70% of cases to stage I‑II with a 10‑fold mortality reduction (3% vs 40%).
Fragmentomics signatures (shorter fragment size, distinct end‑motif patterns) differentiate cancer‑derived cfDNA from normal cfDNA and improve detection AUC to 0.92 for liver cancer.
Integration of fragment size, end‑motif, and methylation data enables tissue‑of‑origin inference, forming the basis of multi‑cancer early detection platforms such as GRAIL’s Galleri test.
open_questions: How does diurnal or physiological variation (exercise, dialysis, menstrual cycle) affect cfDNA concentration and fragmentomics readouts in longitudinal monitoring?
Can histone modification signatures on cfDNA be systematically leveraged to improve tissue‑origin classification?
What are the limits of viral‑derived cfDNA fragmentomics for distinguishing infection‑related cancers versus benign viral carriage?

patent_or_ip_hints: patents on cfDNA fragmentomics and size‑based quantification
licensing agreements between CUHK and Sequenom, later GRAIL

key_findings: The Troplex assay quantifies HER2 and Trop‑2 in absolute units with inter‑ and intra‑assay CV <10% using cell‑line standards.
In a retrospective Yale cohort (n=316), quantitative HER2 levels distinguished patients likely to benefit from trastuzumab‑deruxtecan, with a hazard ratio of 0.70 per 50‑unit increase (p<0.05).
High Trop‑2 expression was associated with significantly shorter overall survival on T‑DXd (median OS 6.2 mo vs 13.9 mo for low Trop‑2, p<0.01).
Combined HER2‑high/Trop‑2‑low tumors showed the best outcomes on HER2‑directed ADCs, suggesting a selective biomarker strategy for drug choice.
The assay received New York State Department of Health (NYSDOH) CLIA approval, enabling clinical deployment.
open_questions: What is the optimal quantitative cutoff for HER2 or Trop‑2 to guide ADC selection?
How do intrinsic molecular subtypes (e.g., PAM50) influence the quantitative protein thresholds?
What is the contribution of the tumor microenvironment and adaptive immunity to ADC durability beyond target density?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: High Trop‑2 expression appears to blunt response to HER2‑directed ADCs, indicating a potential resistance mechanism or competitive target effect.
Patients with both high HER2 and high Trop‑2 had poorer outcomes than HER2‑high/Trop‑2‑low, supporting the need for a selective biomarker rather than a single target assessment.

cited_papers: JCO Precision Oncology 2024 Rim et al.

key_findings: Never smokers comprised ~30% of advanced lung cancer cases in the Japanese national database.
EGFR mutations are the most frequent driver in never-smoker lung adenocarcinoma, while KRAS dominates in smokers.
Passive smoking increases tumor mutational burden via APOBEC signatures but does not affect EGFR mutation frequency.
Air pollution (PM2.5) correlates with higher EGFR-positive lung cancer incidence without directly causing EGFR mutations.
Germline polymorphisms (e.g., TERT, HLA class II) confer greater risk in never smokers, especially for EGFR-positive disease.
open_questions: What are the functional mechanisms by which identified germline variants (TERT, HLA) promote EGFR-driven tumorigenesis?
How does passive smoking interact with APOBEC activity to influence tumor evolution?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: EGFR-positive tumors in smokers often lack SBS4 smoking signature, indicating a smoking-independent development pathway.

key_findings: Young‑onset lung cancer (≤45 y) is enriched for targetable fusions (ALK, ROS1) and EGFR mutations.
Rare pathogenic germline variants in TP53, SMAD6, and IREB2 are significantly enriched in young‑onset or fusion‑driven tumors.
Polygenic risk scores derived from smoking‑associated GWAS still confer modest risk (OR ≈ 1.3 per SD) in never‑smoker cohorts.
Large (>1 Mb) rare deletions are over‑represented in young‑onset, fusion‑positive cases.
A BRCA2 germline pathogenic variant with tumor LOH predicted exceptional response to platinum chemotherapy followed by PARP inhibition.
open_questions: How do germline variants interact with environmental exposures (e.g., air pollution) to shape somatic driver selection?
Can polygenic risk scores be refined to improve predictive power specifically for never‑smoker lung cancer?

key_findings: EGFR TKI hazard ratio 0.7 in never smokers versus smokers, confirming greater efficacy.
Addition of anti‑angiogenic agents to EGFR TKI improves outcomes more in smokers than never smokers.
Never smokers have significantly lower TMB and PD‑L1 scores, resulting in poor ICI monotherapy response (ORR ~10%).
PBAP loss‑of‑function mutations (~10% of never smokers) predict durable ICI responses (5‑year remission).
High DDR1 expression associates with hyperprogression on ICI in never smokers.
open_questions: What molecular mechanisms underlie the differential benefit of anti‑angiogenic agents in smokers versus never smokers?
Can DDR1 inhibition restore ICI sensitivity in high‑DDR1 never‑smoker tumors?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: High DDR1 expression linked to impaired T‑cell infiltration and hyperprogression on ICI.
Low APOBEC signature in never smokers correlates with reduced ICI benefit.

key_findings: Three genomic subtypes (piano, mezzo‑forte, forte) correlate with copy‑number burden and driver mutations.
Endogenous signatures (SBS1, SBS5, APOBEC) dominate; exogenous SBS4 and Signature 22A (aristolochic acid) appear in specific regions.
High outdoor PM2.5 exposure associates with increased SBS5 and reduced telomere length.
KRAS‑mutant tumors have shorter latency (≈5 y) and earlier age at diagnosis compared with EGFR‑mutant tumors (≈6 y).
AT1‑origin methylation signature distinguishes low‑grade, indolent tumors and aligns with the steady transcriptomic group.
open_questions: How does the AT1‑cell epigenetic constraint influence response to targeted therapies?
Can the methylation‑based cell‑of‑origin classifier be applied prospectively for early detection?

key_findings: All 49 MMR‑deficient rectal cancer patients achieved a clinical complete response after 6 months of pembrolizumab, enabling non‑operative management (100% cCR).
Two‑year recurrence‑free survival was 96/49 (≈96%) in the rectal cohort and 85% in the 54‑patient non‑rectal cohort treated with pembrolizumab.

In a ctDNA‑guided MRD trial, 25 ctDNA‑positive patients who received pembrolizumab had recurrence‑free outcomes comparable to 125 ctDNA‑negative patients observed, whereas untreated ctDNA‑positive patients progressed rapidly.
Adverse events of any grade occurred in only 35% of non‑rectal patients, indicating a favorable safety profile for organ‑preserving immunotherapy.
Retrospective analysis of 837 Lynch syndrome carriers showed >80% reduction in secondary cancer incidence among those who had received PD‑1 blockade versus untreated controls.
open_questions: Is a phase III randomized trial required to establish neoadjuvant PD‑1 blockade as standard of care for organ‑preserving treatment of MMR‑deficient rectal cancer?
What are the mechanistic determinants of the observed tissue‑specific variability in response (e.g., prostate vs. bladder)?
Can earlier or longer duration of PD‑1 blockade further improve cure rates in non‑rectal MMR‑deficient cancers?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Lower complete response rates observed in prostate, gastric, and esophageal MMR‑deficient tumors suggest tissue‑specific immune tolerance or microenvironmental barriers.
Barrier tissues (lung, skin, GI mucosa) showed higher responsiveness than non‑barrier sites, indicating possible role of local microbiome or stromal factors.

company_or_sponsor: Philanthropic donor groups (e.g., Chesapeake Bay swimmers fund)

key_findings: Lung cancer incidence in women under age 50 now exceeds that of men, a reversal not explained by smoking prevalence alone.

Birth-cohort analysis shows a fourfold increase in rectal cancer risk and twofold increase in colon cancer risk for cohorts born after 1950, prompting USPSTF to lower colorectal screening start age to 45.
Geographic clusters with 40% higher colorectal cancer mortality identified in the Lower Mississippi Corridor, leading to targeted screening initiatives and legislative action.
Medicaid expansion under the ACA reduced uninsured rates more than private-market subsidies and improved five-year overall survival in high-poverty rural areas.
Dependent coverage expansion increased early-stage diagnosis and fertility-sparing treatment rates for cervical cancer in women aged 21‑25.
open_questions: How can cancer registry data be integrated with genomic and treatment data to better understand rural disparities?
What methods can reduce the lag time in treatment data reporting to inform real-time policy decisions?

key_findings: Integrin αVβ5‑positive EVs from lung‑tropic breast cancer cells home to the lung and establish pre‑metastatic niches, whereas αVβ3‑positive EVs target the brain.
β2‑integrin‑bearing EVs derived from melanoma or pancreatic cancer induce rapid lung clot formation in naive mice; anti‑β2‑integrin antibody reduces fibrin deposition and improves platelet counts.
Exomeres, the smallest EV fraction, preferentially accumulate in the liver, reprogram Kupffer cells to a TNF‑α‑high, fatty‑acid‑low state, and generate fatty‑liver disease in mice.
Pharmacologic blockade of β2‑integrin or TNF‑α prevents EV‑driven thrombosis and fatty‑liver pathology and modestly delays metastatic tumor growth.

Activated T‑cell EVs package granzyme B, enter tumor cell nuclei, up‑regulate antigen‑presentation pathways, and when combined with anti‑PD‑1 produce durable tumor regressions in pancreatic cancer mouse models (median survival extended 30–40 days).
Circulating β2‑integrin‑positive EV levels prospectively predict clot events in pancreatic cancer patients, outperforming standard coagulation tests.
open_questions: How long do tumor‑derived EVs persist in circulation after definitive primary‑tumor resection?
What are the precise molecular mechanisms by which granzyme B‑loaded T‑cell EVs access the tumor cell nucleus?
Do CAF‑derived EVs differ functionally from tumor‑cell EVs in organotropism and metabolic reprogramming?
Can chronic exercise‑induced “healthy” EVs competitively displace tumor EVs in patients, and what biomarkers best capture this shift?

key_findings: EWS‑FLI1 dosage is a Goldilocks dependency: both over‑expression and complete repression are deleterious to Ewing sarcoma cells.
TRIM8 is a selective Ewing sarcoma dependency; its knockout increases EWS‑FLI1 levels and is lethal in vitro and in vivo.
ETV6 competes with EWS‑FLI1 on chromatin; CRISPR or dTAG‑mediated loss of ETV6 leads to excess EWS‑FLI1 activity and cell death.
STAG2 loss predicts metastatic disease and poor prognosis in Ewing sarcoma, validated in isogenic knockout models.
Chemical PRISM screening identified compound R112 as uniquely active in Ewing sarcoma; activity is rescued by UGT3A2 knockout, implicating UDP‑glucose metabolism as a novel vulnerability.
A genomics‑guided case of a pediatric B‑ALL patient with RCST1‑ABL2 fusion achieved durable complete remission when imatinib was added to standard therapy.
Development of high‑throughput GFP‑mCherry reporter assays enabled screening of >100,000 molecules, yielding several candidates that induce proteasome‑dependent degradation of the EWS‑FLI1 fusion.
open_questions: What are the precise molecular mechanisms by which UGT3A2 mediates sensitivity to R112 in Ewing sarcoma?
Can bifunctional degraders be developed that directly engage EWS‑FLI1 without requiring a high‑affinity ligand?
How can the Goldilocks dosage requirement be translated into a therapeutic index that avoids toxicity in normal tissues?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Goldilocks phenomenon indicates that precise modulation of fusion protein levels is required; both hyper‑activation and complete loss are cytotoxic, complicating therapeutic windows.
STAG2 loss creates a selective vulnerability but also promotes metastatic behavior, suggesting potential resistance via lineage plasticity.

key_findings: Identified PRMT5 as a synthetic lethal dependency in MTAP‑deleted cancers, validated by three concurrent manuscripts and ongoing clinical trials of PRMT5 inhibitors.
Discovered WRN helicase dependency in microsatellite instability (MSI) cancers using both CRISPR and shRNA data, leading to multiple manuscripts and clinical development of WRN inhibitors.
Found that loss of the 9p21 region creates dependency on the SKI complex (PELO/HBS1L), with MSI also driving PELO dependency, revealing a novel synthetic lethal axis.
open_questions: How can the map be expanded to capture resistance mechanisms and combination dependencies beyond single‑gene knockouts?
What are the optimal high‑dimensional phenotypes to predict therapeutic efficacy beyond cell viability?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: CRISPR screens exhibit copy‑number–related off‑target toxicity, addressed by the Chronos model to improve selectivity of gene effect scores.

cited_papers: Three concurrent PRMT5 synthetic lethal manuscripts (2024)
Three concurrent WRN synthetic lethal manuscripts (2024)
Two concurrent SKI complex dependency manuscripts (2024)

key_findings: Generated a library of >27,000 paralog pairs and screened ~300 models, revealing context‑specific dependencies such as AKT1 alone versus AKT1+AKT2 co‑knockout.
Integrated 150 organoid and neurosphere models into DepMap, showing lineage‑specific dependencies (e.g., ITGAV vs ITGV1) that differ from 2D cell lines.
Developed the Prism bar‑coded pooled drug sensitivity assay covering 900 cell lines and 265 compounds, enabling rapid assessment of compound selectivity and synthetic lethal interactions.
open_questions: How can high‑dimensional phenotypic readouts be scaled to systematically map resistance mechanisms?
What is the optimal strategy to model metabolic and microenvironmental contexts (e.g., serum vs defined media) in DepMap?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Paralog screens reveal that single‑gene knockouts may miss dependencies masked by redundancy, emphasizing the need for combinatorial targeting.

company_or_sponsor: Stand Up to Cancer (funding for surface proteomics)

key_findings: Developed a novel algorithm to detect recurrent non‑coding regulatory mutations, exemplified by functional validation of a breast cancer XPP1‑proximal region.
Demonstrated germline BRCA2 enrichment in advanced prostate cancer and extended germline risk analysis to CHEK2, DNA‑repair genes, and structural variants in pediatric solid tumors.
Identified loss‑of‑function mutations in PBRM1 as a predictive biomarker for response to nivolumab in renal cell carcinoma, with replication in the Checkpoint 025 trial (nivolumab arm only).

Created an interpretable deep‑learning pathology pipeline that quantifies tumor grade heterogeneity and immune cell features, improving response prediction over single‑gene biomarkers in the same renal cell carcinoma cohort.

Built the “Peanut” biologically‑engineered neural network to classify primary versus lethal prostate cancer, uncovering a novel association with MDM4 amplification that is being pursued for therapeutic targeting.
open_questions: How can germline structural variants be systematically incorporated into clinical decision‑making pipelines?
What are the optimal methods to ensure interpretability and trustworthiness of agentic AI models in oncology?
How should heterogeneous data quality be weighted when training large‑scale foundation models for precision medicine?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: PBRM1 association with ICB response was strong in early cohorts but attenuated in later studies, suggesting context‑dependent resistance mechanisms linked to prior VEGF‑TKI exposure.
MDM4 amplification emerged as a novel driver of lethal prostate cancer, indicating a potential resistance pathway to standard androgen‑targeted therapies.

key_findings: Developed a patent for an antibody targeting Substance P to inhibit the transactivation of EGFR and HER2.

patent_or_ip_hints: patent application for antibody against substance P

key_findings: Identified elongation factor two as a differentially phosphorylated protein in glioblastoma compared to normal white matter.
Licensed a pharmacophore for P-glycoprotein to Vertex, resulting in the compound VX-701.
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Spent 10 years at J&J on elongation factor two but never made a drug selective enough to go forward.

cited_papers: Heit et al. TIBS (Academic Entrepreneurship: Promise and Perils)

key_findings: Guinea pigs are better models for oxidative stress than rats because they do not produce ascorbate like humans.
Pelotonia raised $350 million for cancer research with 100% of funds going to research.
Initial $100,000 funding for ibrutinib in a CLL mouse model contributed to the development of a multi-billion dollar drug that changed the standard of care for CLL.
Co‑founding Foundation Medicine leveraged massively parallel sequencing to create a whole‑panel diagnostic that became a Roche asset.
Discovery of MTAP deletion–PRMT5 synthetic lethality led to Tango Therapeutics, now developing PRMT5 inhibitors in the clinic.
Early career networking (e.g., with Eric Lander) was critical to secure venture capital and industry introductions.
Transitioning from academia to industry required understanding institutional motivations and building cross‑functional teams.
Initial pitch to VCs failed due to lack of clear funding ask; revised pitch led to first round of capital from two venture groups.
Two clinical validation trials published in NEJM 2015 demonstrated diagnostic performance, facilitating acquisition by Veracyte.
Institutional Ignition Fund ($50k) provided critical deck development support and mentorship.
Angel funding from high‑net‑worth individuals helped bridge the gap between seed and Series A.
Rutgers Cancer Institute’s GMP facility enabled rapid IND filing for an HPV‑directed cell therapy.
Early clinical data showed 58% ORR and durable complete responses in HPV‑positive patients.
Pre‑IND meetings can de‑risk programs, but a well‑prepared IND can also prompt rapid FDA feedback.
Academic teams can leverage FDA staff with academic backgrounds for more collaborative interactions.
Incorporated TerraNovir in the US in 2025 to access American capital markets.
Identified a gap in understanding metastatic versus primary tumor biology as a strategic focus.
Described challenges when VCs assign junior analysts unfamiliar with the target, underscoring the need for clear scientific communication.
Alloy’s venture studio seeds projects with both capital and operational support (e.g., CRO services).
Studio model enables academic founders to focus on science while leveraging in‑house expertise for regulatory and business development.
Alternative structures such as Deerfield’s academic partnerships, CurioBio’s pre‑money evaluation, and roll‑up funds are expanding the ecosystem.
First tobacco cessation trial aimed for 6,000 enrollees but enrolled 12,000 patients (100% reach of eligible tobacco users).
COVID rapid‑cycle messaging trial enrolled 107,000 of 160,000 eligible patients (67% reach) using 37 message workflows across 227 cohorts.
Second COVID at‑home test trial enrolled 33,000 participants after pandemic peak.
CDC‑funded colorectal cancer screening program increased screening rates from 36% to 43%, a relative 20% increase and accounted for ~50% of national CHC screening gains.
Cares For You was implemented in four middle schools, reaching 288 students; 95% reported learning new science content during STEM Day.
Bridge to Quit increased patient‑portal enrollment from a baseline of 34‑44% to 61% after 18 months, surpassing the 50% target.
CDC‑funded colorectal cancer screening program raised screening rates from 36% to 43%, representing an almost 20% relative increase.
High satisfaction with educational components: 90% found speakers interesting, 85% learned about new jobs.
The guaranteed income pilot randomized 3,000 participants (2,200 pregnant women, 800 foster youth) to differing cash amounts.
A 75% survey response rate was achieved across baseline, 3‑month, 9‑month, exit, and 6‑month post‑exit assessments.
Planned analyses will examine changes in diet, exercise, sleep quality, and stress using the Hope Index.
EITC focus groups are being used to explore how tax credits influence colorectal cancer screening behaviors.
open_questions: How will increased cash flow translate into measurable reductions in colorectal cancer incidence over longer follow‑up?
What are the mechanisms linking EITC receipt to changes in screening uptake?

key_findings: Version 2 STAR T cells achieved ORR 33.3% and DCR 66.7% in three heavily pretreated AFP-positive gastric cancer patients.
CXCR2-armored STAR T cells improved tumor trafficking in preclinical models.
Membrane-bound IL-15 (Version 3) increased ORR to 15% and DCR to 75% in four patients with advanced HCC or gastric cancer.
Grade ≥3 CRS occurred in 42.9% of patients; no treatment‑related deaths were observed.
open_questions: What mechanisms underlie the limited long‑term persistence despite IL‑15 armoring?
Can further engineering improve safety while maintaining efficacy?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Limited persistence of STAR T cells observed; responders showed sustained expansion while non‑responders had rapid decline in copy number.

key_findings: Three of four acral melanoma patients achieved disease control (75% DCR).
Responder showed >90% T cells in peripheral blood at week 12 versus low levels in stable disease patient.
Effective response linked to higher fractions of TFH and intermediate exhausted CD8 T cells, not total T cell count.
Clonal analysis revealed expanded progenitor‑like TCR clones persisting in blood up to 12 weeks post‑infusion.
open_questions: Can TFH and intermediate exhausted signatures be used prospectively to select patients?
What is the optimal dosing schedule for sustained clonal persistence?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Non‑responders harbored predominantly terminal exhausted CD8 T cells lacking tumor reactivity.

key_findings: TLR4‑signaling CAR‑DC1s induced strong costimulatory molecule upregulation (CCR7, CD86, CD70).
In vitro, CAR‑DC1s cross‑presented OVA and endogenous tumor peptides at markedly higher abundance than control DCs.
In the heterogeneous sarcoma model, 30/30 mice achieved complete tumor rejection after CAR‑DC1 treatment.
Mice cured by CAR‑DC1s rejected rechallenge with both B7‑H3‑positive and B7‑H3‑negative tumors, indicating epitope spreading.
open_questions: Will CAR‑DC1s be effective against low‑B7‑H3 expressing tumors?
What is the optimal dosing route (IT vs IV) for different solid tumor types?

key_findings: GPC2 identified as top oncofetal surface antigen in medulloblastoma via surfaceome analysis.
CAR T cells required CD28 transmembrane domain to detect ~5,000‑6,000 GPC2 molecules/cell.
c‑Jun overexpression reduced antigen‑low escape and enhanced cytokine production.
Phase 1 trial (NCT‑pending) enrolled 4 patients with no dose‑limiting toxicities and detectable CAR T cells in CSF.
open_questions: Will GPC2 CAR T cells be effective against heterogeneous CNS tumors with variable GPC2 expression?
What is the optimal intra‑cerebral dosing schedule?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Tumor escape observed with reduced GPC2 density; c‑Jun engineering mitigated this.

key_findings: TCR‑NK cells killed target tumor spheroids faster than conventional TCR‑T cells (≈2 min vs ≈6 min per target).
In vivo, NK TCR treatment cured 5/5 myeloma‑bearing mice with durable engraftment in blood, bone marrow, and spleen.
No off‑target toxicity observed in peptide‑pulsed LCL assays or in treated patients (no CRS, ICANS, or GvHD).
First patient with NY‑ESO‑1‑positive myeloma achieved complete remission lasting >2 years after a single 22 M dose.
open_questions: Will NK TCR cells retain activity against MHC‑downregulated tumors?
Can additional cytokine support further improve persistence?

key_findings: Synthetic chimeras (e.g., FAS‑OX40) and stemness factors (TCF7L1) consistently enriched across multiple screens.
Lymphoma‑specific hits (ARID family genes) emerged only in Toledo co‑culture screens.
In vivo screen identified similar top hits, with ~71% concordance between in vitro, in vivo, and deep‑learning model predictions.
open_questions: Which of the identified gene edits translate to improved clinical response in patients?
Can CACTEX2 be refined to a minimal set for rapid clinical testing?

key_findings: One patient showed dramatic tumor reduction in 16 days with peak CAR T expansion of 14.7 B cells.
Clonal analysis revealed a dominant TCR clone not present in the infusion product.
Retroviral integrations disrupted CBLB, CCDC6, and ASB2, correlating with the expanded clone.
Triple knockout of these genes in IL‑15 CAR T cells led to greater T cell expansion and complete tumor control in HCC xenograft mice.
open_questions: Is disruption of all three genes required for maximal benefit?
Does IL‑15 synergize with the knockouts or act independently?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Potential autoimmunity risk from CBLB loss; however, monoallelic disruption appeared safe in patient.

patent_or_ip_hints: patent related to triple knockout strategy

key_findings: Y6 synBody targeting CD38, BCMA, and GPRC5D showed in vitro potency approximately 80-fold stronger than BCMA-targeting belantamab in a high-bar myeloma resistance model.
SynBody demonstrated log-order increases in binding strength, internalization, trafficking to lysosomes, and payload delivery compared to monospecific controls.
SynBody is resistant to the presence of soluble targets, whereas belantamab is highly affected.
In vivo dose-ranging experiments showed 100% tumor growth inhibition (TGI) and 2 complete responses (CRs) at the highest dose tested with no body weight loss.
SynBody achieved equivalent efficacy to belantamab MMAE with 11X lower exposure.
A synBody targeting CD19, CD22, and CD79B showed log-order increases in killing potency compared to polatuzumab in both Ramos and HT NHL models.
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Designed to overcome soluble antigen sinks that typically reduce the efficacy of monospecific ADCs.

key_findings: M7437 showed superior anti-tumor activity compared to 9B12 MMAE in head and neck and ovarian PDX models.
In a panel of PDX models, 17 reached the cutoff for preclinical regression and 8 showed complete regression across TNBC, ovarian, head and neck, NSCLC, pancreatic, and gastric cancer.
M7437 demonstrated superior activity compared to DATO-DXd in squamous and SCLC PDX models expressing both LY6E and Trop-2.
M7437 showed promising efficacy in a gastric cancer PDX model that was primary resistant to Enhertu (T-DXd).
GLP toxicity study in cynomolgus monkeys showed the drug was well tolerated, with primary toxicities being hematological (lymphocytes, neutrophils, reticulocytes).
In vitro PBMC assays showed proliferating NK cells were sensitive, while resting NK, B, and T cells were unaffected.
open_questions: Discriminating how much bone marrow toxicity is due to LY6E expression on immune cells versus the known toxicity of the exatecan payload.
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Bystander effect allows for efficacy in tumors with heterogeneous target expression.

key_findings: Humanized mice expressing human Cadherin 17 showed rapid clearance of the ADC, with levels falling below detection within 48 hours, indicating a significant tissue sink in the gut.
In P-gp positive colorectal cancer models, exatecan-bearing ADCs maintained activity while MMAE-bearing ADCs lost activity.
Pharmacological inhibition of P-gp with ensequiror restored the response of MMAE-bearing ADCs in resistant LS513 cells.
Genetic knockout of P-gp in LS513 cells restored sensitivity to MMAE-bearing ADCs in vitro and in vivo.
Switching to an exatecan payload does not mitigate the target-mediated clearance liability caused by normal tissue expression.
TMC is driven by the antibody's binding to normal tissue and is independent of the ADC construct (free antibody showed same clearance rate).
open_questions: Whether P-gp status can be clinically validated as a biomarker to guide payload choice for Cadherin 17 ADCs.
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: P-gp pumps in colorectal cancer act as a primary resistance mechanism for hydrophobic payloads like MMAE.

key_findings: Nuzepha demonstrated significant efficacy in HNSCC xenografts (Fadu, SCC9, Cal27), with doses of 3 and 5 mg/kg producing near complete regressions in aggressive lines.
The BDC format avoids the bleeding toxicity (coagulopathy) associated with antibody-based EphA2 conjugates.
The small size of the molecule allows for rapid delivery and penetration, making episodic dosing sufficient for efficacy.
The binding affinity for EphA2 is 2 nM.
An MMAF version of the construct was found to be decidedly less potent than the MMAE version.
tumor_types: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC)
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: The short half-life is a design feature to reduce systemic toxicity while maintaining efficacy through rapid tumor penetration.

key_findings: HOX16 antibody binds the non-shed portion of MUC16 with sub-nanomolar affinity and is minimally impacted by exogenous CA125, unlike the DMAC antibody which showed a 22-fold IC50 shift.
HOX16 ADC demonstrated sub-nanomolar internalization efficiency.
Bystander effect was demonstrated by the ability to eliminate 100% of cells in a 3:1 mixture where 33% were antigen-negative (Raji-Luc).
In ovarian CDX models, HOX16 caused tumor regressions at 1 mg/kg, whereas the original DAR-4 MMIE construct (DMAC) was incapable of causing regressions at the same dose.
In vitro plasma stability showed <0.4% payload release over 21 days, which is >10-fold higher stability compared to the DRUG-DXd platform (which showed >4% release).
NHP tox studies showed the ADC was well-tolerated up to 60 mg/kg with no mortalities.
open_questions: What are the lower bounds of MUC16 expression by which efficacy can still be achieved in vivo?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Target-mediated drug disposition (TMDD) is a significant challenge for MUC16 due to high levels of shed CA125 in the bloodstream.

key_findings: Screening of 50 ADCs across 25 targets showed that sensitivity strongly correlates with target antigen expression (gene expression and copy number amplification).
Prism AIR showed strong concordance with actual ADC data for the target F3 (tozotamab), validating the AIR format as a proxy for ADC activity.
Differential analysis between datopotamab deruxtecan and datopotamab AIR (MMAF) identified SLC46A3 as a driver of sensitivity for non-cleavable linkers.
Ceticizumab showed poor correlation with its target antigen in the AIR format, which the speaker attributes to the instability of its specific linker chemistry releasing free payload.
open_questions: How do 3D cell culture results differ from the current 2D Prism screening results for ADCs?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Payload-specific differences can lead to outliers in target correlation, such as the difference between SN-38 and MMAF payloads.

key_findings: STRO-004 achieved an overall ORR of 64% and DCR of 90% across 70 PDX models in a mouse clinical trial.
In head and neck models, STRO-004 showed superior ORR (57% vs 38%) and median PFS (45 vs 27 days) compared to the TF-MMAE benchmark.
In pancreatic models, STRO-004 showed an ORR of 70% compared to 50% for the TF-MMAE benchmark.
STRO-004 was well-tolerated in NHPs up to 50 mg/kg with no significant heme toxicities or bleeding/eye toxicity.
Response is multifactorial; combining Tissue Factor and Schlafen 11 expression levels better captures response heterogeneity than either alone.
open_questions: Does the distribution of Tissue Factor between epithelial and stromal cells impact efficacy?
Do extra-tumoral beta-glucuronidase levels correlate with response?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: The use of para-azido phenylalanine via code expansion ensures a homogeneous DAR8, which the speaker claims leads to higher stability and lower systemic payload release.

key_findings: Screened 54 patients, 19 (35%) were mesothelin-positive and eligible.
Seven patients received intraperitoneal CAR T; no dose‑limiting toxicities observed.
CAR T cells persisted in peripheral blood beyond 100 days.
Best radiographic response was stable disease; no objective responses observed.
Low‑grade CRS was common and manageable; one patient experienced grade 3 IE‑CHS resolved with steroids.
open_questions: Will selecting patients with higher mesothelin expression (>75%) improve responses?
Can combining with systemic checkpoint inhibition overcome heterogeneous antigen loss?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Limited efficacy attributed to heterogeneous mesothelin expression across tumor lesions.
Off‑target, on‑tumor toxicities (pharyngitis) linked to mesothelin expression in tonsillar epithelium.

key_findings: Nine patients received at least one infusion; no dose‑limiting toxicities observed.
ORR 28.6% and DCR 57.1% across evaluable patients, with two partial responses.
Transient CAR expression peaks within 1 hour post‑infusion and declines after 8 hours.
Higher dose levels correlated with increased CAR and Lego expression and with central memory CD8 T‑cell expansion.
Low incidence of high‑grade CRS; cytokine release was modest compared with protein CAR T.
open_questions: Will repeated dosing overcome transient expression without increasing toxicity?
Can combining with checkpoint blockade enhance durability?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Transient mRNA expression may limit durability of response.
Potential anti‑drug antibodies (ADA) suggested as cause for reduced PK on repeat dosing.

key_findings: Twelve patients received KSQ001EX; no dose‑limiting toxicities observed.
ORR 33% with one patient achieving a durable partial response >12 months.
Higher cell doses (>5.25 B) correlated with tumor reduction in 100% of patients.
Engineered TILs expanded and persisted in peripheral blood for up to 500 days.
Tumor biopsies showed increased CD8 cytotoxic T cells and remodeling of the microenvironment.
open_questions: Will dual editing of SOX1 and RAG1 improve efficacy without added toxicity?
What is the optimal cell dose to balance efficacy and manufacturing feasibility?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Efficacy appears dose‑dependent; lower doses may require IL‑2 support.

key_findings: Five‑year OS hazard ratio 0.67 with survival doubling from 8% to 16% at 5 years.
Disease control rate improved to 46% versus 27% with investigator's choice.
Baseline ctDNA undetectable patients had markedly better OS (HR 0.5).
ctDNA clearance at week 9 occurred in 37% of patients and predicted superior survival (HR 0.32).
Treatment beyond radiographic progression yielded additional tumor regressions and prolonged post‑progression survival.
open_questions: Can earlier ctDNA monitoring guide treatment continuation versus stopping at progression?
Will combining tebentafusp with other immunomodulators further improve outcomes?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Radiographic RECIST responses underestimated survival benefit; ctDNA proved more sensitive.
Heterogeneous benefit across disease burden and LDH subgroups, but overall favorable.

key_findings: Intratumoral RZ001 combined with atezolizumab‑bevacizumab yielded ORR 40% (RECIST) and 61.5% (mRECIST).
No dose‑limiting toxicities; grade 3/4 treatment‑related AEs occurred in 53% but were manageable.
Rapid onset of responses with durable disease control observed at data cutoff.
All patients expressed hTERT; viral delivery was well tolerated without systemic replication.
open_questions: Would RZ001 synergize with more potent ICI backbones (e.g., tremelimumab/ durvalumab)?
Can biomarker‑guided selection (e.g., hTERT expression level) refine patient benefit?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Potential resistance via loss of hTERT expression not yet observed.

key_findings: In arm 2 (LOAD‑703 + chemo + atezolizumab), ORR was 38% with three complete responses.
First‑line patients (n=13) achieved median OS 14.7 months and 1‑year survival 62%.
Peripheral CD8 effector memory T cells increased while Tregs decreased after treatment.
Tumor biopsies showed upregulation of Th1 cytokines and down‑regulation of fibroblast/TGF‑β signatures.
open_questions: Will a randomized four‑arm trial clarify the contribution of LOAD‑703 versus chemo alone?
Can earlier‑line use (neoadjuvant) convert unresectable disease to resectable?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Patients with rapid progression exhibited high IL‑6 levels, suggesting a potential resistance pathway.

key_findings: Pembrolizumab achieved a 41% complete response rate in BCG‑unresponsive NMIBC.
Adstiladrin (intravesical adenoviral) yielded a 53% complete response rate for CIS at 3 months.
Anctiva (IL‑15 agonist) demonstrated a 71% complete response rate in BCG‑unresponsive disease.
Enfortumab vedotin combined with pembrolizumab (EV‑pembro) doubled median overall survival to 31.5 months in metastatic bladder cancer.
open_questions: How can molecular subtyping be integrated into routine clinical decision‑making for NMIBC?
What is the cost‑effectiveness threshold for adopting these high‑price bladder‑preserving therapies?

key_findings: Adjuvant nivolumab improves disease‑free survival after cystectomy (CheckMate 274).
In IMvigor11, ctDNA‑positive patients derived a DFS benefit from atezolizumab versus placebo.
MODERN trial uses ctDNA to randomize patients to nivolumab ± LAG‑3 (escalation) or surveillance (de‑escalation).
Peri‑operative EV‑pembro achieved a 57.1% pathologic complete response, markedly higher than cisplatin‑based neoadjuvant therapy.
Clinical complete response after neoadjuvant chemo‑PD‑1 therapy predicts excellent metastasis‑free survival, and undetectable ctDNA/utDNA correlates with true remission.
open_questions: What is the optimal ctDNA threshold and timing for initiating adjuvant immunotherapy?
Can urine tumor DNA replace blood ctDNA for surveillance, or should both be used?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Patients with detectable ctDNA after cystectomy are at high risk of recurrence despite surgery, indicating residual micrometastatic disease.
Urine tumor DNA can detect residual bladder disease even when blood ctDNA is negative, highlighting compartment‑specific resistance.

key_findings: APOBEC3A exposure increased neratinib IC50 4.8‑fold and conferred cross‑resistance to HER2‑ADC (T‑DXd), FGFR3 inhibitors, and enfortumab‑vedotin.
A3A‑exposed cells showed persistent late‑S‑phase stasis, γH2AX and p‑RPA32 elevation, and sustained chromatin accessibility at the SOX2 promoter and distal enhancer.
FOXM1 binds the SOX2 promoter 11‑fold more in A3A‑exposed cells, driving SOX2 transcription.
SOX2‑PROTAC sensitized A3A‑driven resistant cells to trastuzumab‑deruxtecan, confirming SOX2 as a therapeutic vulnerability.
DASP signature (FOXM1, SOX2, S‑phase, EMT genes) predicts poorer progression‑free and overall survival across TCGA pan‑cancer cohorts.
open_questions: Can DASP be detected in patient tumors using the transcriptional signature, and does it predict clinical resistance to ADCs?
Would inhibition of FOXM1 upstream of SOX2 provide an alternative strategy to prevent DASP formation?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: A3A‑induced DASP state confers broad cross‑resistance to multiple ADCs and TKIs, independent of target expression.
The resistance is not recapitulated by generic DNA damage (doxorubicin) or TGF‑β‑induced EMT, indicating specificity to deaminase activity.

patent_or_ip_hints: US2025/0123456 – SOX2 PROTAC for bladder cancer

key_findings: CHD7 expression is minimal in pre‑castration prostate tissue, induced early post‑castration, and sustained in terminal NEPC lesions.
CHD7 knockdown reduces NE marker expression, cell growth, DNA synthesis, and increases DNA damage and apoptosis.
CHD7 directly binds and maintains accessibility at ~1,805 loci, regulating 563 transcriptional targets involved in neural fate and DNA replication.
Loss of CHD7 impairs ATR checkpoint phosphorylation and sensitizes NEPC cells to cisplatin (IC50 markedly reduced).
Combining cisplatin with ATR checkpoint inhibition further decreases viability compared with either agent alone.
open_questions: What upstream signals drive early CHD7 induction in NEPC?
Which transcription factors cooperate with CHD7 at its binding sites?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: CHD7 up‑regulation confers cisplatin tolerance via ATR checkpoint activation.

key_findings: KDM5B and SOX9 are co‑overexpressed in ~46% of NEPC cases and correlate with NSE levels.
KDM5B knockout reduces SOX9, NSE, and SYN expression in NEPC cell lines.
Restoring KDM5B rescues SOX9 and NE markers in a dose‑dependent manner.
Castrated PTEN‑p53 mice develop NE recurrence with high KDM5B, SOX9, NSE, and SYN.
Triple knockout of PTEN‑p53‑KDM5B prevents tumor recurrence and NE marker expression.
open_questions: Does KDM5B directly demethylate the SOX9 promoter or act via co‑factors?
Can pharmacologic inhibition of KDM5B prevent therapy‑induced NEPC in patients?

key_findings: Global CpG methylation does not change acutely after BRAF V600E induction.
CGI promoters gain methylation over months in both control and BRAF lineages, independent of replication.
Non‑CGI sites lose methylation in a replication‑dependent manner, accelerated in BRAF organoids.
Transcription factor enrichment differs: control lineage shows stress/viral TFs; BRAF lineage enriches cancer‑related TFs.
External datasets (replication inhibition, mitomycin C) confirm that promoter hypermethylation is replication‑independent while loss is replication‑linked.
open_questions: What enzymatic pathways mediate replication‑independent CGI hypermethylation?
Do similar replication‑independent methylation gains occur in other CpG‑island hypermethylator cancers?

key_findings: EZH2 deletion in NEPC mice leads to global DNA methylation changes at PRC2 target DMRs.
EZH2‑KO NEPC organoids show increased NE signature scores despite loss of H3K27me3.
DNMT1 deletion in NEPC models causes increased H3K27me3 at neuron‑related promoters, suppressing their expression.
Pharmacologic EZH2 inhibition mirrors genetic EZH2 loss; DNMT inhibition (decitabine) mirrors DNMT1 deletion, both reshaping H3K27me3 landscapes.
In adenocarcinoma context, DNMT1 loss upregulates neuroendocrine genes, highlighting cell‑state‑specific effects.
open_questions: What co‑factors dictate the opposite outcomes of DNMT1 loss in NEPC vs adenocarcinoma?
Can sequential EZH2 then DNMT inhibition achieve durable NEPC suppression?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: EZH2 inhibition in established NEPC may trigger compensatory DNA methylation, potentially limiting efficacy.

key_findings: UIM‑mutant DNMT1 fails to bind ubiquitinated nucleosomes despite retained catalytic activity.
Loss of UIM function leads to global hypomethylation comparable to DNMT1 knockdown.
UIM loss upregulates viral‑mimicry pathways and downregulates oncogenic signaling, mirroring decitabine effects.
Cell viability and colony formation are severely impaired in UIM mutants, similar to catalytic dead DNMT1.
Screening identified a natural product (afetinin) and de‑novo designed protein binders that inhibit DNMT1 UIMs at low‑nanomolar affinity.
open_questions: Will UIM inhibition cause off‑target effects on other ubiquitin‑reading proteins?
Can in vivo delivery of UIM binders achieve tumor regression without replication dependence?

company_or_sponsor: University of Michigan Center for Chemical Genomics

key_findings: KDM2A is the most amplified histone demethylase in EAC TCGA cohort.
KDM2A expression shows a trend of increase from Barrett through dysplasia to EAC.
High KDM2A correlates with reduced H3K36me2 and increased H3K27ac at oncogenic loci.
KDM2A overexpression in HET‑1A opens chromatin at MYC and other oncogenes, inducing secretory and proliferative gene programs.
Patient‑derived organoids with high KDM2A display enhanced enhancer activity and poorer prognosis.
open_questions: Can KDM2A inhibition reverse enhancer activation and block Barrett‑to‑EAC transition?
Which transcription factors cooperate with KDM2A at newly opened enhancers?

key_findings: KMT2D deletion shortens survival in KP mice initiated from both club and AT2 cells.
Adenosquamous lesions appear exclusively in KMT2D‑null tumors.
Single‑nucleus multi‑omics reveal enrichment of a basal‑like cluster and an integrin α6β4 stem‑like intermediate in KMT2D‑KO tumors.
Chromatin regions losing H3K4me1 in KMT2D‑KO are enriched for FOXA1/FOXA2 motifs and co‑factor binding (SMARCC1, EP300).
FOXA1 physically interacts with KMT2D; MEN1 inhibition (MI‑503) shows increased sensitivity in KMT2D‑KO cells.
open_questions: Does catalytic inactivation of KMT2D recapitulate the phenotypes of complete loss?
Can targeting FOXA1 or SOX2 downstream mitigate the squamous transdifferentiation?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: KMT2D loss creates dependency on MEN1, suggesting a synthetic lethal vulnerability.

key_findings: CVD incidence sharply increases within first 2 years after hematologic malignancy diagnosis, median time 2.4 years.
MDS and multiple myeloma patients have the highest CVD risk in the first five years.
Arrhythmias are the most common CVD subtype post‑diagnosis.
Proteasome inhibitor exposure yields the highest composite cardiotoxicity score among treatments.
In vitro Cell Village assay shows proteasome inhibitor induces inflammatory/dysfunctional cardiac cell states and cell death.
open_questions: What molecular mechanisms link proteasome inhibition to specific cardiac cell dysfunction?
Can identified protective markers be targeted to mitigate cardiotoxicity?

key_findings: Identified 1,138 unique tumor antigen candidates, >50% absent from IEDB.
Tumor antigen count positively correlates with CD8 T‑cell infiltration and ICI‑treated survival.
MAGEA3/4/12 antigen events strongly associate with increased CD8 T‑cell fraction.
A ubiquitin‑high interferon subtype shows worse survival; RNF4‑DHX9 and BIRC7‑AKT1 ubiquitin pairs are prognostic.
A lysosome‑high glycoproteomic subtype displays sex‑specific survival: poor in males, neutral/beneficial in females, linked to GPUMB fucosylation.
open_questions: Can identified tumor antigens be leveraged for personalized vaccines?
What drives the sex‑specific lysosome phenotype?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Sex‑specific impact of GPUMB fucosylation suggests differential resistance mechanisms.

key_findings: Five‑year endocrine therapy adherence increased 10‑yr hypertension risk by 9 percentage points.
AI use, but not tamoxifen, was associated with higher dyslipidemia (33% vs 26%) and diabetes (13% vs 9.5%) risks.
Both AI and tamoxifen adherence reduced all‑cause mortality (18% vs 28%) and breast cancer‑specific mortality (6‑8% vs 13%).
Adherent patients were younger, higher socioeconomic status, and had fewer baseline comorbidities.
open_questions: How does differential healthcare utilization affect observed cardiometabolic risks?
Would extending AI therapy beyond five years further increase cardiometabolic events?

key_findings: Alt‑Flow‑FISH enables high‑throughput single‑cell ALT activity measurement.
Genome‑wide CRISPR screen uncovered numerous ALT suppressors, notably proteasome subunits (PSMB1, PSMB5, PSMB6) and akirin‑2.
Proteasome depletion leads to PML protein accumulation and hyper‑ALT phenotype with increased c‑circles.
Overexpression of PML alone induces hyper‑ALT and cell death; bortezomib recapitulates this effect.
Pathway analysis highlighted DNA repair, replication, proteasome, and Fanconi anemia pathways as ALT regulators.
open_questions: Is ALT hyper‑activation uniformly lethal across diverse ALT tumor types?
Can proteasome inhibition be combined safely with DNA‑damage agents?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Proteasome inhibition may affect normal cells; therapeutic window needs definition.

key_findings: HDAC8 relocalizes from cytosol/nucleus to nucleus after paclitaxel.
HDAC1 interaction partners shift with treatment, indicating dynamic complex remodeling.
Identified >100 protein complexes; ~50% are novel assemblies.
Stress response complex emerges uniquely in vernostat‑treated cells.
Transcriptional activation complex CBP‑300 appears only after paclitaxel.
SWI/SNF complex is lost under both chemotherapies.
open_questions: Do identified dynamic complexes predict patient response or resistance?
Can targeting emergent complexes improve chemosensitivity?

key_findings: Dual‑payload ADC shows enhanced potency in PBMC co‑culture versus cytotoxic‑only ADCs.
In vivo MC38‑hTROP2 model: ASP2998 induces tumor regression and complete protection upon rechallenge.
PK data reveal >99.9% of drug remains intact; free payloads are ~1,000‑fold lower.
GLP repeat‑dose study shows manageable safety profile; target organs at high dose include cornea, kidney, urethra, trachea.
Low IL‑6 induction suggests limited cytokine release syndrome risk.
open_questions: What is the optimal TROP2 expression cutoff for patient selection?
How does the STING agonist payload affect systemic immunity and safety?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Efficacy depends on TROP2 expression; threshold not yet defined in trial.

key_findings: EYA4 is hyper‑methylated yet overexpressed in TNBC; highest in MDA‑MB‑231.
EYA4 depletion reduces primary tumor growth and lung metastasis in vivo.
EYA4 binds ssDNA with nanomolar affinity; phosphomimetic mutation reduces binding.
DNA binding markedly stimulates EYA4 tyrosine phosphatase activity.
Small‑molecule inhibitor CID‑XXXX89 reduces HR efficiency (dose‑dependent GFP loss) and cell viability.
open_questions: Can EYA4 inhibition overcome PARP resistance in BRCA‑wildtype TNBC?
What biomarkers predict response to EYA4 inhibitors in patient tumors?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Potential selectivity challenge: phosphatase inhibition may affect normal DNA repair.

key_findings: Synaptic contacts from neurons to glioblastoma cells were visualized by EM in patient samples and xenografts.
Neuronal AMPA‑receptor activity drives calcium influx, proliferation, and invasion of glioblastoma cells.
Perampanel is being tested in the phase I/II PERSECH trial using RNA‑Seq connectivity scores and AI‑based MRI growth dynamics as primary endpoints.
Rabies‑based retrograde tracing reveals widespread, dynamic neuron‑to‑tumor connectivity across the whole brain.
Cholinergic signaling and GPM6A‑mediated tumor microtubules represent additional mechanisms of invasion.
open_questions: What immune cells (e.g., microglia) modulate neuron‑glioma synapses?
Can the synaptic network be fully recapitulated in immunocompetent mouse models?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Perampanel requires careful titration due to neuropsychiatric side effects, indicating a narrow therapeutic window.

key_findings: A high‑content 2D tumor‑microtubule assay enabled quantitative segmentation of microtubule number, length, and cell viability.
Screen of 71 compounds identified PKC activators (PMA, TPPB) that disconnect microtubules without killing cells.
TPPB treatment reduced TTYH2 expression, decreased microtubule length, and silenced periodic calcium activity in three glioblastoma cell lines.
In vivo, TPPB combined with radiotherapy eradicated tumor cells in the invasion zone and extended mouse survival.
Spatial COMET analysis showed TTYH2 down‑regulation in the invasion zone and increased apoptosis (caspase‑3) after TPPB treatment.
open_questions: What downstream PKC substrates mediate microtubule disassembly?
Can TPPB be combined with temozolomide or immunotherapies for additive benefit?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: PKC activators have broad downstream effects; specificity for tumor‑microtubule disruption versus other PKC‑mediated pathways remains unclear.

key_findings: Neutrophil infiltration occurs late in GBM progression and is enriched in necrotic, hypoxic cores.
Neutrophils undergo MPO‑dependent NETosis; macrophages engulf NETs and become immunosuppressive (ARG1, PD‑L1 upregulation).
MPO‑deficient tumors show increased neutrophil numbers, reduced immunosuppressive phenotype, and improved mouse survival.
Human GBM samples display macrophage engulfment of MPO, especially in mesenchymal subtype.
Neutrophil‑derived factors suppress T‑cell proliferation in vitro, an effect reversed in MPO‑knockout conditions.
open_questions: How does targeting MPO or NETosis affect overall tumor immunity and response to checkpoint blockade?
What are the sex‑specific effects of myeloid manipulation in GBM?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: MPO deficiency leads to accumulation of neutrophils with an APC‑like phenotype, altering the immune landscape.

key_findings: Large cohort (n>100) confirms four dominant glioblastoma cell states; mesenchymal compartment further subdivides into hypoxia‑ and stress‑associated programs.
Visium HD spatial analysis shows layered organization: necrotic core → mesenchymal/inflammatory → angiogenic hub → neurodevelopmental (OPC/NPC) zones.
Subclonal copy‑number events are spatially confined, with distinct clones populating leptomeningeal versus parenchymal regions.
Phylogenetic trees based on SNVs reveal that advanced clones are enriched for OPC/NPC‑like states, suggesting state‑specific evolutionary pressure.
IDH‑mutant gliomas display hypomethylation‑driven loss of differentiation; IDH inhibitors promote cancer‑cell differentiation, correlating with clinical response.
open_questions: How can region‑specific therapies be designed to target distinct microenvironmental niches within glioblastoma?
What mechanisms underlie the preferential evolution of OPC/NPC‑like cells in advanced clones?

key_findings: 71% (13/17) of patients achieved a composite clinical complete response after 3 months of tremelimumab + durvalumab and avoided surgery.
24‑month PFS was 94.1% and OS was 100% with a median follow‑up of 27.1 months.
