open_questions: How does SPARC‑mediated collagen architecture specifically modulate neutrophil NETosis signaling?
Can therapeutic restoration of SPARC in the stroma reverse immune suppression in established tumors?
readouts: flow cytometry for CD24 and P‑selectin

key_findings: CHIL1 overexpression accelerates lung metastasis in Middle T mice within six weeks.
CHIL1 knockout tumors retain an intact CK14+ myoepithelial layer and fail to metastasize.
Neutrophil depletion (anti‑Ly6G) preserves myoepithelial markers and prevents basement membrane degradation.
Pharmacologic inhibition of neutrophil elastase with Alvestat maintains CK14, calponin, and p63 expression and reduces circulating tumor cells.
CHIL1‑driven neutrophil recruitment leads to extensive laminin and collagen IV degradation, driving myoepithelial loss.
open_questions: Can CHIL1 inhibition synergize with checkpoint blockade to convert immune‑cold tumors to hot?
What is the relative contribution of NET‑associated versus granule‑released elastase in ECM remodeling?
readouts: basement membrane component staining (laminin, collagen IV)
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Neutrophil elastase inhibition blocks ECM degradation without affecting NETosis, indicating distinct neutrophil functions.

cited_papers: Kim Marske lab neutrophil elastase knockout study

key_findings: Smoothened inhibition combined with gemcitabine accelerated tumor progression in humans despite preclinical efficacy.
Pegylated hyaluronidase failed to improve overall survival and worsened outcomes when combined with FOLFIRINOX.
TGF‑β blockade depleted myCAFs but did not improve survival in pancreatic cancer trials.
IL‑1β blockade showed no benefit over chemotherapy in pancreatic cancer.
open_questions: How can fibroblast subsets be selectively reprogrammed rather than globally depleted?
What are the precise mechanisms by which fibroblast depletion worsens outcomes?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Depleting fibroblasts or ECM can increase tumor aggressiveness, suggesting fibroblast subsets have both tumor‑promoting and restraining roles.

key_findings: Kit ligand is highly expressed in normal pancreatic stellate cells but markedly reduced in pancreatic cancer stroma.
Conditional deletion of Kit ligand in mouse pancreas increases CD45+ leukocyte infiltration and perivascular mesenchymal cells.
Kit ligand loss exacerbates cerulein‑induced pancreatitis and promotes acinar‑to‑ductal metaplasia.
In implantable tumor models, stromal Kit ligand deficiency accelerates tumor growth.
open_questions: Can downstream effectors of Kit ligand (e.g., basement membrane components) be therapeutically targeted to mimic its tumor‑suppressive role?
What cues in pre‑invasive lesions maintain Kit ligand expression, and can they be reinforced?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: TGF‑β signaling down‑regulates Kit ligand expression, linking a known tumor‑promoting pathway to loss of a stromal tumor‑suppressive factor.

key_findings: Three of four sites completed local QLoRA fine‑tuning, showing improved extraction accuracy versus out‑of‑the‑box MedGamma (visualized as orange vs blue bars).
One site demonstrated a statistically significant increase in variable extraction performance after fine‑tuning; other sites reported even larger gains.
Federated aggregation of QLoRA weights is scheduled, with the hypothesis that exposure to four centers’ data will further boost model robustness.
open_questions: What is the optimal level of differential privacy that balances privacy guarantees with model accuracy across heterogeneous sites?
readouts: structured data extraction from pathology reports

key_findings: Local fine‑tuning at one site increased extraction performance from baseline (blue) to post‑fine‑tuning (orange).
Two additional sites reported even larger improvements after local QLoRA adaptation.
Federated aggregation of QLoRA weights is planned for the week following the conference.
open_questions: Will federated QLoRA updates yield additive gains beyond the best local fine‑tuned model?

key_findings: Added 104 real‑world Moffitt GBM patients to three public datasets without centralizing data.
Leave‑one‑site‑out evaluation showed consistent Kaplan‑Meier separation across held‑out cohorts.
Time‑dependent 1‑year AUC and C‑index were comparable to prior centralized studies, though absolute performance was not yet sufficient for clinical decision‑making.
Future plans include incorporating an additional private NCI GBM cohort and expanding to radiology reports, other imaging modalities, and clinical markers.
open_questions: How to accurately compute Cox partial likelihood in a federated setting given incomplete at‑risk information across sites?
What is the impact of batch‑wise approximation on survival model bias across heterogeneous cohorts?

cited_papers: AI‑RANO review in The Lancet Oncology

key_findings: Nine weeks of neoadjuvant pembrolizumab achieved a 59% pCR rate in high-risk stage II/III MMRd CRC (n=31).
ctDNA was detected in 100% of patients at baseline, with 24% in the ultrasensitive range (<100 ppm).
100% of 'super molecular responders' (rapid clearance after 1 cycle) achieved pCR.
Post-operative ctDNA surveillance demonstrated 100% specificity and 100% negative predictive value for relapse over a median follow-up of 33 months.
Baseline TCR clonal expansion correlates with pCR, and a combined Bayesian model of TCR and ctDNA kinetics improves response prediction.
open_questions: Whether super molecular responders can be safely managed non-operatively.

key_findings: 100% specificity: all 47 patients achieving pCR were ctDNA negative post-neoadjuvant therapy.
Sustained MRD negativity (76% of patients) resulted in a 63% pCR rate.
Persistent MRD positivity resulted in 0% pCR and 100% residual disease (all RCB2 or 3).
Frequent sampling identified 64% more patients at risk for residual disease compared to a single post-neoadjuvant time point.
Clearance timing varied by subtype: TNBC cleared within 45 days (90% of patients) vs HR+/HER2- which took 16 weeks (90% of patients).
open_questions: Whether a negative test in the presence of residual disease implies a favorable long-term outcome regardless of pCR.

key_findings: Two-year DFS was 71%, an improvement over the historical benchmark of 60% for HR+ IBC.
ctDNA negativity at the end of treatment was associated with 100% disease-free survival at 24 months.
ctDNA positivity provided a lead time to clinical progression of up to 15 months.
Durable responders showed lower maximum variant allele frequency (VAF) in nodal tissue compared to non-responders.
Deletions in the immunoglobulin heavy locus (IGH) were found in durable responders, suggesting B-cell involvement in the response.
open_questions: The specific role of B-cell clones in aiding T-cell effectors in IBC response.

key_findings: A single patient treated with rivocostimib achieved persistent ctDNA clearance and remains disease-free 2 years post-therapy.
ctDNA detection at 8-12 weeks post-therapy had 50% sensitivity for recurrence, which improved to 73% with longitudinal tracking.
HPV DNA sequencing showed higher sensitivity but lower specificity compared to the RADAR assay in OPC patients.
Combining tumor-informed assays and HPV DNA increased sensitivity to 100% in OPC patients.
The study was paused due to lower-than-expected MRD prevalence (only 6 patients eligible for interception).
open_questions: Whether more sensitive assays (<100 ppm) can catch relapses that occur more than a year after the positive sample.
tumor_types: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma

key_findings: Bifetostat 5mg + fulvestrant is the recommended dose for Phase 3 based on superior ctDNA clearance and gene expression changes.
Early ctDNA clearance (within 9 weeks) strongly correlates with clinical response (PR and SD).
Patients with undetectable ctDNA at 9 weeks had a significantly longer median PFS (21.9 vs 5.3 months).
The combination effectively clears ESR1 mutations (63% clearance rate), which are key drivers of endocrine resistance.
open_questions: Determinants of responder vs non-responder among patients who still showed >50% ctDNA drop but progressed.

key_findings: Sustained ctDNA clearance was associated with the best outcomes (median PFS 19.3 months vs 6.2 months for non-clearers).
ctDNA re-emergence occurred 55 days before clinical progression in one representative case.
100% of sustained clearance patients were alive at 12 months, compared to 36% of never-clearers.
The methylation-based assay is viable for SCLC due to the high shedding nature of the tumor.
ctDNA dynamics aligned closely with longitudinal RECIST assessments.
open_questions: Need for prospective randomized trials to determine if ctDNA-guided therapy improves outcomes over standard care.

key_findings: Trained the first multimodal foundation model on 5,003 patients (4,605 publicly released) with paired H&E and spatial proteomics data across 8 cancer types.
Demonstrated that the model can virtually stain unmeasured proteins and predict optimal protein panels, achieving comparable performance to specialized single‑modality models.
Showed that model‑derived signatures stratify responders vs non‑responders in a triple‑negative breast cancer immunotherapy cohort better than existing clinical biomarkers.
Implemented EchoK, a reinforcement‑learning sequential acquisition system that selects a minimal set of proteomic markers (as few as 8) while preserving cell‑typing accuracy.
CellFlux trained on 300 k images achieved higher image‑generation quality than prior baselines; scaling to 11.6 M images further improved performance.
Demonstrated that flow‑matching in latent space (CellFlux v2) enables realistic perturbation simulations and visualizes transformation trajectories.
Created MicroVQA, a benchmark of >1 000 expert‑curated microscopy questions covering higher‑order Bloom’s taxonomy, revealing gaps in current vision‑language models.
Showed that large multimodal LLMs (e.g., Gemini 3 Pro) achieve state‑of‑the‑art scores on MicroVQA but still struggle with fine‑grained visual reasoning.
open_questions: How to effectively model discrete biological events (e.g., apoptosis) within continuous flow‑matching frameworks?
Best strategies for joint training on limited matched multimodal (image‑transcriptomics) data combined with large unimodal datasets.

key_findings: Constructed Myriad, a 6 M QA pair knowledge base derived from peer‑reviewed literature, improving retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) performance on MedExpertQA.
Developed a process‑reward model that checks individual reasoning steps of a language model against guidelines, reducing hallucinations across multiple downstream medical tasks.
Demonstrated an agent that performs step‑wise 3D chest CT analysis with traceable reasoning, achieving higher fidelity than baseline LLMs.
open_questions: How to scale structured knowledge representation while maintaining up‑to‑date clinical guidelines?
Methods for integrating multimodal inputs (imaging, labs, notes) into the agentic reasoning loop.

key_findings: CRDC hosts 533 studies covering over 200,000 subjects and 17 petabytes of data.
Since inception, the cloud resource has performed over 1,600 compute years and offers more than 1,200 public analysis tools.
User engagement includes 100,000 monthly users and 47,000 PubMed citations referencing CRDC data.
CCDI ecosystem currently includes 41 datasets, including Childhood Cancer Survival Study and Pediatric MATCH.
Project Every Child has enrolled >9,000 patients, delivering molecular characterization results within 21 days.
6,000 patients' molecular data from MCI have been released in cBioPortal, with integrated SNV and methylation widgets.
Over 4,000 pathology images are available in the Imaging Data Commons, with AI‑ready processing by DOE.
Netrius DataCord AI‑driven curation platform achieved ≥90% reduction in manual curation time in pilot deployments.
Data Gatherer combines rule‑based and LLM methods to extract dataset metadata from publications, enhancing discoverability.
BioInsight AI chatbot enables plain‑language queries across CRDC genomic, proteomic, and imaging resources.
Each 5 kg/m² increase in BMI raises post‑menopausal breast cancer risk by ~10% (IARC meta‑analysis).
Obesity at cancer diagnosis is associated with >20% higher breast cancer‑specific mortality across 36 studies.
Bariatric surgery reduces overall cancer incidence by ~40% and obesity‑related cancers (breast ~50% reduction, colorectal ~60% reduction).
In the Breast Cancer Weight Loss Trial, the lifestyle intervention achieved a mean 6% weight loss at 1 yr, with 50% of participants losing ≥5% body weight versus 12% in controls.
Weight loss lowered fasting insulin by 21% and reduced HOMA‑IR by 25% at 6 mo, indicating reversal of insulin resistance.
Metabolic improvements (insulin, leptin, CRP) were observed without yet having invasive disease‑free survival data, which are pending.
open_questions: Will randomized weight‑loss trials demonstrate a causal reduction in cancer incidence and mortality comparable to bariatric surgery?
Which metabolic biomarkers (e.g., insulin vs leptin) are most predictive of cancer risk reduction after weight loss?
Can body‑composition metrics (DEXA, bioimpedance) improve risk stratification beyond BMI?

cited_papers: International Agency for Research on Cancer monograph (2022)
Oxford Overview Group breast cancer recurrence analysis (2023)
Look AHEAD trial secondary cancer outcomes (2024)

key_findings: Tirzepatide achieved ~20% weight loss in obese C57BL/6 mice, matching human clinical trial outcomes.

Obesity‑driven tumor growth in EO771, MC38 and PY230 models was reduced to lean‑control levels by tirzepatide; pair‑feeding reproduced most of the effect, indicating weight‑loss as the primary driver.
In the LKB1/p53‑deficient endometrial model, tirzepatide reduced tumor burden even in non‑obese mice, suggesting additional metabolic effects.

Obesity suppressed CD8⁺ T‑cell activation (naive markers TCF7, CCR7) and antigen‑presentation gene sets (18/18); tirzepatide fully restored activated phenotypes (granzyme B, PD‑1) and antigen‑presentation scores.
CD8⁺ T‑cell depletion abolished tirzepatide’s anti‑tumor effect, confirming T‑cell dependence.
Tirzepatide did not affect cancer cell proliferation in vitro, consistent with low GLP‑1R/GIPR expression in human cancer cell lines.
Gut microbiome analysis showed tirzepatide enriched butyrate‑producing bacteria, potentially contributing to reduced inflammation.
open_questions: Which specific metabolic factor (insulin, leptin, IGF‑1) is most critical for the immunologic rescue?
Can tirzepatide synergize with checkpoint inhibitors in obese tumor models?
Does the microbiome shift contribute causally to the restored anti‑tumor immunity?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: No direct cytotoxic effect of tirzepatide on cancer cells observed across a wide concentration range.
Effectiveness appears largely mediated by systemic metabolic improvement rather than tumor‑intrinsic target engagement.

cited_papers: Hursting et al. Nat Commun preprint 2024

key_findings: GLP‑1 users had a 17% lower overall cancer incidence (HR 0.83) compared with matched non‑users in the OneFlorida cohort.
Significant risk reductions were observed for endometrial (HR 0.71), ovarian (HR 0.74) and meningioma (HR 0.68) cancers.
In Medicare type 2 diabetes patients, GLP‑1 vs SGLT2 was associated with a 22% increased kidney cancer risk (HR 1.22).
GLP‑1 vs DPP4 showed a borderline 18% increased endometrial cancer risk (HR 1.18) but was not statistically definitive.
Among cancer survivors with diabetes, GLP‑1 exposure improved overall survival (HR 0.78) and breast cancer‑specific survival (HR 0.71) versus DPP4.
Protective effects were consistent across age groups and most pronounced in non‑Hispanic White patients.
open_questions: What biological mechanisms underlie the observed kidney cancer signal in diabetic cohorts?
Do newer GLP‑1 agents (semaglutide, tirzepatide) confer stronger protective effects than older agents?
How do GLP‑1 effects differ between primary prevention (risk) and secondary prevention (survivorship) settings?
readouts: comparative effectiveness vs SGLT2 and DPP4
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Potential increased kidney cancer risk in diabetic patients may reflect underlying CKD susceptibility amplified by GLP‑1 therapy.

key_findings: Analyzed 350,000 NSCLC liquid biopsy tests from 2015‑2025, representing community practice across 20 self-reported ethnicities.
Technical success rate >90% for both NGS and ddPCR platforms.
KRAS G12C was the most frequent SNV; EGFR L858R and exon 19 deletions were also prevalent.
CCDC6‑RET was the most common fusion; ROS1 and ALK fusions were detected at expected frequencies.
MYC copy‑number gain was the most common CNV among the panel.
Observed variant prevalences were modestly lower than literature reports, reflecting real‑world, non‑referral‑biased populations.
open_questions: How do observed prevalence differences impact selection of targeted therapies in community settings?
Can longitudinal liquid biopsy monitoring improve outcomes compared with tissue genotyping?

key_findings: In 844 never‑smoker lung cancers, adenocarcinoma and carcinoid were over‑represented, while squamous and SCLC were under‑represented compared with smoker cohorts.
Combined IASLC grades 1 + 2 showed better overall survival than grade 3 (HR 0.38 in all stages; HR 0.31 in stage I‑II).
Deep‑learning model improved AUC for five‑year OS when added to clinical variables and grading (integrative model AUC > clinical‑only model).
Model identified a subset of grade 3 tumors with low risk, enriched in East Asian ancestry.
Web‑based heat‑map tool enables pathologists to visualize high‑risk histologic regions.
open_questions: What histologic features drive the deep‑learning model’s risk predictions, especially in East Asian patients?
Can the model be prospectively validated in independent registries?

key_findings: Propensity‑matched cohort of 1,870 patients per arm achieved covariate balance (SMD <0.1).
Early survival similar (1‑yr OS 83% vs 85%); long‑term survival diverged favoring trastuzumab deruxtecan (5‑yr OS 58% vs 49%).
Adjusted hazard ratio for death with chemotherapy vs T‑DXd = 1.14 (caution due to early curve crossing).
Higher incidence of all‑grade interstitial lung disease (12%) and heart failure (9%) in the T‑DXd group.
Hematologic toxicities comparable; fatigue and vomiting more frequent with T‑DXd, diarrhea more common with chemotherapy.
open_questions: Will prospective second‑line trials confirm the observed long‑term OS benefit?
What monitoring protocols best mitigate ILD risk in real‑world use?

key_findings: Cohort of 2.6 M veterans (10% ARB, 90% ACE) followed up to 10 years.
ARB initiation associated with 20‑25% lower overall cancer risk (RR 0.75‑0.80).
No significant difference in diagnosis‑free mortality between groups.
Effect stronger in patients >70 years (≈30% risk reduction).
Consistent risk reduction across major solid‑tumor subtypes.
open_questions: What biological mechanisms underlie the observed cancer risk reduction with ARBs?
Can findings be replicated in non‑veteran, more gender‑balanced populations?

key_findings: Cohort of 105,000 ART users and 105,000 matched non‑ART controls (mean age 47).
Breast cancer events: 1,774 (ART) vs 1,581 (non‑ART).
Ovarian cancer events: 235 (ART) vs 161 (non‑ART).
Endometrial cancer events: 261 (ART) vs 252 (non‑ART).
Adjusted HRs: breast cancer 1.12, ovarian cancer 1.46, endometrial cancer 1.03 (not significant).
Risk persisted after excluding women with endometriosis or PCOS.
open_questions: Would inclusion of family history, BMI, and screening data modify the observed associations?
Is the risk dose‑dependent on number of ART cycles?

key_findings: German WGS pipeline achieved >85% clinically actionable reporting across 20 tumor types.
Pilot Indian cohort demonstrated feasibility of generating WGS, imaging, and pathology data for under‑represented patients.
AI models trained on German data successfully applied to Indian cases for therapy recommendation and risk stratification.
open_questions: How to ensure data governance and patient ownership across jurisdictions?
What cost‑effective sequencing strategies can broaden access in low‑resource settings?

key_findings: Classifier achieved ROC‑AUC >0.85 on held‑out validation using C‑circle assay as ground truth.
ALT prevalence recapitulated known high‑ALT cancers (glioma, sarcoma, osteosarcoma) and identified estimates for >30 additional tumor types.
ATRX/DAXX truncations enriched for ALT but many ALT‑positive tumors lacked these alterations.
Missense mutations in RB1 and POT1 associated with ALT activity in wild‑type ATRX/DAXX tumors.
ALT positivity correlated with better OS in glioma but worse OS in sarcoma and osteosarcoma.
open_questions: Can the classifier be adapted to whole‑genome or other panel platforms?
Will prospective trials of ALT‑targeted agents use this model for patient selection?

key_findings: A wiki‑survey of >2,000 Black and White adults identified distinct top‑ranked messages for each racial group.
In a subsequent RCT (≈2,000 participants), all message conditions increased screening intention versus control.
Black‑preferred messages produced the highest mean intention scores among Black participants, outperforming median‑ranked and White‑preferred messages.
White participants showed no significant increase in screening intention across any message condition.

Message sharing intentions aligned with racial preference: Black participants were more likely to share Black‑preferred messages, and White participants were more likely to share White‑preferred messages.
open_questions: How can participatory (user‑generated) messages be optimized without compromising scientific accuracy?
What mechanisms can integrate religious or community‑based messengers into evidence‑based prevention campaigns?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Participants reported that messages not aligned with their racial identity were perceived as less effective, highlighting the importance of cultural relevance.

key_findings: Segmentation identified high‑ vs low‑mistrust clusters among Black patients, each with distinct messaging needs.
Perceptual mapping revealed that high‑mistrust patients prioritized concerns about privacy, insurance exploitation, and genetic discrimination.
GenePilot incorporated persona‑based modules (Fly, Glide, Soar, Navigate) addressing these concerns.
In the RCT (≈100 Black patients), GenePilot significantly lowered decisional conflict and increased self‑efficacy compared with usual care.
Usage analytics showed mandatory progression through all four modules, ensuring exposure to core content.
open_questions: How can the GenePilot platform be adapted for other under‑served populations beyond Black patients?
What is the long‑term impact of GenePilot on actual genetic testing completion rates and downstream clinical outcomes?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: High‑mistrust patients expressed fear that genetic information could be used against them financially or racially.
Low‑mistrust patients were less concerned about privacy but still valued clear explanations of testing purpose.

patent_or_ip_hints: GenePilot decision support tool patent pending

key_findings: Microdissected metaplastic glands display ~2‑fold higher SNV burden and ~3‑fold higher indel rate than adjacent non‑metaplastic glands.
Mutational signature SBS18 (ROS injury) and increased ID2/ID1 ratio emerge early in metaplasia, resembling MSI tumor signatures.
Single‑cell RNA‑seq defines hybrid gastric‑intestinal cells and a fetal gut signature (TROP2, TACSTD2) in metaplastic organoids.
Chromosome 20 gain is frequent in metaplastic organoids and enables growth without Matrigel, suggesting an early tumor‑initiating event.
Claudin‑18.2 expression declines during metaplastic progression, potentially mediating resistance to CLDN18.2‑targeted therapies.
open_questions: Can chromosome 20 gain be used as a predictive biomarker for progression to invasive gastric cancer?
What molecular events trigger the transition from hybrid to fully intestinal metaplasia?
How can the fetal reversion signature be therapeutically targeted to prevent tumor initiation?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Loss of CLDN18.2 expression in advanced metaplastic organoids may represent an escape mechanism from CLDN18.2‑targeted antibodies.

key_findings: Zanidatamab induces HER2 cap formation and hexamerization not observed with trastuzumab, pertuzumab, or their combination.
In the fourth‑line setting, zanidatamab monotherapy produced durable responses absent with standard HER2‑targeted therapy.
Phase II zanidatamab + chemo yielded a median PFS advantage of 4 months over trastuzumab + chemo (HR 0.65, p < 0.001).
Adding tislelizumab to zanidatamab + chemo further improved OS (HR 0.72, ~7‑month gain) compared with trastuzumab + chemo.
Diarrhea was the most common toxicity in the zanidatamab‑chemo arms, requiring proactive management.
open_questions: Will zanidatamab benefit HER2‑low (2+ without amplification) gastric cancers?
What biomarkers predict response beyond HER2 IHC/FISH status?
Can earlier‑line use of zanidatamab improve cure rates in resectable disease?

key_findings: Neoadjuvant durvalumab + FLOT achieved a 19% pCR rate and 19% MPR rate, markedly higher than historic chemotherapy alone.
Patients with pCR had durable disease‑free survival with median follow‑up >4 years.
Clinical complete response was observed in 83% of early‑cohort patients after six cycles of neoadjuvant therapy.
ctDNA clearance correlated with pathologic response but 38% of ctDNA‑negative patients still recurred, highlighting residual risk.
Chromosomal instability (CIN) signatures predicted poorer immunotherapy benefit, suggesting a need for additional biomarkers.
open_questions: What molecular or immune signatures can reliably identify patients who will achieve pCR and may be candidates for non‑operative management?
How can CIN‑driven cGAS‑STING suppression be therapeutically reversed to improve immunotherapy response?
What is the optimal duration of neoadjuvant immunotherapy to balance efficacy and toxicity?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: CIN tumors showed reduced benefit from durvalumab‑FLOT, likely due to cGAS‑STING mediated immune evasion.

key_findings: Carcinogenic effect is calculated as the odds ratio of cancer vs. normal tissue mutation frequencies.
TP53 shows a carcinogenic effect in the thousands in esophageal SCC, confirming strong driver status.
NOTCH1 mutations are more frequent in normal esophagus than in cancer, suggesting a tumor‑inhibiting role.
PIK3CA, FAD1, EP300 show low carcinogenic effects, indicating limited contribution to malignancy.
In AML, classic drivers (e.g., FLT3) have high carcinogenic effects, while TET2/DNMT3A have low effects.
open_questions: Can age‑dependent mutation frequency be used prospectively to identify high‑risk individuals?
How do environmental exposures alter the normal‑tissue mutation frequencies used in the model?

key_findings: A single DMBA dose creates ~30,000–50,000 mutations, including HRAS Q61L, which remains latent for up to a year.
TPA promotion induces massive clonal expansion of HRAS Q61L, accounting for >90% of tumors.
Spontaneous KRAS G12D/G13R clones expand with TPA but disappear unless HRAS is knocked out.
HRAS knockout mice develop KRAS‑driven tumors, revealing competitive clonal interactions.
Promotion requires innate immune cells; NSG mice (immune‑deficient) develop few tumors.
open_questions: What precise molecular signals from neutrophils/monocytes drive HRAS‑clone expansion?
How do different genetic backgrounds modulate promotion sensitivity?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: HRAS and KRAS mutants show reciprocal competition; removal of HRAS permits KRAS‑driven tumorigenesis.

key_findings: Off‑target reads from panel sequencing can accurately impute common germline variants (R²>0.8).
Pan‑cancer GWAS identified a 1q32/M​DM4 locus associated with TP53 mutations; replicated in Dana‑Farber and TCGA cohorts.
CRISPR deletion of the implicated enhancer reduced MDM4 expression, confirming functional relevance.
The MDM4 risk allele is enriched in stage IV disease and lung metastasis in breast cancer, independent of TP53 status.
Ancestry‑specific germline variant explains part of the higher ERG fusion frequency in European‑ancestry prostate cancer.
open_questions: How many additional germline‑somatic associations remain undiscovered at larger sample sizes?
Can germline‑driven selection be leveraged for preventive interventions?

key_findings: MutRisk predicts highly unequal per‑site mutation probabilities; some TP53 codons are orders of magnitude more likely to mutate.
Estimated numbers of TP53‑mutant stem cells range from ~18 000 in colon to ~1.5 million in smoker lung tissue.
Combinations of driver mutations (e.g., APC + APC + KRAS) are exceedingly rare without clonal selection (<1 per million individuals).
Duplex sequencing of normal bladder reveals strong positive selection for RBM10 truncations and TP53 mutations, with higher DN/DS in males.
TERT promoter mutations show strong selection only in smokers, linking exposure to clonal expansion.
open_questions: How do specific environmental exposures reshape the selection landscape in different tissues?
Can MutRisk be integrated with longitudinal sampling to predict individual cancer risk?

cited_papers: López‑Bigas et al. 2024 Nat Rev Cancer

key_findings: 25% of TRACERx patients have >1 primary tumor, 12% have >1 lung primary
10% discordance between clinical and genomic relatedness leads to potential mistreatment
Multiple primaries show similar genomic divergence as tumors from different patients
Higher cumulative tobacco exposure associated with multiple lung primaries
open_questions: What host immune factors influence independent tumor initiation within the same patient?

key_findings: Two-thirds of KRAS-driven mouse pancreatic cancers acquire a second mutant KRAS copy early in tumor evolution
KRAS dosage increase occurs late (carcinoma stage) in lung and intestinal KRAS-driven cancers
CDKN2A loss is required for KRAS dosage gain in pancreas but not in intestine or lung
Wnt pathway activation precedes KRAS amplification in intestinal tumors
open_questions: How do KRAS dosage dynamics translate to human tumor evolution across tissues?

key_findings: Smoking signature SBS4 directly implicated in KRAS G12C, G12V, G13C mutations
Clock-like signatures SBS5/40 associated with KRAS G12A, G12D, G13D, Q61H mutations
KRAS mutant tumors show higher smoking signature burden than KRAS-wt
Subtype-specific signature contributions suggest smoking does not drive all KRAS variants
open_questions: Can signature-based attribution inform personalized prevention or early detection strategies?

key_findings: ecDNA-bearing cells display a broad 100‑1000 copy number range per cell, correlating with HER2 protein levels
Gene expression scaling with ecDNA dosage is stronger and more coordinated than in HSR cells
PVT1 transcriptional output and Myc program are highly dependent on ecDNA architecture
Sorted high‑ecDNA and low‑ecDNA populations reconverge to original distribution within 2‑3 generations via biased segregation and growth advantage
open_questions: What therapeutic strategies can exploit the dependence of specific oncogenic programs on ecDNA architecture?

key_findings: Transformed tumors display greater phenotypic diversity than de novo small cell
A basal intermediate state marked by NF‑κB, JAK‑STAT, hypoxia precedes neuroendocrine transformation
FOXF2B overexpression induces neuroendocrine markers and suppresses EGFR signaling
SDK1 and KEAP1 mutations may define a neuroendocrine‑to‑GI plasticity axis in large‑cell neuroendocrine carcinoma
open_questions: Can targeting the basal hypoxic program prevent lineage plasticity and improve outcomes?

key_findings: ZEB1 knockdown biases cells toward epithelial state regardless of initial phenotype
GRL2 loss biases toward mesenchymal state
SUV39H1/2 loss enhances bidirectional plasticity, increasing state transitions
Dual‑guide approach enables detection of epistatic interactions (e.g., ZEB1 vs GRL2)
open_questions: Can pharmacologic inhibition of SUV39H1/2 modulate PDAC plasticity in vivo?

key_findings: IDH‑mutant gliomas share clonal astrocyte‑like cells with 1p/19q codeletion
Mismatched methylation and 3D genome states suggest early chromatin remodeling during cell‑state transitions
ecDNA (EGFR, CDK4) present only in IDH‑wt GBM, with structural variants correlating with methylation subclones
Oncogene‑specific TF motif enrichment (MAPK for EGFR ecDNA, Hedgehog for GLI1 ecDNA) links ecDNA structure to epigenetic reprogramming
open_questions: How does ecDNA‑driven methylation remodeling influence therapeutic response in GBM?

key_findings: BCL6‑BRD4 TSIP activates a BCL6‑dependent reporter with EC50 ~5 nM via a hook‑shaped ternary complex.
BRD4 recruitment relocalizes to BCL6 loci, inducing NOXA and other apoptotic genes more potently than BCL6 loss.
In lymphoma xenografts with high BCL6, the TSIP suppresses tumor growth at modest doses, while BCL6‑low models are resistant.
TRAP‑1 (p53‑BRD4 glue) induces p21 and MDM2 expression in p53 Y220C cells, demonstrating gain‑of‑function activation.
dTag‑based glue redirects EWS‑FLI1 to BCL6 sites, upregulating SOX2 and illustrating programmable transcriptional rewiring.
open_questions: How does low‑occupancy gluing affect long‑term cellular homeostasis?
Can other effectors (e.g., CDK9, p300) be optimized for stronger gain‑of‑function outcomes?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Hook effect observed: supra‑optimal concentrations reduce ternary complex formation.
Efficacy depends on target expression; low BCL6 or mutant p53 levels diminish response.

key_findings: Cryo‑EM shows UM171 occupies HDAC active site and contacts KBDBD4 2B2C loop.
Cancer insertions (+2 aa) in KBDBD4 2B2C loop drive CoREST degradation without UM171.
Deep mutational scanning of 5,000 KBDBD4 variants identified insertions as the most potent neodegraders.
Structural superposition reveals UM171 arms recapitulate side‑chains of PR and TTYML insertions.
Activation‑lethality phenotype correlates with co‑REST degradation; mutants in lower‑right quadrant of DMS plot are both degradative and cytotoxic.
open_questions: Can small‑molecule design replace the 2B2C loop insertions to create synthetic glues for new neosubstrates?
What determines which neosubstrates are recruited by the mutant ligase versus UM171?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Mutant KBDBD4 shows broad cytotoxicity across many cancer cell lines, indicating limited selectivity.

key_findings: TRIM21 expression is a strong predictive biomarker for PRLX sensitivity across >4,000 compounds screened.
CRISPR KO of TRIM21 completely rescues cells from PRLX‑induced death; overexpression confers sensitivity.
PRLX directly binds TRIM21 PRY/SPRY domain (crystal structure) and recruits TRIM21 to NUP98 APD, leading to NPC ubiquitination and degradation.
Degradation of NPC components reduces cytoplasmic MCL1 and MYC, causing rapid caspase activation.
In KRAS‑mutant pancreatic xenografts, oral JWZ8103 induces tumor regressions with favorable pharmacokinetics.
Selectivity index shows ~23‑fold greater sensitivity in cancer vs normal immortalized cells after 24 h exposure.
open_questions: What is the therapeutic index of NPC degradation in normal tissues?
Why do chemically diverse TRIM21 glues all recruit NUP98 despite structural differences?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Efficacy depends on high TRIM21 expression; low‑expressing tumors are resistant.
Potential therapeutic window suggested by 23‑fold cancer‑vs‑normal cell sensitivity.

key_findings: JWJ‑0136 degrades ZBTB11 with Dmax ~80 % in resistant cells, dependent on cereblon and proteasome.
Degradation is abolished by a K866A ZBTB11 mutant, confirming on‑target ternary complex formation.
ZBTB11 loss normalizes mitochondrial biogenesis and reduces basal/maximal OCR in resistant cells.
Combination of JWJ‑0136 with KRAS inhibitors restores drug sensitivity across multiple KRAS‑mutant resistant lines and organoids.
Neuronal assays show no significant impact on mitochondrial health or viability, indicating a favorable therapeutic window.
open_questions: Can ZBTB11 degraders be optimized for in vivo pharmacokinetics and oral bioavailability?
Will long‑term ZBTB11 degradation lead to compensatory resistance mechanisms?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Selectivity achieved via cereblon expression pattern and ZBTB11 dependency unique to KRAS‑resistant cancer cells.
Neurons are spared because ZBTB11‑regulated mitochondrial genes are not essential in neuronal context.

key_findings: FMT from responder patients into germ-free mice restored anti-PD-L1 efficacy, a phenotype retained generationally in offspring.
Single-cell RNA-seq of FMT mice showed that responder microbiota induced an inflammatory macrophage gene signature and flipped granulocytes away from an MDSC-like phenotype.
Conditional deletion of PKC delta in hematopoietic cells led to spontaneous tumor control and markedly improved anti-PD-1 efficacy.
GPNMB is dominantly expressed in SPP1+ macrophages; its knockout resulted in substantial spontaneous tumor control in B16-SIY and orthotopic breast cancer models.
GPNMB-mediated suppression is driven by tissue-resident macrophages rather than bone marrow-derived cells, as Lysozyme M-Cre deletion showed a phenotype while Vav1-Cre did not.
open_questions: Identification of the relevant receptor for GPNMB to enable pharmacological blockade.
Whether the GPNMB pathway is generalizable to other cold tumors like pancreatic or colon cancer.
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: STING agonists have limited efficacy in cold tumors because they require the presence of CDC1 cells to function.

key_findings: Inactivation of TRAF2 or RNF31 tips the balance from pro-survival to pro-death, leading to tumor regression in immune-proficient mouse models.
DEP5 knockout in primary T cells boosts global translation and proliferation, leading to significant tumor control in adoptive transfer models.
CD8 T cell clusters comprise ~1.4% of all cells in melanoma lymph node metastases, with ~12% of total CD8 T cells residing in clusters.
T cells isolated from clusters show a 9-fold increase in melanoma killing capacity in vitro across 11 patients.
MGT2 was identified as a top hit in proximity labeling and cluster screens; its knockout in T cells enhances tumor killing in vitro and in vivo.
open_questions: Whether these heterotypic clusters can be detected in peripheral blood for non-invasive monitoring.
Whether T cells at the tumor margin of 'cold' tumors form stable clusters with APCs to enable isolation of reactive T cells.

key_findings: Sipuleucel-T induces T cells that are 'excluded' at the invasive margin, limiting clinical efficacy.
SPP1-high TAMs produce adenosine via CD73; blocking the A2A receptor with zafirlukast combined with anti-PD-1 showed clinical responses in 20% of CRPC patients.
Bone metastases are uniquely enriched for IL-1beta-high mature neutrophils, which are functionally immunosuppressive in vitro and in vivo.
Inhibition of CXCR1/2 or IL-1beta receptor rescued the efficacy of combination checkpoint inhibition in bone metastasis mouse models.
open_questions: Whether the role of IL-6 contributes to the immunosuppressive phenotype of neutrophils in bone metastases.
Whether epigenetic subtypes (e.g., neuroendocrine vs AR-positive) drive the different myeloid compositions across metastatic sites.
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Bone metastasis environments are dominated by neutrophils rather than TAMs, requiring different therapeutic strategies than soft tissue metastases.

key_findings: CRISPR screens revealed SHMT1/2 as selective vulnerabilities in T‑ALL, validated by RZ2994 treatment that reduced bone‑marrow and spleen disease in mice.
GLIS2‑rearranged AML models depend on JAK1/2; ruxolitinib inhibited leukemia growth and modestly prolonged mouse survival.
Resistance to JAK inhibition was mediated by loss of RASA2, which activated MAPK signaling and conferred ruxolitinib resistance in CRISPR screens.
FLT1 is highly expressed in GLIS2 AML; the FLT1‑ADC STRO‑02 eradicated leukemia in mouse xenografts and induced MRD‑negative CR in >40% of 40 pediatric patients on compassionate use.
FLT1‑CAR‑T cells are being developed as a follow‑up strategy for FLT1‑positive AML and osteosarcoma.
open_questions: What structural modifications could improve the drug‑likelihood of SHMT1/2 inhibitors for clinical use?
Can targeting RASA2 or downstream MAPK components overcome ruxolitinib resistance in GLIS2 AML?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: RASA2 loss activates MAPK signaling and drives resistance to ruxolitinib in GLIS2 AML.
SHMT1/2 inhibitor RZ2994 had limited clinical availability, highlighting drug‑access challenges.

key_findings: Covalent BTK inhibitors achieve median frontline PFS of 8.9 years (ibrutinib) and 62–75.8% PFS at 5–6 years (acalabrutinib, zanubrutinib).
BTK C481S and PLCγ2 hotspot mutations are present in 81% of lymphocytosis‑type relapses after covalent BTK inhibitors.
Non‑covalent BTK inhibitor pirtobrutinib yields >80% ORR with median PFS 19.6 months in relapsed CLL, but selects for BTK T474I and L528W mutations.
BTK degraders (Bexarotenoag, BGB16673) produce median PFS of 22.1 months and 65.9% PFS at 16 months respectively in patients resistant to both covalent and non‑covalent BTK inhibitors.
A428D BTK mutation emerges after degrader therapy and may confer cross‑resistance to all current BTK inhibitors and degraders.
open_questions: Will frontline use of non‑covalent pirtobrutinib alter the spectrum or timing of resistance mutations compared with covalent agents?
Can BTK degraders be combined with BCL2 inhibitors to achieve deeper, more durable remissions?
What is the clinical impact of low‑frequency BTK mutations detected in compartments other than peripheral blood?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: C481S converts irreversible binding to reversible, reducing drug potency.
Gatekeeper (T474I) and kinase‑impaired (L528W) mutations confer differential sensitivity to acalabrutinib vs. zanubrutinib.
A428D disrupts the binding pocket of both inhibitors and degraders, representing a pan‑resistance mutation.

key_findings: KRAS/NRAS‑mutant myeloma cells display markedly increased macropinocytosis compared with wild‑type cells.
A nanobody‑MMAE conjugate is selectively internalized by RAS‑mutant myeloma via macropinocytosis, leading to tumor shrinkage in mouse models.
No significant off‑target toxicity was observed in wild‑type myeloma or normal tissues in preclinical studies.
The approach is potentially applicable to other RAS‑driven cancers (pancreatic, colorectal, lung).
open_questions: Will macropinocytosis‑mediated delivery be effective in heterogeneous patient tumors with subclonal RAS mutations?
What is the safety profile of nanobody‑MMAE in non‑malignant tissues that may exhibit basal macropinocytosis?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Selectivity relies on macropinocytosis; cells lacking RAS‑driven macropinocytosis are spared.

key_findings: One‑dose HPV vaccination showed durable antibody levels up to 11 years post‑vaccination with only a four‑fold reduction versus three‑dose levels.
ESCUDO randomized trial (≈20,000 girls) met co‑primary non‑inferiority endpoints for both Cervarix and Gardasil 9, demonstrating >80% efficacy for one‑dose versus two‑dose schedules.
Global HPV vaccine uptake in 2020 was only 20% overall and ~9% in low‑resource settings, but one‑dose schedules are now adopted in ~90 countries, raising one‑dose coverage to 63%.
Meta‑analyses of single‑dose trials (Kenya, Tanzania, India) confirm high efficacy against virologic and histologic endpoints across vaccine platforms.
open_questions: Efficacy of a single dose in adult women and men, and at non‑cervical sites (oropharynx, anal).
Long‑term durability beyond 20 years and correlates of protection.

key_findings: The SHIP trial enrolled 2,088 participants across 24 US sites, with 495 completing the SO1 protocol.
Self‑collected vaginal samples achieved 89.2% sensitivity for CIN 3+ (vs 96.9% for clinician samples) and 83.7% for CIN 2+ (vs 90.7%).
Positive percent agreement between self‑collection and clinician collection was 92% for overall high‑risk HPV, 94% for HPV‑16, and ~89% for other types.
The FDA granted the first pre‑market approval for a self‑collection HPV assay (BD/Waters Onclarity) based on these data.
The trial population was diverse (23.6% Hispanic, 37.6% Black) and included 42% previously vaccinated, supporting generalizability to underserved groups.
open_questions: How will the remaining sub‑protocols (Roche, Abbott) perform in terms of accuracy and regulatory approval?
What implementation strategies will maximize uptake and follow‑up in safety‑net settings?

key_findings: Mailed self‑collection kits in the PRESTESS trial doubled screening participation (47% vs 21% usual care) among under‑screened safety‑net patients.
Adding patient navigation to mailed kits further improved uptake (41% vs 21%).
Meta‑analyses show self‑sampling yields 2‑2.5‑fold higher participation compared with clinician‑collected screening in underserved populations.
Implementation context (mail, door‑to‑door, clinic integration) drives effectiveness more than the specific HPV assay used.
Cost‑effectiveness analyses indicate self‑sampling is highly sensitive to implementation design, with navigation and high return rates essential for value.
open_questions: How can door‑to‑door outreach be sustainably funded in safety‑net health systems?
What are the most effective models for ensuring timely follow‑up (colposcopy, treatment) after a positive self‑sample?

key_findings: Organoid establishment success was ~50% across 186 biopsies, with failure associated with markedly longer patient survival.
Ex vivo gemcitabine/nab‑paclitaxel sensitivity in PDOs predicted better clinical outcomes compared with FOLFIRINOX in the randomized trial.
A transcriptional oxaliplatin‑response signature derived from hypersensitive organoids stratified patients receiving FOLFIRINOX and correlated with overall survival.
Pan‑RAS inhibitor showed heterogeneous activity across KRAS‑mutant and wild‑type organoids, highlighting the need for functional testing beyond genotype.
High‑content microscopy reduced assay turnaround to <30 days while maintaining strong correlation with traditional ATP‑based readouts.
open_questions: Can the organoid establishment rate be increased to >80% to capture the most chemosensitive patient subset?
Will prospective use of the transcriptional signature alone replace the need for PDO testing in routine care?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Organoids that failed to grow were derived from less aggressive tumors, indicating that culture failure itself is a prognostic marker.
Fibroblast co‑culture increased the IC50 of the pan‑RAS inhibitor three‑fold, demonstrating microenvironment‑mediated drug resistance.

key_findings: Cell state signatures (stem‑like vs monocytic) explain response to >70% of 120 tested drugs.
Venetoclax is highly effective against stem‑like AML but ineffective against monocytic AML.
Panobinostat shows the opposite pattern, being active in differentiated AML.
Venetoclax + palbociclib demonstrates superior ex vivo activity and synergy, especially in RAS‑mutant or monocytic‑like samples.
The pharma‑type composite ex vivo signature predicts clinical response to venetoclax + HMA with near‑perfect accuracy in newly diagnosed AML.
open_questions: Can cell‑state‑guided therapy be prospectively validated in a randomized AML trial?
What additional biomarkers (e.g., protein synthesis signatures) can refine patient selection for venetoclax + CDK4/6 inhibition?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Monocytic differentiation confers resistance to BCL2 inhibition by upregulating protein synthesis pathways.
RAS mutations sensitize AML cells to the venetoclax + palbociclib combination.

key_findings: ChemoID‑guided therapy extended median OS by 4.5 months in recurrent glioblastoma (12 vs 7.5 months).
In ovarian cancer, objective response rate increased from 5% to 55% with ChemoID guidance.
Median PFS improved from 3 months to 11 months in the ChemoID arm for ovarian cancer.
A ≥50% cell‑kill threshold in both bulk and cancer stem cell compartments predicted clinical response.
The assay achieved CLIA/CAP accreditation and received FDA breakthrough device designation for brain tumors.
open_questions: Can the ChemoID platform be scaled for broader tumor types and integrated with genomic biomarkers?
What is the optimal cell‑kill cutoff for cancer stem cells to maximize clinical benefit?
readouts: flow cytometry immunophenotyping (CD44, CD24, CD117, CD184)
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Patients whose tumors showed <50% kill in cancer stem cell assays experienced progressive disease despite bulk sensitivity.
Monocytic‑like cancer stem cells persisted after many standard agents, indicating a resistant subpopulation.

key_findings: Identified 16 consensus reduced penetrance BRCA1/2 variants across Myriad and Ambry labs, with multiple families carrying the same variant but showing divergent cancer histories.
Described a family with an 84‑year‑old metastatic breast cancer patient and two unaffected BRCA2‑positive daughters, illustrating late‑onset disease despite pathogenic classification.

Showed a 61‑year‑old woman with both ER‑positive and triple‑negative breast cancers carrying a BRCA2 VUS that was classified as pathogenic by six labs and VUS by two, underscoring discordant interpretations.
Highlighted that ClinVar entries often label such variants as pathogenic but note hypomorphic potential in buried comments, leading to counseling challenges.
Emphasized that reduced penetrance variants can still warrant standard risk‑reducing interventions (e.g., breast MRI) while allowing shared decision‑making for prophylactic surgery.
open_questions: How should clinicians integrate reduced penetrance classifications into NCCN guidelines and counseling?
What standardized terminology (e.g., reduced penetrance vs. low penetrance) should be adopted across labs?

key_findings: Developed a VARcall two‑component mixture model that separates neutral from pathogenic activity distributions and flags intermediate‑activity variants as potential reduced penetrance pathogenic variants.
Demonstrated that known hypomorphic BRCA1 variants (e.g., R1699W, V1736A) fall in the intermediate activity zone and correlate with atypical family segregation patterns.

Showed that large‑scale functional screens (e.g., from Shendure and Couch labs) can identify a subset of missense variants with activity scores between clearly benign and clearly pathogenic, providing a pool of candidate reduced penetrance variants.
Proposed a calibration strategy where a few functionally validated reduced penetrance variants are used to set activity thresholds for genome‑wide classification.
open_questions: Which specific functional assays best predict clinical cancer risk for intermediate‑activity variants?
How many validated reduced penetrance variants are needed to reliably calibrate activity‑to‑risk thresholds?
readouts: linear regression of activity vs. risk

key_findings: Attenuated FAP caused by 5' APC variants can be managed using polyp burden (Spiegelman score) to dictate duodenal and colorectal surveillance intervals, avoiding premature colectomy.

A specific MSH6 missense variant present in ~4% of MSH6 carriers showed no statistically increased risk for colorectal, ovarian, or uterine cancer compared with population risk, suggesting a reduced penetrance phenotype.

Proposed extending colonoscopy intervals to the maximum guideline‑allowed three years for carriers of the low‑risk MSH6 variant and deferring prophylactic hysterectomy to age 50 or possibly omitting it.
Emphasized that gene‑specific guidelines (e.g., earlier colonoscopy for MLH1/MSH2 vs. later for PMS2) remain essential, but variant‑specific data are needed to refine recommendations.
open_questions: What is the optimal calibration method to integrate polygenic risk scores with reduced penetrance variant risk estimates?
Should prophylactic surgeries be universally recommended for reduced penetrance Lynch syndrome variants, or can they be safely omitted?

key_findings: Anti‑PD‑1 treatment induces dense collagen I/III deposition in 4T1 and Lewis lung tumors via CD8 T‑cell‑derived BMP1.
SCID mice lacking T cells do not show ECM remodeling after anti‑PD‑1, which is rescued by adoptive transfer of T cells.
BMP1 expression is up‑regulated in CD8 T cells and plasma after anti‑PD‑1 in mice and in head‑and‑neck SCC patients.
Combination of anti‑PD‑1 with the BMP1 inhibitor UK‑383367 restores tumor sensitivity and reduces ECM density.
A BMP1‑ADC (antibody‑drug conjugate delivering the BMP1 inhibitor) retards tumor growth in multiple models.
open_questions: Does BMP1 expression in CD8 T cells predict response or hyper‑progression to ICI in larger patient cohorts?
What upstream signals drive BMP1 release from activated T cells?
tumor_types: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: BMP1-mediated ECM creates a barrier that limits T‑cell infiltration and contributes to ICI resistance.

key_findings: Aged lung and liver exhibit markedly higher ARG1 expression in CD45+ myeloid cells and fibroblasts.
Recombinant ARG1 administration to young mice reactivates dormant melanoma cells and increases liver colonization.
ARG1 treatment selectively reduces NK cell infiltration and activation in metastatic sites.
ARG1 inhibition with CB‑1158 in aged mice significantly decreases liver metastasis and restores NK cell frequency and activation markers (decreased PD‑1, increased DNAM‑1).
ARG1 high expression in TCGA melanoma patients correlates with poorer overall survival and is enriched in patients >55 years.
open_questions: What upstream aging signals drive fibroblast and myeloid ARG1 up‑regulation?
Can ARG1 inhibition synergize with checkpoint blockade in aged hosts?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: ARG1-mediated arginine depletion selectively impairs NK cell cytotoxicity without affecting primary tumor growth.

key_findings: Peritoneal metastasis occurred in 70.8% of stage IV gastric cancer patients (n=3,200) and was associated with markedly poorer overall survival compared with lymph‑node‑only disease.
HER2‑negative gastric cancers showed a higher peritoneal metastasis rate (≈75%) than HER2‑positive cases (≈50%).
FGFR2 amplification was significantly enriched in peritoneal metastasis tissues versus primary tumors, suggesting a potential therapeutic target.
Spatial profiling identified four CAF subtypes (remodeling, immune‑controlling, mesothelial, stress‑related) with remodeling and immune‑controlling CAFs markedly increased in peritoneal lesions.

Peritoneal lesions exhibited higher fibroblast, endothelial, macrophage, and T‑cell infiltration but reduced T‑cell activation and granzyme expression, indicating an immunosuppressive microenvironment.
Antigen‑presentation genes (e.g., cloudin) were down‑regulated in peritoneal metastases, implying reduced efficacy of cloudin‑targeted ADCs in this compartment.
open_questions: Can CAF‑targeting agents or matrix‑modulating therapies improve drug delivery and immune infiltration in gastric peritoneal metastasis?
What is the optimal timing and modality (systemic vs intraperitoneal) for delivering FGFR2‑directed therapies?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Dense CAF‑derived extracellular matrix physically blocks immune cell contact and drug penetration, contributing to resistance.
Down‑regulation of cloudin and other ADC targets in peritoneal lesions suggests loss of target expression limits efficacy of ADCs.

key_findings: CMS4 is significantly over‑represented in colorectal peritoneal metastases compared with primary tumors and liver metastases.
Within CMS4, three molecular subgroups (RAS‑mutated mucinous, inflamed, and others) exhibit distinct RAS/TP53 mutation patterns and microenvironment compositions.
Genomic landscapes (TP53, APC, KRAS) are largely conserved between primary and peritoneal lesions, indicating polyclonal seeding rather than subclonal divergence.
CMS4 peritoneal metastases display poor prognosis (HR 0.56 vs non‑CMS4) and are less responsive to oxaliplatin‑based HIPEC, but show greater sensitivity to mitomycin C in vitro.
Targeting stromal proteins moesin or PAI‑1 with monoclonal antibodies reduced tumor burden in preclinical peritoneal models, suggesting a novel therapeutic avenue.
open_questions: Can CMS4 classification be reliably performed on limited peritoneal biopsy material to guide therapy?
Will combining stromal‑targeted agents with systemic chemotherapy improve overall survival in CMS4 patients?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Oxaliplatin‑based HIPEC shows limited efficacy in CMS4 peritoneal metastases, likely due to stromal barrier and drug penetration issues.
Poly‑clonal seeding leads to heterogeneous therapeutic vulnerabilities, reducing the effectiveness of single‑target agents.

key_findings: ≈50% of high‑grade serous ovarian cancers are HR‑deficient, identifiable by tandem‑duplication (BRCA1‑like) or interstitial deletion (BRCA2‑like) signatures.
HR‑deficient tumors up‑regulate type‑I interferon and JAK‑STAT pathways and show higher expression of antigen‑presentation machinery compared with HR‑proficient (FBI) tumors.
Clonal 6p LOH (HLA loss) is enriched in BRCA1‑like HRD‑DUP tumors and correlates with increased T‑cell dysfunction.
All tumors contain genome‑doubled cells; genome doubling drives extensive cell‑specific aneuploidies and micronucleus formation.
cGAS‑positive micronuclei are abundant in diploid cells but inversely correlated with cGAS‑STING signaling in genome‑doubled cells, suggesting adaptive suppression of innate immunity.
Multiplex IF reveals significantly more PD‑1/PD‑L1 proximal interactions in HRD‑DUP tumors, indicating a distinct immune checkpoint landscape.
open_questions: What determines the selective suppression of cGAS‑STING signaling after genome doubling?
Can HLA loss be reversed or compensated to restore immunogenicity in HR‑deficient lesions?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Clonal HLA loss (6p LOH) provides a mechanism of immune escape in HR‑deficient peritoneal lesions.
Genome doubling suppresses cGAS‑STING signaling, allowing cells with high chromosomal instability to survive.

key_findings: DESI imaging identified glutamine depletion and high SLC7A5 expression in APC KRAS colorectal tumor epithelium versus normal tissue.
Genetic deletion of SLC7A5 in APC KRAS mouse models caused accumulation of glutamine, glutamate, and alanine and resulted in the strongest tumor suppression observed in colorectal cancer models.
SLC7A5 loss reduced phospho‑S6 signaling, sensitizing tumors to rapamycin and MAPK inhibition.

KRAS G12D inhibitor treatment eliminated phospho‑ERK signaling but did not eradicate tumors; however, it rapidly altered neutrophil, lymphocyte, and monocyte counts and remodeled macrophage and CAF spatial organization.
In pancreatic KPC mice, SLC7A5 deletion slowed tumor genesis, shifted tumors toward a more homogeneous squamous subtype, and increased immune infiltration.
open_questions: What is the precise mechanism by which SLC7A5 deletion remodels the tumor vasculature and immune cell infiltration?
Can the metabolic phenotypes observed in organoid models be fully recapitulated in patient-derived xenografts?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: KRAS inhibitors showed poor efficacy in colorectal models despite target inhibition, indicating intrinsic resistance mechanisms linked to metabolic context.

key_findings: Chronic TCR stimulation plus hypoxia uniquely upregulates SLC25A1 in terminally exhausted CD8+ T cells.
SLC25A1 mediates export of mitochondrial citrate, leading to cytosolic acetyl‑CoA accumulation, lipid droplet formation, and widespread protein acetylation.
CRISPR knockout of SLC25A1 increases mitochondrial respiratory capacity, glycolysis, and reduces lipid droplet burden in exhausted T cells.
SLC25A1‑deficient T cells exhibit lower PD‑1, TIM‑3, and CD39 expression, retain IL‑2 production, and display superior polyfunctionality in tumors.
Adoptive transfer of SLC25A1‑KO T cells yields greater tumor regression and synergizes with anti‑PD‑1 therapy in mouse models.
open_questions: Does SLC25A1 inhibition affect PD‑L1 expression on tumor cells via increased IFN‑γ production?
What is the impact of SLC25A1 loss on myeloid cell populations within the TME?
Can selective SLC25A1 inhibitors be developed with acceptable safety for clinical use?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: SLC25A1 expression persists despite PD‑1 blockade, suggesting a resistance mechanism independent of checkpoint inhibition.

key_findings: NK cells cultured in lipid‑rich APEL media acquire higher mitochondrial mass, elongated morphology, and increased spare respiratory capacity versus standard media.
CIS knockout NK cells display upregulated mTOR signaling, glycolysis, and improved survival in aggressive Raji lymphoma mouse models.
TGFBR2‑KO CD70 CAR NK cells demonstrate superior anti‑AML activity in preclinical models and have entered a Phase 1/2 trial (NCT‑pending).
E4ORF1 overexpression in NK cells enhances glycolysis, OXPHOS, fatty‑acid oxidation, and glutaminolysis, leading to robust killing of multiple solid tumor lines even under nutrient starvation.
AMPK activity is required for the E4ORF1‑mediated metabolic boost; inhibition of AMPK abrogates the enhanced cytotoxic phenotype.
open_questions: Which specific media components in APEL drive the observed metabolic reprogramming?
Can E4ORF1 overexpression be safely applied to CAR T cells without oncogenic transformation?
How does metabolic reprogramming affect NK cell receptor repertoire and ADCC function?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: TGF‑β signaling in the TME suppresses NK cell metabolism; TGFBR2 knockout overcomes this resistance.

patent_or_ip_hints: CRISPR‑mediated TGFBR2 knockout NK cell IP filing 2023

key_findings: Overall response rate of 50% and disease control rate of 97% in a high‑risk PD‑L1 negative NSCLC cohort (n=39).
In STK11/KEAP1/SMARCA4 altered subgroup, ORR increased to 61% with 100% disease control.
STK‑12 induced robust expansion of 4‑1BB+ CD8 T cells and >10‑fold clonal expansion of pre‑existing TCR clones.
Minimal classic IL‑2 toxicities observed; most common AE was reversible maculopapular rash in ~50% of patients.
open_questions: Does STK‑12 generate de‑novo neoantigen responses or rely solely on pre‑existing clones?
What is the optimal dosing schedule to maximize T‑cell expansion while minimizing rash?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: STK‑12 did not expand NK cells or Tregs, preserving a favorable safety profile.
Efficacy appears limited in patients lacking pre‑existing antigen‑experienced T cells, suggesting dependence on recall responses.

key_findings: TLS‑associated immune module (Tfh‑like CD4+, LAMB3+ mature DCs, cycling B cells) is enriched in pretreatment tumors of patients achieving PCR.
Spatial analysis shows co‑localization of these cell types within 20‑µm niches, defining TLS structures.
Higher TLS niche fraction predicts PCR (p<0.01) and correlates with increased intratumoral CD8+ T cells post‑treatment.
CellChat indicates CD4+ Tfh cells activate B cells via IL‑2, CD40, and ICAM pathways within TLS.
open_questions: Do post‑treatment biopsies show expansion of TLS structures, confirming dynamic induction?
Can specific TLS‑associated taxa be modulated to further improve response?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: High‑endothelial venules and specific dendritic subsets (XCR1+) were not fully characterized, suggesting heterogeneity in TLS composition.

key_findings: SMG1 inhibition increased PD‑1+ CD8 T‑cell activation in ex vivo tumor fragments without affecting adjacent normal tissue.
In Lewis lung carcinoma, SMG1 inhibitor monotherapy matched anti‑PD‑1 efficacy; combination yielded superior tumor control.
Immunopeptidomics identified six neoantigen peptides up‑regulated only after NMD inhibition; four were immunogenic in vitro.
MHC‑I blockade abolished T‑cell activation induced by SMG1 inhibition, confirming antigen‑dependent mechanism.
open_questions: Will chronic SMG1 inhibition lead to autoimmunity due to presentation of self‑derived PTC peptides?
What is the optimal dosing schedule to maximize tumor antigen presentation while minimizing potential off‑target effects?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: SMG1 inhibition showed minimal toxicity in normal tissue ex vivo and no significant weight loss in mice, suggesting tumor selectivity.

key_findings: High‑fiber diet did not alter overall alpha/beta diversity but increased patient‑specific enrichment of known response‑associated taxa.
Serum bile acid profiling showed a significant decrease in secondary/primary bile acid ratio in the high‑fiber arm.
Classical monocyte immunosuppressive cluster decreased over time only in high‑fiber patients.
Digital spatial profiling revealed greater CD8+ T‑cell and cytotoxic lymphocyte density post‑intervention in responders receiving high‑fiber diet.
open_questions: Would isolated fermentable fiber supplements recapitulate the benefits of whole‑food high‑fiber diets?
What are the long‑term durability of immune benefits after cessation of the diet?

key_findings: Identified a disease‑specific POLR6+ CD4+ PD‑1+ TH17‑like cell cluster producing IL‑17, MCP1, CCL11, granzyme B, etc.
Higher POLR6+ cell burden correlated with greater PET‑measured neuroinflammation and worse cognitive scores.
Clonal T‑cell expansions persisted up to 12 months, indicating ongoing antigen‑driven response, with NMDA‑R1 as a dominant neuroantigen.
Retrospective anti‑IL‑17A treatment was associated with reduced neuroinflammation and improved neurologic function without affecting cancer outcomes.
open_questions: What is the source of NMDA‑R1 antigen driving TH17 expansion?
Can prospective anti‑IL‑17A therapy prevent IRAE‑CNS when given prophylactically?

key_findings: NAT10 is overexpressed in MSS CRC and predicts worse overall survival.
NAT10 knockout increases CD8+ T‑cell infiltration and tumor regression in mice.
Combination of NAT10 inhibition with anti‑PD‑1 yields complete tumor regression in 80% of mice.
MYC transcriptionally up‑regulates NAT10; NAT10‑mediated ac4C stabilizes MYC mRNA, forming a feed‑forward loop.
open_questions: Will NAT10 inhibition synergize with other immunotherapies (e.g., CTLA‑4 blockade) in MSS CRC?
What biomarkers best predict response to NAT10‑targeted therapy in patients?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: NAT10 inhibition may affect normal cells due to global RNA modification, but preclinical data show limited toxicity.

key_findings: Versican overexpression in MC38 tumors induced immunotriad formation and cured >70% of mice with anti‑PD‑1 alone.
In VCAN‑high LSC tumors, versican plus dual checkpoint blockade (PD‑1 + CTLA‑4) was required for tumor control.
Exogenous versican delivered via LNP mRNA or recombinant protein showed monotherapy activity in VCAN‑low models and synergized with ICB.
Efficacy depended on cDC1 dendritic cells and CD8+ T cells; depletion abrogated therapeutic benefit.
open_questions: Which tumor types beyond CRC and lung cancer exhibit VCAN proteolysis deficiency and could benefit from versican therapy?
What is the optimal dosing schedule for versican protein versus mRNA delivery to maximize immune activation while minimizing potential pro‑metastatic effects?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Potential concern that matrix remodeling could facilitate tumor cell dissemination; however, versican fragments appear to act primarily on immune cell recruitment rather than tumor invasion.

key_findings: Among ~7,000 HIV+ lung cancer patients, 75% were diagnosed at metastatic stage.
People with HIV had a 15% increased risk of metastatic lung cancer diagnosis compared to non‑HIV patients.
Socioeconomic factors (ZIP‑code education, income, care location) predicted higher probability of metastatic diagnosis.
The R01 aims to (1) describe LDCT screening patterns, (2) estimate direct/indirect effects of social determinants, and (3) explore patient decision‑making via qualitative interviews.
Implementation planning group generated 36 potential strategies, refined to top five themes (patient education/communication, clinical flow).
Top four selected strategies: identify/prep champions; develop low‑literacy educational materials; organize quality monitoring (UDS metrics); conduct implementation meetings.
Pilot clinic A achieved 77% screening among diabetic patients (higher among uncontrolled diabetes), using champion‑driven Cologuard outreach.
Pilot clinic B, with lower baseline screening (28%), improved to 60% using adapted postcards, QR‑code videos, and staff training.
Uncontrolled diabetes patients comprised the largest unscreened subgroup in both clinics.
After 12‑month implementation, HPV vaccine initiation increased significantly at three pilot clinics, driven by higher uptake at ages 9‑10.
18‑month follow‑up showed sustained provider discussion of vaccination at age 9 (88% of staff) and increased confidence addressing parental hesitancy (69%).
CSAT scores indicated staff found the strategies easy to use, integrable into workflow, and clinically meaningful (median 5‑7/7).
Turnover of clinic staff remained a major barrier to sustainment; half of staff changed within 24 months.
Scale‑out to AltaMed, Chinatown Service Center, and Riverside San Bernardino IHS required adaptation of training modality (in‑person, virtual, hybrid) and cultural tailoring of materials.
readouts: surveys of clinic staff and providers
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: High staff turnover limits long‑term maintenance of implementation gains.

key_findings: Developed a targeted-exome assay to detect the colibactin SBS88 signature in >80,000 clinical tumors, finding enrichment in colorectal, esophageal, bladder, and head/neck cancers.
Colibactin signature-positive tumors occur in significantly younger patients and are more often located in the rectosigmoid region.
Identified a specific APC splice-site mutation occurring in the AT-rich colibactin context, enriched in young-onset colorectal cancers, suggesting colibactin-driven initiation.
Inverted-polarity organoid model exposed to pks+ E. coli recapitulated colibactin mutational signatures and induced upregulation of LGR5 and ASCL2 stem cell markers.
pks+ E. coli exposure increased functional stem cell capacity (organoid formation) and proliferation compared to Δpks controls.
Thermal proteomics and ATAC-seq revealed colibactin-induced repression of AT-rich transcription factor motifs, notably CDX2, leading to loss of differentiation and promotion of stemness.
Young colon organoids showed greater regenerative response to colibactin-induced injury than aged organoids, linking age-dependent stem cell capacity to early-onset tumorigenesis.
open_questions: Does inhibition of colibactin production or colonization by pks+ E. coli prevent early-onset colorectal cancer in high-risk populations?
Can therapeutic restoration of CDX2 activity counteract colibactin-induced stemness and tumor initiation?
What host factors (diet, microbiome composition) modulate susceptibility to colibactin-mediated mutagenesis?

key_findings: A universal rate‑versus‑Dmax relationship was observed across diverse degraders (BRD9, EP300, CBP) regardless of target or cell line.
The rate inflection point (0.7–1.8) predicts ≥85–90% Dmax; compounds below this "cliff" show target recovery.
AUC of rate‑versus‑concentration curves distinguishes compounds with identical DC50 but up to five‑fold differences in maximal degradation rate.
Faster degraders exhibit higher ubiquitination levels and form more stable ternary complexes with slower koff rates measured by SPR.
In vivo PK/PD mapping of CBP degraders demonstrates that dosing at Cmax and trough samples the maximal degradation rate, leading to robust target loss in mouse models.
83% overall response rate in a heavily pre‑treated CLL population, including patients who progressed on the approved BTK inhibitor pirtobrutinib.
Median duration of response reached 20 months, exceeding the ~12‑month DOR reported for the best current inhibitor.
Degrader retained activity against all known BTK resistance mutations, whereas inhibitors showed gaps in coverage.
Higher dose (600 mg) improved progression‑free survival without increasing adverse‑event frequency, indicating a wide therapeutic index.
Comprehensive proteomics showed BTK as one of the top‑down‑regulated proteins with minimal off‑target degradation.
No QT prolongation observed in healthy volunteers or patients, differentiating this degrader from earlier molecules.
open_questions: What therapeutic strategies can overcome the emergent A428D BTK mutation that blocks degrader binding?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: A novel BTK A428D mutation abolishes binding of both inhibitors and degraders, representing a potential resistance mechanism.

key_findings: High‑throughput screen of 170,000 compounds identified 13 hits; lead chemotype 7907 degraded both AR and ARV7 via proteasome.
Medicinal chemistry optimization yielded analogs 15 and 64 with sub‑micromolar EC50s and rapid (≤4 h) degradation of both proteins.
Compound 15 suppressed AR‑driven transcription in 22RV1 cells, outperforming enzalutamide and ARV110 in RNA‑seq AR‑score analysis.
In vivo, oral dosing of compounds 15 and 64 markedly inhibited growth of ARV7‑positive 22RV1 xenografts, achieving greater tumor regression than enzalutamide or ARV110.
Mechanistic studies mapped activity to the AR N‑terminal TAL1 and AF1 subdomains; degradation required Cullin‑RING ligase activity (blocked by MLN4924) and was partially reversed by DDB1 knockout.
Global proteomics showed AR and ARV7 among the top‑down‑regulated proteins with minimal off‑target effects; compounds were well tolerated with no weight loss.
open_questions: What is the precise E3 ligase complex (beyond DDB1) mediating degradation?
Can off‑target degradation be further minimized in primary prostate cells?

key_findings: SPEN truncation co-occurs with Notch2 truncation in BN2 DLBCLs and predicts inferior survival in a 4,500-patient cohort.
Female BN2 DLBCL mice develop X‑chromosome hypomethylation, increased TLR7 expression, and are more sensitive to IRAK inhibitors than males.
African ancestry DLBCLs harbor frequent ATM, MGA, and SETD2 mutations (>50%) and show elevated senescence (GLB1) and exhausted CD4 T‑cell infiltrates.
SETD2‑heterozygous DLBCL cells are hypersensitive to a clinical SETD2 inhibitor, offering a potential ancestry‑specific therapy.
IRAK inhibition reduces tumor growth in female BN2 DLBCL xenografts, supporting a sex‑specific precision therapy approach.
open_questions: What molecular mechanisms link X‑chromosome hypomethylation to TLR7 overexpression in female BN2 DLBCLs?
Can GDF15 modulation improve outcomes in the described DLBCL subtypes?
Are there additional sex‑specific vulnerabilities beyond IRAK signaling?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Female BN2 DLBCLs display selective IRAK inhibitor sensitivity due to X‑linked TLR7 overexpression.
SETD2‑mutant African ancestry DLBCLs are resistant to standard therapies but vulnerable to SETD2 inhibition.

key_findings: Older breast cancer patients exhibit distinct molecular landscapes: ER+ tumors lose immune/metabolic activity, while TNBCs gain an inflamed EMT phenotype.
In mouse models, aged mice show slower NET1 tumor growth but reduced response to paclitaxel + anti‑PD‑L1, despite higher CD8 infiltration and Treg expansion.
Barcode 25 subclone is enriched by age and paclitaxel, displays intrinsic paclitaxel resistance, and can be eliminated by HDAC inhibition.
Panobinostat combined with anti‑PD‑L1 dramatically extends survival in aged mice, whereas the same combination is less effective in young mice without chemotherapy.
open_questions: What mechanisms drive the EMT and immune exhaustion programs uniquely in aged TNBC?
Can selective HDAC isoform inhibitors improve efficacy while reducing toxicity in older patients?
How does the middle‑aged cohort (40‑60 yr) molecularly differ from young and old groups?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Barcode 25 subclone confers paclitaxel resistance and limits combination efficacy in aged mice.
HDAC inhibitors selectively target the age‑enriched resistant clone.

key_findings: Aged mice develop larger orthotopic KPC tumors and exhibit markedly reduced CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration compared with young mice.
Circulating GDF15 is low in young mice but rises sharply in aged mice and further increases after tumor implantation.
Genetic or antibody‑mediated GDF15 neutralization halves tumor size in aged mice and restores CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration; effect is lost after T‑cell depletion.
GDF15 neutralization enhances KRAS mutant peptide vaccine‑induced IFN‑γ T‑cell responses in aged mice.
In a PDAC GVAX trial, high tumor GDF15 expression correlates with ~2‑fold worse overall survival, independent of age.
open_questions: What is the precise receptor and downstream signaling pathway by which GDF15 suppresses CD8⁺ T‑cell trafficking in PDAC?
Can GDF15 neutralization improve responses to standard chemotherapy or other immunotherapies in human PDAC trials?
Are there biomarkers beyond circulating GDF15 that predict benefit from GDF15‑targeted therapy?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: GDF15‑mediated immunosuppression is age‑specific; young mice show minimal response to GDF15 blockade.
Tumor‑intrinsic KRAS vaccine efficacy is limited in aged hosts unless GDF15 is neutralized.

key_findings: High-fat diet mice develop increased breast cancer liver metastasis compared to control diet.
RAG2 gamma knockout mice show increased liver and lung tumor burden, implicating innate lymphocytes in surveillance.
Selective depletion of conventional NK cells increases lung but not liver metastasis, indicating liver ILC1s are essential for hepatic surveillance.
ILC1s mediate tumor killing via TRAIL binding to DR5 on cancer cells; DR5 loss increases liver metastasis.
GLP-1 receptor agonist restores hepatic ILC1 numbers in steatotic mice and reduces liver tumor burden.
open_questions: What upstream signals regulate ILC1 activation in the liver microenvironment?
Can GLP-1 agonist synergize with checkpoint blockade in metastatic breast cancer?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: DR5 loss in tumor cells enables escape from ILC1-mediated killing.

key_findings: PAD4 knockout mice show decreased tumor necrosis and fewer liver metastases compared to wild-type.
Disulfiram treatment reduces NETs, necrosis, and liver metastasis burden in AKPS organoid mice.
NET inhibition combined with FOLFOX chemotherapy further decreases liver metastasis compared to chemotherapy alone.
Necrotic tumor regions exhibit higher EMT markers (vimentin, SNAI1) and inflammatory pathways.
Mice with NET inhibition display increased neutrophil activation markers (citH3) reduction.
open_questions: What upstream signals trigger NET release in colorectal tumors?
Can NET inhibition improve response to immunotherapy in CRC?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Disulfiram is a non-specific aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibitor, raising potential off-target concerns.

key_findings: ODC1-deficient tumor debris is less efficiently taken up by dendritic cells in vitro and in vivo.
Blocking polyamine transport (AMTX) impairs dendritic cell uptake of tumor debris.
