Polyamine deficiency reduces RAC1 expression and activation in dendritic cells.
Inhibition of NPC1 or statin treatment diminishes CCR7 and other maturation markers on dendritic cells.
AXL knockout dendritic cells accumulate more cholesterol, lipid nanodomains, and display heightened maturation and improved tumor control.
open_questions: Can pharmacologic modulation of polyamine transport improve dendritic cell vaccines in patients?
What is the impact of systemic statin use on dendritic cell function in cancer patients?

key_findings: IL1β pathway activity rises from normal to pre‑cancer to invasive adenocarcinoma in both human and mouse samples.
Anti‑IL1β antibody suppresses tumor growth when given at pre‑cancer stage but not at advanced stage in two mouse models.
Anti‑IL1β treatment paradoxically increases IL1β plasma levels in mice and humans.
Spatial analysis shows pre‑cancer blockade reduces IL1R1‑positive epithelial cells within the IL1β network, whereas advanced stage blockade reduces IL1R1‑positive fibroblasts.
Location‑aware cell‑cell interaction analysis reveals that IL1β‑IL1R1 contacts are disrupted in pre‑cancer but persist in advanced disease.
open_questions: Which fibroblast subtypes sustain IL1β signaling in advanced NSCLC?
Can simultaneous targeting of IL1β and fibroblast pathways improve outcomes in late‑stage patients?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Advanced tumors retain fibroblast‑driven IL1β signaling, providing a resistance mechanism to IL1β blockade.

key_findings: Antibiotic‑induced gut dysbiosis accelerates death of mice after tail‑vein breast cancer cell injection.
Lung mast cell density inversely correlates with survival in dysbiotic mice.
Ketotifen (mast cell stabilizer) improves survival of dysbiotic mice, implicating mast cells in metastasis promotion.
Single‑cell RNA‑seq reveals dysbiotic lung mast cells upregulate IL‑6 and degranulation genes.
Fibroblasts and endothelial cells in dysbiotic lungs show STAT3‑driven fibrotic and angiogenic transcriptional programs.
Macrophages shift toward M2 phenotype with increased CCL2 and MMP‑related genes in dysbiotic lungs.
open_questions: Do primary bile acids mediate the gut‑lung signaling that activates mast cells?
Does lung microbiome alteration contribute independently to the pro‑metastatic niche?

key_findings: Systemic IFN‑γ neutralization increases tumor number and burden in liver metastasis model.
Myeloid‑specific IFNγR2 KO mice exhibit larger tumor burden and higher TAM numbers.
KO TAMs show decreased CD80/CD86/MHC‑II and increased ARG1/CD206/SPP1 expression.
T‑cell proliferation (Ki67) and cytokine production (IFN‑γ, TNF‑α) are reduced in KO mice.
Bulk RNA‑seq reveals down‑regulation of IFN‑γ response and up‑regulation of fibrosis pathways in KO tumors.
Single‑cell RNA‑seq identifies expansion of SPP1‑high macrophages with ECM and TGF‑β signatures in KO.
open_questions: Do resident Kupffer cells versus monocyte‑derived macrophages differ in IFN‑γ responsiveness?
Can exogenous low‑dose IFN‑γ rescue the fibrotic phenotype without promoting tumor immune evasion?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Loss of IFN‑γ signaling shifts macrophages toward a pro‑fibrotic, immunosuppressive phenotype.

key_findings: uPAR is co‑expressed on tumor cells, CAFs, and myeloid suppressor cells in >10 solid tumor types.
Single dose of uPAR‑CAR T yields durable tumor regression and protects against rechallenge in multiple xenograft models.
Cisplatin treatment up‑regulates uPAR on ovarian cancer cells, sensitizing them to uPAR‑CAR T killing.
uPAR‑CAR T reduces collagen deposition and fibrosis, leading to increased CAR T cell infiltration.
In humanized mice, uPAR‑CAR T shows antitumor activity without significant depletion of myeloid or granulocyte compartments.
open_questions: Can uPAR‑CAR T be combined with checkpoint blockade to further boost antitumor immunity?
What is the long‑term impact on normal monocyte populations and infection risk?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Potential on‑target off‑tumor effects on monocytes due to uPAR expression.

key_findings: Audited 23,000 street‑view locations with standardized protocol achieving high kappa agreement, demonstrating reliable measurement of physical disorder.
Internal consistency analysis (Cronbach's alpha) justified collapsing multiple disorder items into a single composite disinvestment score.
Spatial kriging based on the fitted semivariogram provided continuous disinvestment estimates for cohort participants lacking exact address‑level data.
In the breast cancer cohort, each unit increase in the disinvestment score was associated with reduced survival time for stage 2 and stage 3 patients in accelerated failure‑time models.
The methodology enables rapid, reproducible, and scalable exposure assessment for built‑environment research across large urban areas.
open_questions: How can temporal variation in street‑view imagery be incorporated to capture changes in neighborhood disorder over the life‑course?
What is the optimal spatial scale (parcel vs. census tract) for linking disinvestment scores to individual health outcomes?

key_findings: Identified multiple census‑tract clusters in Pennsylvania with significantly higher lung cancer incidence after age, sex, and race adjustment.

In multivariate models, smoking prevalence, ambient air‑pollution levels, traffic density, and proportion of old housing (asbestos proxy) were each significantly associated with cluster status (p<0.05).
Philadelphia‑specific analysis revealed high‑mortality neighborhoods with greater tobacco outlet density and elevated environmental exposures.

Neighborhood‑wide association study of >14,000 Census variables pinpointed five SSDOH factors (e.g., public‑transport use, housing disinvestment) linked to aggressive prostate cancer in Black men and 17 factors in White men.
Combining three top SSDOH variables into an exposure score markedly improved prostate cancer risk prediction beyond PSA alone (probability ≈30% vs 8% for high vs low exposure scores).
Community‑outreach pilots were launched in identified high‑burden areas, including smoking‑cessation programs and air‑quality monitoring collaborations.
open_questions: How can longitudinal residential histories be incorporated to capture cumulative SSDOH exposure over the cancer latency period?
What is the optimal spatial resolution (ZIP code vs. census tract vs. block group) for linking SSDOH variables to molecular biomarkers such as epigenetic age acceleration?

key_findings: EGFR‑directed siRNA achieved ~90% tumor cell uptake after 2 h in xenograft mice.
Selective KRAS G12V silencing at RNA and protein levels with no effect on wild‑type KRAS.
Single‑agent EFTX G12V induced significant tumor growth control and complete responses in KRAS G12V lung (H727) and colon models.
Sustained tumor tissue accumulation and KRAS protein knockdown observed up to 96 h after dosing.
Immunocompetent MPK195 model showed comparable anti‑tumor efficacy and robust CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration.
open_questions: Can the EGFR‑targeted siRNA platform be adapted for other KRAS mutants (e.g., G12C, G12D)?
What is the therapeutic window in larger animal models and humans?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Selectivity for KRAS G12V over wild‑type KRAS minimizes on‑target toxicity in normal tissues.
Kidney shows highest off‑target delivery but no KRAS inhibition observed.

key_findings: ORC1A is up‑regulated in KRAS‑mutant CRC and induced after KRAS inhibitor treatment.
Combining olaparib with KRAS inhibitors reduces KRAS inhibitor IC50 by ~10‑fold in SLIC14‑63 cells.
Synergy is driven by marked down‑regulation of MCL1 via GSK3β‑mediated proteasomal degradation.
MCL1 knockdown or pharmacologic inhibition phenocopies ORC1A inhibition, confirming MCL1 as functional driver.
Dual inhibition leads to robust tumor regression in KRAS G12C CRC PDX models without overt toxicity.
open_questions: Will ORC1A inhibition sensitize KRAS G12D or G13D CRC models similarly?
Can the combination be tolerated in vivo with standard chemotherapy?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: RESTORATION of MCL1 levels by proteasome inhibition rescues viability, confirming on‑target mechanism.
Potential for resistance via MCL1 stabilization.

key_findings: Motif‑based scoring accurately identified BRAF/ERK activity dynamics after BRAF inhibitor treatment in melanoma cells.
DNA‑damage kinases (ATM/ATR) were temporally resolved after UV exposure, matching known kinetics.
The platform can predict upstream kinases for >95% of phosphosites, vastly expanding annotation beyond PhosphoSitePlus.
Open‑source Python package and web interface released for community use.
open_questions: How to integrate quantitative phosphosite intensity with motif scores for improved activity inference?
Can the library predict off‑target kinase inhibition of novel inhibitors?

key_findings: ImmunoTar pipeline identified CHRNA3/B4 as a neuroblastoma‑specific surface complex.
DISCO binders specifically bind cells co‑expressing CHRNA3 and CHRNB4, not single‑positive or negative cells.
DISCO CAR T cells mediate potent in‑vitro killing of CHRNA3/B4‑positive neuroblastoma lines.
Single and double‑dose DISCO CAR T treatment induced tumor regression and prolonged survival in neuroblastoma PDX models.
Intravitreal DISCO CAR T delivery eradicated retinoblastoma tumors in mice, preserving ocular integrity.
open_questions: Will CHRNA3/B4 expression be stable in patients after CAR T pressure?
Can DISCO CAR be combined with checkpoint blockade for synergistic effect?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Antigen loss observed in low‑expressing tumor variants; double dosing improved control.
No off‑target activity detected on normal tissues with low CHRNA3/B4 expression.

key_findings: CRISPRa screen identified REST as a top chemoresistance hit in SCLC PDX.
REST overexpression in PDX abrogates cisplatin/topotecan‑induced tumor regression.
REST drives Notch activation (↑ NICD1/3, Hes1) which mediates resistance; gamma‑secretase inhibition restores chemosensitivity.
REST‑high tumors display increased MHC‑I, CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration, and respond to anti‑PD‑1 therapy.
Single‑cell analysis revealed a REST‑associated tumor cell cluster enriched for Notch signaling and CX3CL1 expression.
open_questions: Will combined Notch inhibition and PD‑1 blockade provide additive benefit?
What proportion of patient SCLC tumors exhibit REST‑high phenotype?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: REST expression defines a chemoresistant, immunogenic SCLC subset.
Gamma‑secretase inhibition reverses chemoresistance but not yet tested with immunotherapy.

key_findings: Aged skin fibroblast conditioned media sensitizes melanoma cells to GPX4 inhibition.
WNT5A expression inversely correlates with MITF and directly with GPX4 down‑regulation.
Aged mice (24 mo) exhibit higher tumor lipid peroxidation and respond to IKE with tumor growth suppression.
Lipid‑peroxidation inhibitor rescues IKE efficacy, confirming ferroptosis as the mechanism.
WNT5A spatially co‑localizes with 4‑HNE in both mouse and human melanoma samples.
open_questions: Will systemic ferroptosis induction cause toxicity in aged patients?
Can WNT5A inhibition reverse ferroptosis sensitivity?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Normal aged tissues may have increased ferroptosis susceptibility; tumor‑specific WNT5A‑driven GPX4 loss provides therapeutic window.

key_findings: Fluorine-18 labeled PSMA small molecule provides high-contrast PET images of tiny prostate lesions, including bone marrow metastases.
PSMA-617 radioligand therapy yields PSA 50% declines superior to cabazitaxel with milder side effects.
Alpha-emitting astatine-labeled PSMA agents enable intracellular targeting and potential precision dosimetry.
FAP-targeted radiopharmaceutical detected pancreatic cancer lesions missed by CT/MR, suggesting utility for hard-to-image tumors.
open_questions: How to optimize patient dosing and precision dosimetry for alpha emitters?
What strategies will overcome tumor heterogeneity and PSMA-negative clones?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Heterogeneous PSMA expression can lead to residual disease; combination with stereotactic radiation (LUNAR trial) aims to address residual clones.

key_findings: ZW291 achieved >50% ORR in FRα‑positive patients despite using a non‑maximally potent Top1 payload.
Dual‑binding (avidity) approach enabled selective killing of cells with >10,000 receptors/cell, improving therapeutic window.
Pan‑RAS ADC showed tumor regression at 1 mg/kg in CDX models with sustained target inhibition for 14 days, while sparing normal tissue.

Linker stability critically influences ADC PK: moderate‑stable linkers can still yield long half‑life (e.g., T‑DXd), whereas unstable linkers produce rapid payload release (e.g., sacituzumab govitecan).
Bispecific ADCs (e.g., EGFR/HER3) demonstrate activity independent of single‑target expression, suggesting broader applicability.
open_questions: What is the optimal balance of payload potency vs. linker stability for different tumor types?
Can truly tumor‑specific cleavable linkers be engineered to further improve safety?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Target downregulation (e.g., HER2 after T‑DXd) can reduce efficacy; bispecific formats aim to mitigate this.
Efflux pump overexpression (ABCC1, Pgp) correlates with reduced ADC benefit in some trials.

key_findings: Talatamab achieved median OS 13.6 mo vs 8.3 mo chemotherapy in SCLC (Phase 3).
Frontline talatamab + atezolizumab increased median OS to 25.3 mo, maintaining manageable safety.
Zalyuritamic’s bivalent STIP1 binding yields activity only on cells with >10 k receptors/cell, sparing normal tissue.
AMG 305 shows potent killing of CDH3/mesothelin double‑positive cells with minimal toxicity in preclinical models.
open_questions: Can dual‑target logic gating be generalized to other antigen pairs?
What is the optimal CD3 affinity to balance potency and cytokine toxicity?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Off‑tumor CD3 engagement can cause cytokine release syndrome; silent Fc reduces FcγR binding.
Target heterogeneity addressed by dual‑target logic gating to limit activity on single‑positive normal cells.

key_findings: TIL therapy improved PFS and ORR versus ipilimumab in PD‑1‑refractory melanoma (HR significant).
Responders harbored abundant CD25+ tumor‑reactive CD8 TILs with IL‑2/STAT5 signaling signatures.
Dropout screens revealed responders recognized more neoantigens and tumor‑associated antigens, while non‑responders showed viral antigen bystander activity.
In real‑world data (n≈100), anti‑PD‑1 pretreated patients achieved 45% ORR, comparable to trial results; prior ipilimumab+nivolumab patients had lower ORR (30%).
open_questions: Can engineered TILs (e.g., TCR‑modified) overcome the lack of tumor‑reactive clones in non‑responders?
What biomarkers best predict durable expansion of tumor‑reactive TILs post‑infusion?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Non‑responders lacked sufficient tumor‑reactive CD8 clones or had highly dysfunctional phenotypes, limiting expansion.
High LDH and prior combination checkpoint therapy associated with poorer outcomes.

key_findings: AEON achieved an average one‑vs‑rest AUROC of 0.996 across 124 tumor subtypes in the internal MSK test set.
Multimodal integration of AEON with the GDENS genomic classifier improved performance in both primary and metastatic validation cohorts.
Paladin correctly identified 9 of 11 ovarian granulosa cell tumors and outperformed DeepHistology on most molecular alteration predictions.
Only ~4% of examined molecular alterations showed a strong phenotype‑genotype signal on H&E, confirming limited but actionable predictive value.
Digital pathology aided variant‑of‑unknown‑significance annotation, low‑purity sample inference, and phenocopy detection.
open_questions: Can allele‑specific effects of mutations be resolved by the current models?
How can the approach be extended to rare tumor subtypes with limited image data?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Most molecular alterations lacked a detectable histologic phenotype, limiting the utility of H&E‑based prediction for many targets.

key_findings: Preliminary cohort of 19 GBM patients shows that short‑recurrence tumors exhibit disrupted tissue architecture and necrosis, whereas long‑recurrence tumors retain normal segmentation.
UniHeal embeddings cluster tiles into biologically meaningful groups (e.g., necrotic vs. vascular regions).
Spatial alignment of Xenium and Codex data reveals that longer recurrence is associated with enhanced immune activity, while short recurrence shows immunosuppressive signatures.
A K‑means spatial domain analysis identified an oligodendrocyte‑enriched niche (cluster 8) with increased immune engagement in long‑recurrence tumors.
open_questions: Will the model generalize to larger, multi‑institutional GBM cohorts?
How robust is the approach to varying adjuvant therapies (e.g., PD‑1 inhibition)?

key_findings: SP1‑macrophage expansion is associated with lymph‑node and bone metastasis and predicts worse overall survival.
mCAF enrichment co‑localizes with SP1‑macrophage in a stromal niche (CN7) linked to poor outcomes.
Anti‑SP1 treatment in bone‑metastasis mouse models reduced tumor burden, pain, and prolonged survival.
NEPC emergence aligns with specific epithelial lineage‑positive states and distinct transcription factor programs.
open_questions: Can SP1‑targeted therapy be safely combined with checkpoint inhibition?
What are the mechanisms underlying SP1‑macrophage recruitment to bone metastases?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: SP1‑macrophage mediates TGF‑β–driven immunosuppression, representing a selective vulnerability.

key_findings: High regulatory disruption scores are associated with significantly worse progression‑free survival across TCGA pan‑cancer cohorts.
Severity of regulatory impact, not the number of regulatory variants, drives the prognostic signal.
Clonal versus subclonal disruption severity provides complementary prognostic information.
Six patient clusters based on disruption profiles show distinct pathway enrichments (e.g., immune vs. cell‑cycle).
open_questions: How do regulatory disruption scores integrate with coding‑mutation drivers for therapy selection?
Can the approach be adapted to rare pediatric cancers with limited variant data?

key_findings: Mesenchymal‑like cell states are enriched in hypoxic tumor cores, while AC‑like cells produce TGF‑β2 that activates tumor‑associated macrophages.
SP1‑macrophage and mCAF co‑localization defines an immunosuppressive niche associated with poor survival.
MasSpec Pen can detect metabolic signatures of proliferating (Ki‑67+) tumor cells intra‑operatively, potentially guiding resection margins.
CRISPR‑KO of TGF‑β receptors in engineered macrophages reduces tumor burden and pain in a glioblastoma bone‑metastasis mouse model.
open_questions: Will intra‑operative metabolomic signatures reliably predict residual aggressive cell states across patients?
How will engineered macrophages perform in the immunosuppressive brain microenvironment in humans?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: TGF‑β signaling from AC‑like cells creates a selective immunosuppressive pressure on macrophages.

key_findings: ADT Norm aligns background and signal peaks across heterogeneous CITE‑seq batches, achieving superior batch mixing and cell‑type separation compared with SeR normalization.
The method quantifies antibody staining quality, flagging markers with poor signal‑to‑background separation.
An AI‑agent interface enables natural‑language driven parameter tuning for large‑scale multi‑technology integration.
open_questions: How does ADT Norm perform on highly multiplexed spatial proteomics (e.g., CODEX) where signal bleed is prominent?
Can the AI‑agent be extended to automatically select optimal markers for downstream analyses?

key_findings: The GNN model trained on 2% of the data matches or exceeds NetMHC‑II Pan performance on DRB1 alleles.
Zero‑shot AlphaFold3 scoring (Fisher score) provides moderate predictive power, but the GNN substantially improves AUC.
Orientation errors in AlphaFold3 predictions for HLA‑DP alleles reduce performance, suggesting a need for orientation‑aware modeling.
Training NetMHC‑II Pan on the same limited dataset yields a 10% lower AUC, confirming the data efficiency of the new approach.
open_questions: Can orientation‑corrected AlphaFold3 models further improve predictions for HLA‑DP alleles?
How will the model perform on rare HLA alleles with minimal PepSeq data?
readouts: AUC on IEDB CD4 epitope benchmark
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: AlphaFold3 sometimes predicts reverse peptide orientation for HLA‑DP, leading to reduced binding prediction accuracy.

key_findings: EIPA delivery via microdevice decreased tumor amino‑acid levels in KRAS‑mutant xenografts, confirming macropinocytosis‑driven nutrient uptake.
DQ‑BSA fluorescence showed lysosomal processing of extracellular protein in KRAS‑mutant but not KRAS‑wildtype cells.
Spatial metabolomics identified two macrophage metabolic states: purine‑rich (pro‑inflammatory) versus lipid‑rich (pro‑tumor).
Logistic regression on metabolite data predicted immune neighborhoods with ROC AUC >0.85, suggesting metabolites can serve as surrogate immune biomarkers.
Microdevice can co‑deliver diverse agents (small molecules, base editors, antisense oligos, ADCs) with release kinetics tuned by PEG molecular weight.
open_questions: What temporal dynamics govern the shift from purine‑driven to lipid‑driven macrophage states during treatment?
Can stabilized isotope tracing be integrated with the microdevice to quantify metabolic fluxes in vivo?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Macropinocytosis inhibition selectively affected KRAS‑mutant cells, indicating a metabolic vulnerability not present in KRAS‑wildtype tumors.

key_findings: Implantable microdevices were placed in >350 patients across 13 trials with no serious adverse events.
Local drug concentration gradients correlated with apoptosis (cleaved caspase‑3) and proliferation inhibition (PCNA) in GBM xenografts.
Spatial transcriptomics confirmed on‑target pathway inhibition for osimertinib (EGFR), lapatinib (HER2/EGFR), everolimus (mTOR), and abemaciclib (cell‑cycle).
In a pilot GBM cohort, microdevice‑derived biomarkers predicted clinical temozolomide response in 5/5 patients, outperforming MGMT methylation status.
Interferon response programs were strongly associated with high‑efficacy temozolomide zones, suggesting a role for innate immunity in alkylator sensitivity.
Combination testing on the device (e.g., palbociclib + anti‑CD4) identified synergistic immune remodeling that translated to superior efficacy in preclinical models.
The platform enables rapid, patient‑specific drug selection and early human PD data for investigational agents, accelerating IND‑enabling studies.
open_questions: How do microdevice‑induced spatial drug gradients compare to systemic pharmacokinetics in heterogeneous tumors?
Can the platform be adapted for real‑time monitoring of immune checkpoint inhibitor activity in lymph nodes?
What is the minimal drug dose required locally to achieve systemic‑equivalent efficacy while avoiding toxicity?
readouts: IHC (cleaved caspase‑3, PCNA, DNA damage markers)
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Device insertion causes limited local inflammation confined to 3–4 cell layers, distinguishable from drug‑induced effects.
Variable drug diffusion can create concentration‑dependent resistance zones; precise polymer formulation mitigates this.

key_findings: Glee1 knockout mice retain normal gastric architecture despite Helicobacter infection, implicating Glee1‑positive myeloid cells in metaplasia.
SLFN4 expression marks granulocytic MDSCs; knockdown of SLFN4 increases apoptosis and reduces T‑cell suppression in vitro.
IL1B overexpression plus MNU yields gastric tumors in 45‑90% of mice; sildenafil treatment reduces tumor size and SLFN4‑positive cell infiltration.
In a human neoadjuvant window trial (n≈14), 2 weeks of tadalafil 20 mg daily decreased SLFN12L‑positive granulocytic MDSC frequency in tumor biopsies.
Subsequent FLOT chemotherapy after tadalafil further eliminated MDSCs and exhausted T‑cells while expanding cytotoxic CD8 T‑cells.
Bulk RNA‑seq of sorted SLFN4‑positive cells identified strong up‑regulation of PDE6, providing a mechanistic link to cyclic GMP metabolism.
open_questions: Can cyclic GMP phosphodiesterase inhibition prevent progression from intestinal metaplasia to invasive gastric cancer in a true preventive setting?
What is the relative contribution of PDE5 versus PDE6 inhibition to MDSC apoptosis, and can selective PDE6 inhibitors improve therapeutic index?
Does SLFN4 expression in T cells have functional relevance, and how does it affect overall immune remodeling?

key_findings: SHP2 phosphatase activity is dispensable for RAS activation, indicating a non‑catalytic role in SOS‑mediated signaling.
A covalent inhibitor targeting KRAS histidine‑95 can engage both GDP‑ and GTP‑bound KRAS, overcoming the limitation of off‑state inhibitors.
Binding of the inhibitor to the switch‑two pocket forces switch‑one into an unproductive state‑one conformation, blocking effector interactions.
The PI3K‑alpha breaker increases KRAS‑PI3K binding affinity to low‑nanomolar range, enabling selective disruption of KRAS‑driven PI3K signaling.
Structural studies reveal distinct conformations of RAF activation complexes that may be exploitable for next‑generation RAF inhibitors.
3034 monotherapy slowed tumor growth in KRAS G12D HPAC xenografts but did not induce regression.
Combination of 3034 with cetuximab produced tumor regressions in the majority of mice and deep partial responses in patients.
≥90% reduction in KRAS G12D ctDNA correlated with radiographic responses across colorectal, pancreatic, and endometrial cohorts.
No increase in cetuximab‑related rash or Grade ≥3 adverse events observed with the combination.
Acquired resistance manifested as KRAS wild‑type amplification after ~300 days of therapy, highlighting a limitation of the current inhibitor’s coverage of wild‑type KRAS.
open_questions: How can wild‑type KRAS amplification be effectively targeted alongside mutant KRAS inhibition?
What is the optimal dosing strategy to achieve EC90 coverage across all KRAS alleles while maintaining tolerability?
readouts: tumor volume measurements in xenograft models
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Acquired KRAS wild‑type amplification led to disease progression despite continued KRAS G12D inhibition.

key_findings: Endometrioid endometrial cancer patients showed robust and durable responses despite co‑occurring PI3K pathway alterations.
Combination of 3034 with cetuximab prevented outgrowth observed with monotherapy in preclinical models.
Preclinical mouse studies demonstrated tumor shrinkage at low oral doses (10‑30 mg) with reduced gastrointestinal adverse events compared with earlier KRAS inhibitors.
open_questions: What specific genotypic features (e.g., PI3K mutation status) drive the observed responses in endometrial cancer?
Does PI3K wild‑type versus mutant status affect early ctDNA suppression and durability of response?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Monotherapy led to outgrowth over time, suggesting adaptive resistance mechanisms.
Preliminary data indicate possible KRAS allele amplification as a resistance mechanism in patients.

key_findings: Resolute‑302 met its primary and secondary endpoints with a disease control rate of 95% in KRAS mutant patients.
PFS and OS curves showed lower confidence‑interval bounds exceeding those of standard second‑line chemotherapy, supporting a survival benefit.
Preclinical models demonstrated durable tumor regression and prevention of relapse when Deruxon Rasib was combined with covalent KRAS G12C inhibitor (Aleron) or G12D inhibitor (Zoldon).
Combination of Deruxon Rasib with gemcitabine/nab‑paclitaxel improved durability of response in pancreatic cancer models, informing the frontline RESOLUTE‑303 trial design.
Resistance mechanisms identified include amplification of the mutant KRAS allele (≈60% of resistant cases) and non‑genomic adaptations (~40%).
open_questions: What are the specific non‑genomic mechanisms driving resistance in the 40% of patients without KRAS amplification?
Can cyclophilin A expression levels predict response or resistance to tricomplex inhibitors?
readouts: in vivo tumor xenograft growth curves
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Amplification of mutant KRAS allele observed in ~60% of resistant patient samples.
Non‑genomic resistance mechanisms (e.g., pathway re‑activation) account for the remaining resistant cases.

patent_or_ip_hints: US Patent Application for KRAS tricomplex inhibitors (filed 2022)

key_findings: CRISPR screens identified KEAP1 knockout as a top driver of resistance to KRAS G12D (MRTX1133) and pan‑RAS (RMC7977) inhibitors.
KEAP1 KO cells show NRF2 and NQO1 up‑regulation and reduced sensitivity to KRAS inhibitors in both pancreatic and NSCLC models.
A glutamine antagonist (DRP104) combined with KRAS inhibitors suppresses tumor growth in three resistant in vivo models.
Patient and PDX datasets reveal higher expression of a KEAP1‑deficiency gene signature in KRAS inhibitor‑resistant cases.
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: KEAP1 loss drives resistance via NRF2‑dependent transcriptional program distinct from RAS, MYC, TEAD pathways.

key_findings: 2088 shows higher cellular affinity than existing ULK1 inhibitors in NanoBRET assays.
Combination of 2088 with trametinib (MEK inhibitor) or sotorasib (KRAS G12C inhibitor) yields strong synergy in NSCLC H2030 cells.
In vivo, 2088 plus sotorasib significantly improves tumor growth inhibition compared to monotherapy in Calu‑1 xenografts.
DNA barcode tracking indicates the combination delays clonal outgrowth and reduces drug‑tolerant persister populations.
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: ULK1 inhibition overcomes adaptive autophagy‑mediated resistance; no specific resistance to 2088 observed.

key_findings: Y64D mutation abolishes RMC‑6236 binding to KRAS and prevents tri‑complex formation with RAF.
KRAS Y64D engineered cell lines show >50‑fold increase in IC50 to RMC‑6236 compared with wild‑type.
In xenografts, Y64D tumors exhibit markedly reduced response to RMC‑6236 at both low and high doses.
MEK inhibitor restores sensitivity in Y64D mutant models, indicating downstream MAPK blockade can bypass resistance.
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Resistance driven by a single point mutation (Y64) that blocks molecular glue engagement; not due to KRAS amplification.

key_findings: Combination of BBI 825 with adagrasib or sotorasib completely prevented resistance emergence in ecDNA‑positive RW7213 cells.
BBI 825 suppressed KRAS amplification in resistant subclones and reduced MEK amplification in deraxurib‑treated cells.
In RW7213 xenografts, BBI 825 plus adagrasib markedly delayed tumor growth and lowered KRAS amplification frequency.
In CLR142 PDX, addition of BBI 825 enhanced efficacy of sotorasib plus cetuximab and reduced c‑MYC expression.
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Resistance driven by ecDNA‑mediated oncogene amplification; BBI 825 selectively impairs this process.

key_findings: Acquired KRAS G12D inhibitor‑resistant PDAC cells display up‑regulated JAK1/STAT3 signaling.
An oral STAT3 inhibitor selectively kills KRAS‑resistant cells and synergizes with KRAS G12D inhibitor in vitro.
Combination of KRAS inhibitor and STAT3 inhibitor leads to durable tumor regressions in KPC CDX models, overcoming relapse seen with KRAS inhibitor alone.
JAK1 inhibitor tofacitinib also blocks phospho‑STAT3 and enhances KRAS inhibitor efficacy.
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: STAT3 activation acts as both acute and chronic resistance mechanism to KRAS inhibition.

key_findings: Resistant PDOs show increased VEGF‑A expression and phospho‑VEGFR2 activation.
CRISPR‑mediated VEGFR2 knockout or DC101 treatment sensitizes resistant cells to MRTX1133.
PI3Kγ inhibition reduces VEGF‑A/VEGFR2 signaling and re‑sensitizes resistant models.
Combination of MRTX1133 with DC101 markedly suppresses tumor growth in multiple resistant xenograft models.
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Resistance mediated by a KRAS‑PI3Kγ‑SP1‑VEGF‑VEGFR2 autocrine loop; targeting VEGFR2 overcomes this specific pathway.

key_findings: KRAS G12C inhibitor LY3499446 induces variable DNA damage and micronuclei across NSCLC lines.
Aurora kinase A inhibitor LSN3321213 shows the strongest synergy with KRAS G12C inhibition, especially in micronuclei‑high cells.
Combination treatment leads to prolonged G2/M arrest and mitotic catastrophe, markedly reducing colony formation.
In vivo, low‑dose AURKA inhibition combined with KRAS G12C inhibitor produces tumor regression and extends relapse‑free survival.
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Synthetic vulnerability limited to KRAS‑inhibitor‑induced chromosomal instability; not observed in CIN‑low lines.

key_findings: 24% of treatment‑naïve lung cancers show cancer‑cell selective TAP2 downregulation; only 6% show TAP1 loss.
Low TAP2 expression predicts an 80% increased risk of death (HR 1.8) after immunotherapy, with no effect on chemotherapy outcomes.
TAP2 knockout reduces tumor‑antigen specific CD8 T‑cell killing more than TAP1 loss; re‑expression of TAP2 rescues killing.
TAP2 loss leads to a 10‑15% reduction in total HLA‑bound peptides but causes a >50% decrease in interferon‑γ‑induced gene expression (e.g., IDO1, PD‑L1) via SOX1 up‑regulation.
IL‑4 secreted by CD11b+ myeloid cells epigenetically closes the TAP2 promoter, an effect not reversed by exogenous IFN‑γ/TNF‑α.
HDAC inhibitors (vorinostat), taxanes, and dasatinib up‑regulate TAP2 without increasing PD‑L1, restoring antigen presentation and T‑cell killing in vitro.
Secreted phospholipase PLA2G10 acts as a T‑cell excluder; overexpression in mouse models accelerates tumor growth and reduces CD8 infiltration, while anti‑PLA2G10 antibody restores T‑cell entry.
Spatial analysis of 250 lung cancers identifies ~20% with a dominant immune‑excluded phenotype, which correlates with poorer immunotherapy survival.
open_questions: What upstream signals drive IL‑4 production by myeloid cells in TAP2‑low tumors?
Can plasma IL‑4 levels reliably predict TAP2 epigenetic silencing across cancer types?
What are the precise molecular mechanisms by which PLA2G10 impairs T‑cell migration?
Will TAP2‑restoring epigenetic therapies improve clinical outcomes when combined with checkpoint inhibitors in a prospective trial?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: TAP2 loss confers resistance specifically to checkpoint blockade, not to chemotherapy.
IL‑4–mediated epigenetic silencing of TAP2 is not overcome by IFN‑γ/TNF‑α stimulation, indicating a durable resistance mechanism.

key_findings: CDK4/6 inhibition increases chromatin‑bound Rb at >10,000 sites, 75% at promoters and many at active enhancers.
Rb binding at non‑promoter enhancers is associated with increased H3K27ac and up‑regulation of nearby estrogen‑response genes.
CRISPR disruption of Rb‑bound enhancers attenuates estrogen‑response gene induction and cyclin D1 protein up‑regulation.
Combining CDK4/6 inhibitors with endocrine therapy yields deeper suppression of cell‑cycle genes and prevents cyclin D1‑mediated resistance.
open_questions: Which E2F family members are recruited by Rb at non‑cell‑cycle sites?
Can selective Rb mutants separate E2F repression from estrogen‑response activation?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Rb‑driven estrogen response may limit monotherapy efficacy and contribute to resistance in ESR1‑mutant tumors.

key_findings: Linear and gap RNA sensors selectively activate reporter expression in cells harboring the target fusion RNA.
In MCF7 cells with an endogenous ARFGAP2‑SOX2 fusion, gap sensors drive mNeon fluorescence with >10‑fold specificity over fusion‑negative MCF10A.
Fusion‑targeted sensors coupled to iCaspase9 reduce MCF7 viability to ~80% versus ~100% for non‑targeting controls.
High‑throughput sensor library screening begins to define design rules for effective RNA‑sensor constructs.
open_questions: What are the optimal payloads (immune‑stimulating, secreted factors) for in‑vivo efficacy?
How can delivery be achieved at scale (LNP, viral nanoparticles) to reach tumor cells in patients?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Variable sensor performance suggests sequence‑context dependent efficacy; loss or mutation of the fusion breakpoint could confer resistance.

key_findings: Only ~7% of cancer patients enroll in trials, whereas ~8% would be needed to fill open slots.
Approximately 50% of trials fail to meet enrollment targets.
Public data sources (e.g., ClinicalTrials.gov, TEFCA) provide trial listings but lack granular inclusion/exclusion criteria.
Private sector investment in trial‑matching technologies exceeds $2 billion, roughly matching public investment.
Current solutions are fragmented (within‑system vs. cross‑system) and often expose patients to only a subset of available trials.
Future focus should shift toward study design that aligns trials with patient care needs, leveraging AI for faster, smaller trials.
MSK’s first‑generation nudge system sends daily email alerts about potential trial matches based on genomic profiling.
A randomized trial of progression‑timed nudges showed a small, non‑significant increase in accrual (a few percentage points).
Clinician time and health‑system money were identified as the top barriers to trial accrual.
Patient trust, rather than travel logistics, was highlighted as the primary barrier to enrollment.
Telehealth, video‑informed consent, and home‑based monitoring were proposed as operational solutions to reduce patient burden.
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: AI prescreening cannot replace dynamic eligibility checks (e.g., pregnancy test on day of enrollment).
Overly strict matching criteria risk excluding eligible patients; overly lax criteria increase clinician workload.

key_findings: 37% of NSCLC patients had an actionable alteration on first plasma PCGP.
In treatment‑naive patients, 36% harbored FDA‑approved genotype‑matched alterations.
22% of treatment‑naive patients started genotype‑matched therapy within 30 days of plasma result.
Undetectable ctDNA was associated with significantly longer overall survival versus detectable ctDNA.
Patients receiving genotype‑matched therapy based on plasma findings had significantly improved overall survival.
open_questions: How does plasma PCGP performance compare with tissue NGS in low‑tumor‑burden settings?
Can earlier serial sampling improve detection of emerging resistance?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: MET amplification and secondary EGFR alterations were the most common resistance mechanisms to osimertinib.
Resistance landscapes differed between first/second‑generation EGFR TKIs (T790M‑driven) and osimertinib (MET, C797S).

key_findings: MET amplification is significantly more common in lung cancer brain metastases (16.4%) than in primary tumors (3.7%).
Plasma ctDNA detects MET amplifications in ~10% of patients at progression, but concordance with tissue is limited.
In paired pre‑ and post‑craniotomy samples, only 1 of 2 tissue MET amplifications were captured in plasma.
Radiation therapy appears to increase ctDNA shedding, leading to higher VAF/CNV signals post‑radiation.
open_questions: Can assay sensitivity be improved to reliably detect brain‑specific MET amplifications?
What is the optimal timing of plasma collection relative to radiotherapy for maximal ctDNA yield?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Technical challenges capture MET amplification by ctDNA, especially with low tumor burden or intrathoracic disease.

key_findings: AXL mRNA is overexpressed in CTCs of ~13% of NSCLC patients at baseline and increases after the first osimertinib cycle.
AXL overexpression persists in a subset of patients at disease progression, indicating a possible resistance mechanism.
During anti‑PD‑1 therapy, AXL overexpression emerges in a few patients, suggesting adaptive resistance.
CTC‑derived AXL expression provides complementary information to ctDNA and tissue analyses.
open_questions: What is the therapeutic threshold of AXL mRNA expression in CTCs for initiating AXL‑targeted therapy?
How does CTC‑derived AXL expression correlate with tissue AXL protein levels?
readouts: Droplet digital PCR for EGFR mutations
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: AXL overexpression is linked to EMT and resistance to EGFR TKIs and immune checkpoint inhibitors.

key_findings: 87% of PDAC patients had CTCs expressing at least one CAR‑NK target (mesothelin or MUC4).
MUC4‑positive CTCs were enriched in metastatic patients.
IL‑12 and IL‑15 armed CAR‑NK cells achieved near‑complete tumor eradication in 2D killing assays and eliminated spheroids by day 12.
Synergistic cytokine‑armed CAR‑NK cells provided superior tumor suppression and survival benefit in mouse models compared with conventional CAR‑NK.
open_questions: How will CTC target expression evolve during therapy and affect CAR‑NK efficacy?
Can this pipeline be adapted for other solid tumors with distinct CTC antigens?
readouts: Granzyme B and IFN‑γ flow cytometry
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Target expression heterogeneity (exclusive mesothelin vs. MUC4) underscores need for personalized CAR‑NK selection.

key_findings: 73% of MSI‑high mCRC patients were ctDNA positive before ICI therapy.
77% achieved ctDNA clearance at least once after ICI start, median time 96 days.
Early clearance (<4 months) occurred in 44% and correlated with 4‑year OS of 95% vs 81% for ctDNA‑positive patients.
Any clearance conferred a 10‑fold OS advantage (95.5% vs 66.1% 4‑yr OS).
Sustained clearance (≥6 months) was observed in 63% of patients.
open_questions: Do ctDNA dynamics differ between pembrolizumab monotherapy and ipilimumab/nivolumab combination?
Can ctDNA monitoring guide optimal duration of ICI therapy in MSI‑high mCRC?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Persistent ctDNA positivity identified a high‑risk group with markedly inferior survival.

key_findings: RBC DNA fragments are shorter (avg 4.3 kb) than genomic DNA but longer than cfDNA.
Distinct genome‑wide coverage patterns differentiate CRC patients from healthy donors.
A binary classifier achieved AUC 0.95, 85% sensitivity for advanced adenomas and 95% for CRC at 90% specificity.
Performance remained robust across external validation cohorts and was not confounded by blood counts or lifestyle factors.
In a prospective head‑to‑head comparison, RBC‑DNA testing outperformed FIT for detecting advanced adenomas and Stage 1 CRC.
open_questions: What are the specific genomic regions driving the RBC‑DNA signal and their biological relevance?
Can RBC‑DNA signatures be extended to other cancer types or pan‑cancer early detection?
readouts: Low‑coverage whole‑genome sequencing of RBC DNA

key_findings: CUPIA 2 achieved 77% top‑1 accuracy and 93% top‑3 accuracy across 19 cancer types in internal validation.
On independent MSK cohort (12,000 samples) top‑1 accuracy was 62% and top‑3 accuracy 82%.
Model provided rationale linking co‑mutations (e.g., KRAS G12D + TP53 R175H) to predicted tissue origins.
Chairman LLM overwrote 24% of ensemble predictions during training.
open_questions: How to improve performance on under‑represented cancer types such as small‑cell lung cancer and endometrial cancer?
Can multimodal inputs (RNA‑seq, imaging) be incorporated to boost accuracy?

key_findings: PalboVNN stratified UCSD patients (n=36) into responders vs non‑responders with HR 0.38 and median PFS benefit of 14 months.
In the larger MSK cohort (n=474) the model retained significance (HR 0.56) with an 18‑month median PFS advantage.
Model performance was specific to palbociclib‑containing regimens and did not stratify letrozole‑only patients.
Interpretation identified 18 protein assemblies (11 shared) driving predictions, including DNA integrity and AKT signaling.
A prospective phase‑II trial has been launched based on these findings.
open_questions: Can the VNN framework be generalized to other CDK4/6 inhibitors (ribociclib, abemaciclib) with comparable performance?
How will inclusion of clinical covariates (ancestry, comorbidities) affect model accuracy?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: ROS1 mutation was a dominant driver of predicted resistance in a non‑responding patient.

key_findings: Fibroblast density was a negative prognostic marker in both IO and chemo arms (high density → worse OS).
Immune cell density showed a predictive interaction: high density correlated with improved OS only in the immunotherapy arm.
Multivariate Cox model adding H&E features to PD‑L1/TMB achieved significant separation (p<0.05) whereas clinical features alone did not.
At 18‑month follow‑up, high‑risk group defined by H&E features had 21% event rate, supporting enrichment potential.
open_questions: Will prospective validation confirm the added predictive value of H&E‑derived biomarkers?
Can these AI features be integrated with other omics (e.g., RNA‑seq) for further improvement?

key_findings: Across 21 cancer types, 87% of 450 pathway‑cancer models achieved AUC > 0.5.
9% of models (top 10 pathways) reached AUC 0.65–0.85, notably nucleotide metabolism (AUC 0.85 in TGCT) and nuclear transport (AUC 0.79 in COAD).
Metabolic pathways with high predictability clustered in nucleotide synthesis, nuclear/mitochondrial transport, and fatty‑acid β‑oxidation.
Demonstrated feasibility of using H&E morphology to infer functional metabolic states, suggesting utility for trial enrichment.
open_questions: Will external validation on independent cohorts confirm the high‑performing pathways?
Can predicted metabolic activity be linked to response to pathway‑targeted therapies?

key_findings: Hybrid architecture achieved near‑perfect AUC (0.99) at year 1 and maintained 0.94 at year 6 on NLST test set.
Hybrid model outperformed Bi‑fusion and Tri‑fusion across all horizons and also generalized to external Moffitt cohort after fine‑tuning.
Statistical tests confirmed significant performance differences (p < 0.05) between hybrid and other models.
Model handles missing time points via attention masking, making it applicable to real‑world screening data.
open_questions: How will incorporation of clinical/demographic risk factors affect long‑term prediction?
Can federated learning across institutions improve robustness to variable scan intervals?

key_findings: CRT model achieved AUC 0.97 for response prediction in training set and validated across two external cohorts.
Predicted PR patients had significantly longer PFS and OS (HR ≈ 0.45–0.48) after multivariate adjustment for age, sex, PD‑L1 CPS.
Pathway analysis showed enrichment of immune‑activating signatures (alpha/gamma response) in predicted PR group versus immune‑inhibitory pathways (IL‑10, NF‑κB) in non‑PR group.
Model outperformed PD‑L1 CPS and unimodal radiomics or pathomics models in precision‑recall and confusion matrix metrics.
open_questions: Will prospective multicenter trials confirm the CRT model’s predictive power for treatment selection?
Can the model be adapted for other immunotherapy regimens or combination therapies?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: High fibroblast density (from pathomics) was linked to non‑PR status and immune‑inhibitory gene expression.

company_or_sponsor: Yangtze River Delta Guochi Intelligent Medical Technology Co.

key_findings: Olaparib treatment of BRCA‑deficient mice increased tumor‑infiltrating macrophages expressing PD‑L1, CSF1R, CD36 and TREM2.
Anti‑CSF1R combined with olaparib doubled median overall survival from ~100 to ~200 days in the mouse model, an effect dependent on CD8 T cells.
TREM2‑CAR monocytes specifically phagocytosed TREM2‑positive target cells in vitro, whereas irrelevant CARs did not.
In vivo, a single IV dose of TREM2‑CAR monocytes increased intratumoral CD8 T cells and reduced tumor burden by ~50% in a breast cancer model, further enhanced by anti‑PD‑1.
The AXLAP phase 1b trial (axcitilimab + olaparib) is >50% enrolled in metastatic HER2‑negative, BRCA1/PALB2‑mutated breast cancer, enabling correlative studies of macrophage modulation.
open_questions: Can CAR‑monocytes be further engineered with cytokine payloads to enhance durability of anti‑tumor immunity?
What is the optimal sequencing of PARP inhibition, CSF1R blockade, and CAR‑monocyte therapy in patients?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: PARP + PD‑L1 showed no benefit in a prior trial, likely due to expansion of lipid‑associated macrophages.
CAR‑monocytes avoid the poor tumor penetration seen with CAR‑T cells because monocytes naturally home to hypoxic, macrophage‑rich niches.

key_findings: CNMF identified 14 myeloid programs across glioma, with four activity programs accounting for >90% of cells.
The scavenger immunosuppressive program (hypoxia‑linked) was enriched in non‑responders to checkpoint blockade and CAR‑T therapy.
Microglial inflammatory program was enriched in responders and associated with improved overall survival.
CAR‑T infusion induced a dose‑dependent surge of the complement immunosuppressive program in CSF myeloid cells across all patients.
Baseline high scavenger program levels in CSF predicted worse overall survival after CAR‑T treatment.
open_questions: Can selective inhibition of the dexamethasone‑driven program improve CAR‑T efficacy without compromising steroid benefits?
What upstream signals trigger the hypoxia‑linked scavenger program in brain metastases?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Dexamethasone treatment drives a distinct immunosuppressive myeloid program that may blunt immunotherapy efficacy.

key_findings: Dupilumab added to ongoing PD‑1 blockade induced remission and complete pain relief in a patient with progressive NSCLC.
Approximately one‑third of PD‑1‑refractory NSCLC patients achieved disease control after three dupilumab doses, allowing continuation of checkpoint therapy.
IL‑4 neutralization reduced emergency myelopoiesis and tumor‑associated macrophage accumulation in KRAS‑mutant mouse lung cancer.
Combined IL‑4Rα and PD‑1 blockade synergistically reduced tumor burden in KP1 mouse model compared with either monotherapy.
Dual IL‑1α/β blockade (anakinra) suppressed age‑related inflammasome activation and tumor growth in old mouse models of colorectal and pancreatic cancer.
open_questions: What biomarkers predict which NSCLC patients will respond to IL‑4Rα blockade combined with PD‑1 inhibition?
Can simultaneous targeting of IL‑4 and IL‑1 pathways overcome resistance in tumors with mixed myeloid programs?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: CCR2/5 inhibition depleted TREM2⁺ macrophages but also unexpectedly reduced peripheral lymphocytes, potentially limiting efficacy.
CD47 antibodies caused hemolysis due to CD47 expression on red blood cells, leading to halted development.

key_findings: Kinase‑inhibitor “metronomic rest” improves CAR T memory phenotype (Ramos et al.).
Self‑clustering of Cilta‑cel‑like CARs drives cytokine release and neurotoxicity in vitro, which can be mitigated by selecting non‑clustering VHH binders.
Bispecific/tandem CARs (e.g., CD19/CD20) show variable efficacy depending on transmembrane and co‑stimulatory domain configuration.
Armoring with IL‑18 or anti‑PD‑1 scFv linked to IL‑12 improves tumor control in murine models.
TGF‑β during manufacturing preserves central‑memory phenotype and enhances in vivo persistence of CAR T cells.
open_questions: What is the optimal balance of CAR clustering to avoid tonic signaling‑induced exhaustion while preserving potency?
Can in vivo CAR T manufacturing achieve comparable memory phenotypes without ex vivo cytokine conditioning?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Antigen loss (CD19 splice variants, CD22 down‑regulation) identified as a major resistance mechanism.
CAR self‑association can cause cytokine‑independent proliferation, raising safety concerns.

key_findings: Allogeneic gamma‑delta T cells can be expanded from donors without causing graft‑versus‑host disease.
Donor fitness (exercise, age) correlates with expansion potential and CD16 expression.
TGF‑β during manufacturing preserves central‑memory phenotype and markedly improves in vivo persistence and osteosarcoma killing.
Triple combination (temozolomide + zoledronate + dinutuximab) with gamma‑delta T cells yields superior neuroblastoma killing in preclinical models.
BiTE or CAR expression in gamma‑delta T cells achieves comparable cytotoxicity to conventional alpha‑beta CAR T cells.
open_questions: What is the optimal donor selection algorithm to maximize expansion and functional potency?
Can large‑scale bioreactor processes achieve consistent Vδ1/Vδ2 ratios for allogeneic products?
readouts: flow cytometry for CD16, NKG2D, memory markers
in vivo tumor growth inhibition in mouse xenografts
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Gamma‑delta T cells lack HLA restriction, reducing risk of tumor immune evasion via HLA loss.
CD16 down‑regulation during TGF‑β expansion may limit ADCC, requiring genetic replacement.

patent_or_ip_hints: Gamma‑delta T cell expansion protocol patents

key_findings: Multi‑domain fusion particles achieve rapid (≤10 min) high‑avidity binding to human T cells in vitro.
Co‑stimulatory‑enhanced particles generate polyfunctional CAR T cells with superior serial killing versus anti‑CD3‑only particles.
In NSG MHC‑KO humanized mice, particles encoding anti‑CD19 CAR produce durable tumor control at low vector doses.
In cynomolgus macaques, a single IV dose yields ~40% CAR‑positive T cells, peaks at days 7‑10, and induces rapid, complete B‑cell depletion.
Transient low‑grade CRS observed; no severe infusion reactions despite high in vivo transduction.
RACR activation with rapamycin markedly expands CAR T cells and improves tumor clearance in low‑antigen (CD22‑low) models.
open_questions: What is the optimal balance of anti‑CD3 affinity to achieve efficient transduction without excessive activation?
Can the RACR system be safely cycled on/off in patients to modulate CAR T persistence?
readouts: in situ hybridization for vector copy
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Anti‑CAR immune response (against Lu16 scFv and hinge) caused B‑cell recovery in macaques, indicating potential immunogenicity of murine scFv components.
No off‑target transduction of endothelial or hepatocyte cells detected at therapeutic doses.

key_findings: Developed Circle Cell Segmentation Across Scales (CCSAS) tool that outperforms existing segmentation methods qualitatively and quantitatively.
Implemented a ranked hierarchy pixel‑by‑pixel classification approach for immune phenotyping that improves cell type assignment compared with simple dimensionality reduction.
Demonstrated that accurate segmentation dramatically impacts downstream spatial analyses such as pairwise cell interaction and cellular neighborhood quantification.
open_questions: How can segmentation algorithms be further optimized for heterogeneous tumor architectures and nerve‑rich regions?
What are the best practices for integrating multi‑modal spatial data (RNA, protein, metabolomics) in a single analysis pipeline?

key_findings: A bulk RNA‑derived classifier predicts perineural invasion and uncovered missed PNI cases on histology.
Spatial profiling revealed PDGFD‑PDGFRB as the only ligand‑receptor pair overlapping between sequencing‑based (GeoMx) and imaging‑based (SMI) datasets.
CRISPR activation of PDGFD in PDAC organoids increased 3D neural invasion index, which was dose‑dependently blocked by the PDGFRB inhibitor SU16f.
Recombinant PDGFD stimulates neurite outgrowth from DRG neurons; this effect is abolished by PDGFRB inhibition.
In vivo, PDGFD overexpression augments orthotopic tumor nerve invasion, while PDGFRB inhibition reduces sciatic nerve invasion.
open_questions: Will PDGFRB inhibition improve response to immunotherapy in PNI‑positive pancreatic cancer?
What are the downstream signaling pathways in neurons and Schwann cells mediating PDGFD effects?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: PDGFRB inhibition selectively blocks PDGFD‑driven invasion without affecting baseline tumor growth in control lines.

key_findings: Half of anti‑PD‑1 non‑responders exhibited histologic perineural invasion, whereas responders had significantly lower rates.
Bulk RNA‑seq of non‑responders showed enrichment of nerve injury pathways (ATF3, C‑JUN) and neurodegeneration GO terms.
Applying neurodegeneration signatures to TCGA head‑and‑neck cohort stratified patients by survival, with high‑signature tumors having worse outcomes.
Spatial profiling demonstrated co‑localization of nerve injury markers with immunosuppressive cells (FoxP3+ Tregs, myeloid cells) but not with effective anti‑tumor immune signatures.
NanoString GeoMx analysis confirmed that nerve‑adjacent regions in non‑responders express higher checkpoint molecules (PD‑L1, CTLA‑4) compared with responders.
open_questions: Can nerve‑injury signatures be used prospectively to stratify patients for combination neuro‑targeted therapies with immunotherapy?
What are the optimal biomarkers (RNA vs protein) for detecting nerve‑mediated immunosuppression in routine clinical samples?
readouts: IHC for NFH and immune markers
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Nerve injury signatures correlate specifically with immunosuppressive phenotypes, suggesting a selective resistance mechanism rather than a global tumor aggressiveness effect.

key_findings: Mice engineered to carry ultra‑long telomeres live significantly longer and develop 40% fewer spontaneous tumors compared with wild‑type controls.
AAV‑mediated, non‑integrative TERT gene therapy administered at 1 yr or 2 yr of age extends median lifespan by ~15% and markedly reduces progression of bleomycin‑induced pulmonary fibrosis.

POT1 knock‑in mice recapitulate human telomere‑biology disease phenotypes: short telomeres, multi‑telomeric FISH signals, reduced litter size, intestinal and testicular atrophy, and accelerated lung and kidney fibrosis.
Genetic or pharmacologic inhibition of TRF1 reduces tumor burden by ~50% in KRAS‑driven lung cancer and glioblastoma mouse models without increasing normal tissue toxicity.

TRF1 stability is controlled by Akt‑mediated phosphorylation at threonine 330; phospho‑dead (T330A) mice exhibit shorter telomeres, increased DNA damage, and higher papilloma formation after chemical carcinogenesis, whereas phospho‑mimetic (T330E) mice maintain longer telomeres but display rapid telomere attrition in adult tissues.
Screening of FDA‑approved drugs identified PI3K/Akt and RAS pathway inhibitors as indirect TRF1 destabilizers, linking extracellular signaling to telomere protection.
open_questions: What molecular mechanisms determine the species‑specific rate of telomere shortening and its link to DNA‑repair efficiency?
How does TRF1 support pluripotency and adult stem‑cell function, and can pathways that rescue TRF1 loss be therapeutically exploited?
Will long‑telomere, POT1‑mutant cancers be selectively vulnerable to agents that exacerbate telomere fragility?
What are the long‑term safety implications of systemic telomerase gene therapy in humans, especially regarding potential tumor promotion?

key_findings: cDC1 cells display mitochondrial high and low populations across multiple tumor models (B16, lung, osteosarcoma, pancreatic).
Mitochondrial‑high cDC1 have higher oxidative phosphorylation, ATP production, and superior ability to prime CD8 T cells in vitro and in vivo.
Tumor progression shifts cDC1 toward the mitochondrial‑low, dysfunctional state, reducing T cell priming capacity.
Adoptive transfer of mitochondrial‑high cDC1 slows tumor growth and synergizes with anti‑PD‑L1, anti‑CTLA‑4, and anti‑PD‑1 therapies, leading to durable immunity upon rechallenge.

OPA1 is up‑regulated in tumor‑infiltrating cDC1; its conditional knockout impairs mitochondrial cristae, oxidative phosphorylation, and anti‑tumor immunity, leading to uncontrolled tumor growth in multiple models.

NRF1 expression is down‑regulated in OPA1‑deficient cDC1; NRF1 knockout phenocopies OPA1 loss, while NRF1 overexpression rescues mitochondrial function and T cell priming, dependent on intact electron transport chain.
open_questions: What upstream tumor microenvironment signals repress OPA1 expression in cDC1?
Can in vivo metabolic re‑programming of cDC1 (e.g., via micropinocytosis modulation) replace adoptive transfer?
Do other DC subsets (e.g., cDC2) exhibit similar mitochondrial heterogeneity and therapeutic potential?
readouts: flow cytometry for T cell proliferation

key_findings: A transition cell state (20‑30% of tumor cells) links proliferative, invasive, and hypoxic clusters and predicts T‑cell exclusion in TNBC.
BACH1 is identified as a top regulator of this transition state; knockout reduces the transition population, overexpression expands it.
High BACH1 activity signature correlates with poor response to pembrolizumab + chemotherapy and low TILs in I‑SPY and other TNBC cohorts.
BACH1 knockout in mouse TNBC models increases CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration, activation, and reduces lung metastasis; phenotype rescued by BACH1 re‑expression.
Mechanistically, BACH1 directly binds and represses IFI21 (type I IFN) locus; loss of BACH1 elevates type I IFN signaling, enhancing anti‑tumor immunity.
Combination of BACH1 loss with anti‑CTLA‑4 yields superior tumor control compared with either alone, indicating synergy with checkpoint blockade.
open_questions: Which additional stressors (e.g., low glucose, iron deprivation) modulate BACH1 activity in human TNBC?
Can pharmacologic BACH1 inhibitors be developed with acceptable toxicity given its developmental roles?
What are the downstream effectors of BACH1‑mediated immune evasion beyond type I IFN repression?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Long‑term BACH1 knockout tumors eventually resume growth, suggesting compensatory pathways emerge.
BACH1‑deficient tumors show early T‑cell activation but later develop increased Treg/CTLA‑4‑mediated resistance.

key_findings: Short‑term PD‑1 blockade yields a transient T cell reinvigoration peak; continuous blockade does not improve long‑term outcomes compared with short‑term treatment.
A drug holiday (2‑week treatment, 2‑month washout, re‑treatment) produces a second robust reinvigoration, leading to better viral control in chronic LCMV infection.
Continuous PD‑1 blockade depletes the intermediate exhausted T cell population (CD63⁺) while preserving terminally exhausted cells.
Progenitor exhausted T cells exposed to long‑term PD‑1 blockade up‑regulate CD22, a B‑cell inhibitory receptor that dampens TCR signaling.
Anti‑CD22 antibody or PD‑1×CD22 bispecific restores intermediate exhausted cell expansion and improves disease control in both viral and tumor models.
Bispecific therapy outperforms either monotherapy in the AT3‑OVA tumor model, increasing T cell numbers, proliferation, and cytokine production.
open_questions: What is the optimal timing and duration of PD‑1 drug holidays in patients?
How prevalent is CD22 expression on human progenitor exhausted T cells across cancer types?
Can CD22 ligands (sialic acids) be modulated to enhance the effect of CD22 blockade?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Chronic PD‑1 loss leads to adaptive resistance via CD22 up‑regulation on Tpex cells.
Long‑term PD‑1 blockade skews differentiation toward terminal exhaustion, reducing therapeutic efficacy.

key_findings: KRAS G12C covalent inhibitors achieve ~80% disease control in KRAS G12C NSCLC patients but relapses are common.
In mouse models, a minor resistant G12D subpopulation expands under G12C inhibition, limiting response.
Combining a KRAS G12C inhibitor with anti‑PD‑1 therapy increases complete response rate to ~45% versus 7% with inhibitor alone.
Mice achieving complete responses reject rechallenge with 100% G12D tumors, indicating immune memory.
open_questions: What is the optimal sequencing of KRAS inhibitor and checkpoint blockade in patients?
Can biomarkers such as early neoantigen‑specific T‑cell expansion predict durable responses?
readouts: flow cytometry for neoantigen‑specific T cells
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Intrinsic resistance due to co‑occurring KEAP1, SMARCA4, CDKN2A alterations predicts inferior outcomes.
Acquired cis‑mutations at KRAS residues 95, 96, 68 prevent inhibitor binding.

key_findings: Combination of KRAS G12C inhibitor with SOS1 inhibitor yields superior tumor regression in KRAS G12D mouse models compared with monotherapy.
KRAS G12C plus MEK inhibitor produces the greatest tumor shrinkage among tested combinations.
Preclinical data support ongoing clinical trials testing KRAS inhibitor + SOS1 or MEK inhibitor combinations.
open_questions: Which biomarker panel best predicts benefit from KRAS inhibitor + SOS1 or MEK combinations?
Can adaptive resistance mechanisms be pre‑emptively targeted in early‑line therapy?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Intrinsic resistance linked to KEAP1, SMARCA4, CDKN2A co‑mutations reduces efficacy of KRAS monotherapy.

key_findings: MEK inhibition leads to loss of RND3 within 24 h, causing rapid YAP target gene up‑regulation.
FAK inhibitor defactinib combined with a TEAD inhibitor produces tumor regressions in uveal melanoma models where each agent alone is cytostatic.
In mouse models, the combination restores CD8+ T‑cell infiltration and improves survival compared with monotherapy.
Hippo‑YAP activation also induces chemokines (CXCL1, CXCL5, CXCL8) that recruit immunosuppressive myeloid cells.
open_questions: What biomarkers can predict which patients will develop Hippo‑YAP mediated adaptive resistance?
Can TEAD inhibitors be safely combined with checkpoint blockade in humans?
readouts: flow cytometry for CD8 T cells
tumor_types: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Adaptive resistance via Hippo‑YAP activation occurs across KRAS, BRAF, and GNAQ‑driven tumors.
FAK inhibition does not markedly affect normal immune cell function at therapeutic doses.

key_findings: HA-based 3D invasion device enables separation of invasive rim and core GBM cells for comparative analysis.
Invasive GBM cells show enrichment of ROS and transsulfuration pathway genes, matching patient tumor data.
Leader GBM cells deposit a trail of HYAL2, degrading HA and facilitating faster follower cell invasion.
Inhibition of hyaluronidase activity or genetic targeting of the transsulfuration pathway reduces GBM invasion in vitro.
open_questions: What upstream signals trigger HYAL2 secretion by leader cells?
Can targeting the transsulfuration pathway synergize with standard GBM therapies?

key_findings: Stiff ECM induces nuclear translocation of Twist1 without changing its protein level.
G3BP2 binds Twist1 in soft ECM, preventing nuclear entry; stiffness‑dependent phosphorylation by LIN releases Twist.
TYK2 membrane localization is lost on stiff matrices, acting as a metastasis suppressor; TYK2 inhibition drives invasion on soft matrices.
TYK2 deletion or inhibition increases lung dissemination of TNBC PDX without affecting primary tumor size.
Twist deletion abrogates the invasive phenotype induced by TYK2 loss, confirming epistatic relationship.
open_questions: What upstream mechanosensor triggers TYK2 membrane dissociation on stiff ECM?
Does TYK2 have similar metastasis‑suppressive roles in other epithelial cancers?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: TYK2 inhibition unexpectedly promotes invasion, suggesting potential resistance mechanism if used clinically for other indications.

key_findings: GSTT1 is absent in primary PDAC but highly expressed in liver and lung metastases and its knockout abolishes metastatic outgrowth while primary tumor growth is unaffected
GSTT1 overexpression induces ectopic metastases in multiple organs and promotes fibronectin secretion via glutathione conjugation

SLC30A4 is specifically up‑regulated in metastatic lesions, and its loss impairs 3D colony formation and metastatic colonization; overexpression increases serine uptake and rescues growth in serine‑depleted conditions
MAT2A shifts from cytoplasmic to nuclear localization in metastatic cells, supporting nuclear SAM production for histone methylation; nuclear MAT2A is required for metastatic growth
open_questions: What transcription factors drive the coordinated up‑regulation of GSTT1, SLC30A4 and MAT2A in disseminated tumor cells?
Can pharmacologic inhibition of GSTT1 or SLC30A4 antibodies prevent metastatic colonization in vivo?

key_findings: IMPDH2 expression is high in primary and metastatic PDAC and correlates with poor patient survival
Long‑term MPA exposure selects for PDAC cells with increased glutathione metabolism (up‑regulation of SLC7A11, GPX4) and a 20‑fold increase in IC50
Sulfasalazine sensitizes MPA‑resistant cells to MPA in vitro and modestly reduces tumor burden in vivo
Combination of MPA with the ferroptosis inducer RSL3 enhances cell killing and decreases liver metastasis size in mouse splenic injection models
open_questions: Will combining MPA with KRAS inhibitors improve efficacy in metastatic PDAC?
Can dietary serine or methionine restriction augment the anti‑metastatic effect of IMPDH2 inhibition?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Acquired MPA resistance is mediated by up‑regulation of cystine‑glutathione axis, conferring cross‑resistance to oxidative stress

key_findings: NUDT5 deficiency confers resistance to 6‑thioguanine and to de novo pathway inhibitors (methotrexate, leflunomide)
NUDT5 directly interacts with PPAT; the R70A mutation abolishes binding without affecting catalytic activity
Wild‑type NUDT5 (or catalytic dead) induces PPAT tetramerization and reduces its enzymatic activity by ~80% in vitro
In xenografts, tumors expressing NUDT5‑binding‑defective PPAT remain resistant to 6‑TG, whereas WT NUDT5 restores drug sensitivity
open_questions: What cellular signal triggers NUDT5‑PPAT binding during purine abundance?
Does NUDT5 regulate purinosome dynamics in vivo and can this be therapeutically exploited?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: NUDT5‑mediated PPAT tetramerization provides a novel mechanism of metabolic drug resistance

key_findings: GAA is the most overabundant metabolite in high‑grade glioma compared to normal brain (563 metabolites screened).
AGAT expression correlates with glioma grade; AGAT knockout mice show increased survival despite unchanged tumor growth in flank.
GAA induces neuronal hyperexcitability via GABA_A receptors; effect is blocked by gabazine and KCC2 agonist CLP257.
Dietary ornithine supplementation with arginine restriction lowers tumor GAA and extends survival, mimicking AGAT knockout.
A surgical window trial will enroll 12 patients to test ornithine supplementation and arginine‑restricted diet pre‑operatively.
open_questions: Will dietary modulation of GAA translate to clinical benefit in glioma patients?
What is the impact of GAA reduction on seizure frequency and overall neurologic outcomes?

key_findings: Clonal barcoding identified ~12% of PDAC clones driving gemcitabine relapse.
Chemotherapy‑responsive clones upregulate OXPHOS and mitochondrial fission (phospho‑DRP1).
IM‑156 more potent than metformin/phenformin, inhibits OCR at 10 µM without lactic acidosis.
Gemcitabine + IM‑156 prolongs regrowth delay, increases apoptosis, and reduces relapse‑clone frequency in mice.
Phase 1/2 trial (n=18) showed 50% partial responses, 80% disease control, median PFS 6 mo, OS 18 mo, with acceptable safety at 400 mg PO daily.
open_questions: What mechanisms underlie eventual resistance to Complex I inhibition after prolonged treatment?
Can biomarkers (e.g., phospho‑DRP1) predict patients who will benefit from IM‑156?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Potential resistance may emerge via alternative ETC bypass or metabolic rewiring; ongoing studies to combine with KRAS inhibitors.

key_findings: KPL mice develop rapid weight loss, fat and muscle wasting, and anemia despite tumor size similar to KP controls.
HIF‑2α inhibition with rezotibib restores body weight, fat, and muscle but induces anemia due to reduced EPO.
E2 pellet treatment in cachectic male mice maintains body weight, fat, and muscle, normalizing serum catabolic metabolites.
Estrogen reprograms peripheral tissues: upregulates OXPHOS/TCA, downregulates proteolysis pathways in muscle and adipose.
Ovariectomy abolishes female protection from cachexia, indicating ovarian hormone dependence.
open_questions: Does estrogen therapy benefit cachexia in human cancer patients, and how does hormone receptor status affect response?
Can combined HIF‑2α inhibition and estrogen therapy provide additive benefits without anemia?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: HIF‑2α inhibition alone fails to address anemia, requiring adjunct EPO therapy.

key_findings: Ketogenic diet slows tumor growth and extends mouse survival but does not eradicate tumors.
Tumors on ketogenic diet show increased TCA cycle metabolites and a 4‑fold rise in intratumoral glutamine.
Isotope tracing shows tumor does not synthesize glutamine de novo; liver produces excess glutamine under low‑protein ketogenic diet.
Glutamine transporter and utilization enzymes are upregulated in ketogenic‑diet tumors.
Combination of ketogenic diet with glutaminase inhibitor CB‑839 or DON yields greater tumor suppression than either alone.
open_questions: How does ketogenic diet affect immune cell function within the PDAC microenvironment?
Can patient stratification biomarkers (e.g., baseline glutamine transporter expression) predict response to diet‑plus‑glutamine inhibition?
readouts: stable_isotope_tracing (U‑13C glucose, ketone bodies, capric acid)
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Ketogenic diet alone leads to metabolic adaptation; tumors become glutamine‑dependent, suggesting a potential resistance pathway if glutamine is not co‑targeted.

cited_papers: Vander Heiden et al. 2022 Nat Metab

key_findings: Senescent CAFs (P16+ α‑SMA+) increase tumor collagen deposition and fiber thickness.
Senescent CAFs display higher mitochondrial content but lower per‑mitochondrion membrane potential.
Metabolomics shows accumulation of glycolytic intermediates and early TCA metabolites (citrate, αKG) with reduced downstream TCA metabolites.
IDH2 and IDH3 expression is upregulated in senescent CAFs, suggesting enhanced αKG production for collagen hydroxylation.
Depletion of senescent cells (Ink‑Tag model) reduces collagen abundance in PDAC tumors.
open_questions: Will inhibition of IDH2/3 in senescent CAFs affect tumor growth or immune infiltration?
Are there systemic effects of targeting αKG production in fibroblasts?

key_findings: BRCA2 loss upregulates PKM1 (constitutively active) while PKM2 remains unchanged.
PKM2 activator (dasatinib or mitapivat) selectively kills BRCA2‑KO cells and increases γH2AX.
Overexpression of PKM1 in WT cells sensitizes them to PKM2 activation, confirming PKM1’s role.
In vivo, mitapivat (400 mg PO daily) delays growth of BRCA2‑KO tumors without weight loss or organ toxicity.
PKM activation reduces glucose oxidation in TCA cycle, downregulates ETC complexes, and impairs PINK1‑mediated mitophagy, leading to mitochondrial superoxide accumulation.
open_questions: What transcriptional or splicing mechanisms drive PKM1 upregulation after BRCA loss?
Can PKM1/PKM2 isoform ratio serve as a biomarker to select patients for PKM activation therapy?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: BRCA‑deficient cells may develop resistance via alternative ATP‑generating pathways; combination with PARP inhibitors shows additive effects.

key_findings: A stromal osteomimicry signature, including periostin, distinguishes high‑grade prostate tumors that metastasize to bone.
Periostin is enriched in neuroendocrine prostate cancer stroma and colocalizes with αVβ3/αVβ5 integrin signaling.
Mouse models recapitulate human stromal changes; fibroblast clusters acquire AP1 motifs and lose AR/GR motifs.
Co‑culture of periostin‑expressing fibroblasts or recombinant periostin induces neuroendocrine differentiation (FOXA2) in organoids.
Spatial analysis shows reduced distance between periostin‑positive fibroblasts and neuroendocrine cells in bone metastases versus primary tumors.
open_questions: Can periostin inhibition prevent neuroendocrine transdifferentiation and bone metastasis in vivo?
What are the distinct ECM compositions produced by periostin‑high versus periostin‑low fibroblast clusters?

key_findings: Metabolic gene signatures predict overall metastatic potential with 86% accuracy; metabolic‑only features improve prediction.
Organ‑specific dependencies identified: FASN in brain, PC in lung, GLS1 in bone metastases.
Bone‑metastatic clones exhibit heightened glutamine uptake, increased GLS1 activity, and sensitivity to GLS1 inhibitor CBA39.
Depleting serine/glycine reduces metastasis in bone, kidney, ovary but not in brain, liver, lung.
Integrated MetaboForm platform infers tumor metabolomes from transcriptomics, revealing distinct metabolic landscapes across metastatic sites.
open_questions: Can metabolic dependencies be exploited clinically to prevent organ‑specific colonization?
What determines the heterogeneity of metabolic phenotypes within a single patient’s metastatic lesions?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: GLS1 inhibition shows specificity for bone‑derived clones; transporter inhibition (SLC1A5, SLC38A12) ineffective due to compensatory uptake.

key_findings: CTC burden correlates tightly (R>0.9) with metastatic score in GEM mice.
Single CTCs can be cultured into organoids; organoid size segregates into hypoxic (large) vs. ox‑phos (small) phenotypes.
TMPO knockdown does not affect primary tumor growth but reduces circulating CTCs and bone metastasis in both subcutaneous and intracardiac models.
TMPO activity correlates with hypoxia signatures and organoid size; loss of TMPO shifts metabolism toward oxidative phosphorylation.
Human CRPC CTCs show high nuclear TMPO co‑expressed with lamin, supporting clinical relevance.
open_questions: Does TMPO regulate dormancy versus active dissemination in CTCs?
What upstream signals control TMPO expression in circulating cells?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: TMPO inhibition selectively impairs hypoxia‑adapted CTCs while sparing ox‑phos clones.

key_findings: Only mice colonized with the CRC isolate 11G5 (pks+, clbQ+) showed severe CRC phenotypes, whereas Nissle 1917 did not despite both being pks+.
Deletion of clbQ abolished the tumor‑promoting effect of 11G5, confirming colibactin dependence.
FimH or FimLH loss in 11G5 eliminated epithelial binding, γ‑H2AX induction, and CRC exacerbation.
High‑affinity 11G5 FimH variants restored binding and genotoxicity when expressed in Nissle, demonstrating variant‑specific adhesion strength.
Sibofimlock, a small‑molecule FimH inhibitor, dose‑dependently reduced bacterial adhesion and colibactin‑driven tumor development in vivo.
open_questions: What cellular receptor or transport mechanism mediates colibactin entry into the nucleus after epithelial adhesion?
Do other Enterobacteriaceae employ similar adhesin variants to modulate colibactin toxicity?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: E. coli Nissle 1917, although pks+, fails to promote CRC due to poor epithelial adhesion, highlighting adhesion as a selectivity determinant.

key_findings: High sulfur amino‑acid diet increased inner mucus thickness without increasing goblet cell numbers.
M. schaedleri bloomed in high‑diet mice across three tumor models (MC38, ApcMin, orthotopic organoids).
Diet‑induced tumor protection was lost in Batf3‑KO mice lacking CDC1 dendritic cells.
Neutralizing XCL1 abolished the anti‑tumor benefit of the high diet, implicating NKT‑derived XCL1 as essential.
Conditioned media from M. schaedleri stimulated NKT cells to produce XCL1 in an MR1‑independent manner.
