Tumor‑associated NK cells are heterogeneous; NK2 (CD56bright) are scarce in tumors, indicating subset‑specific targeting challenges.

key_findings: Memory‑like NK cells persisted up to 200 days in some post‑transplant AML patients, far exceeding the typical 10‑12 day lifespan of conventional NK cells.
Four of eight AML patients achieved MRD‑negative complete remission after a single infusion of memory‑like NK cells.
In heavily pre‑treated head and neck cancer patients, 7 of 10 achieved disease control, including one dramatic partial response lasting ~12 months.
CAR‑NK cells armed with a TGF‑β‑responsive IL‑12/IL‑18 circuit cured >90% of mice in aggressive pancreatic and kidney cancer models without systemic toxicity.
Combining engineered tumor‑targeting bacteria expressing IL‑12 and adenosine deaminase with CAR‑NK cells doubled survival in pancreatic cancer mouse models.
open_questions: What is the optimal cytokine payload combination (IL‑12 vs IL‑18 vs others) for maximal NK activation without toxicity?
Can memory‑like NK cells achieve durable remission without subsequent allogeneic stem cell transplant?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Tumor‑derived TGF‑β suppresses NK function; the engineered TGF‑β sensor converts this suppressive signal into IL‑12 production, flipping inhibition into activation.
Adenosine pathway up‑regulation (CD39) on NK cells after bacterial exposure may limit efficacy, addressed by co‑expressing adenosine deaminase in the bacterial vector.

key_findings: Overall response rate of ~50% in heavily pre‑treated relapsed/refractory AML patients.
CR/CRh achieved in 30‑40% of patients with median CR duration of 7.6 months.
High MRD‑negative conversion rates observed across responders.
NK‑cell related adverse events were limited to Grade 1‑2 pyrexia; cytokine release syndrome was minimal compared with CAR‑T therapies.
Platelet and neutrophil counts recovered rapidly after lymphodepletion, indicating limited bone‑marrow toxicity.
open_questions: Will SENTI‑202 demonstrate durable benefit without subsequent allogeneic stem cell transplant?
Can the logic‑gate platform be expanded to other AML antigens or solid tumor indications?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Patients with low baseline hematopoietic stem cell counts showed MLFS responses, suggesting limited efficacy when healthy stem cells are already depleted.
Potential escape via loss of CD33/FLT3 expression remains a concern; ongoing monitoring planned.

key_findings: Enrolled >11,500 high‑risk participants across 65 centers, surpassing the original 10,000 target.
Identified 42 screen‑detected pancreatic cancers, 72% of which were high‑grade dysplasia or Stage I.
Cohort includes >3,000 BRCA carriers and ~900 ATM carriers, providing a rich population for MCED studies.
open_questions: What genomic trajectories (gradual vs. punctuated) underlie early pancreatic tumorigenesis?
Can methylation‑based blood tests (Advantech, PancraSure) achieve sufficient sensitivity/specificity longitudinally?

cited_papers: Nature 2010 mathematical modeling of PDAC trajectory

key_findings: EsaCheck/EsaGuard achieved 90% sensitivity and 92% specificity for non‑dysplastic Barrett's in a pilot of 120 high‑risk asymptomatic subjects.
In four clinical cohorts, Barrett's detection sensitivity ranged 80‑90% and cancer detection was ~100% (one miss).
BAD Very Bad score detected 96% of cancers and 68% of high‑grade dysplasias while flagging only 7% of non‑dysplastic lesions.
Methylated CCNA1 positivity post‑ablation conferred a 25‑fold increased risk of recurrence (13/27 vs 1/53).
EsaCheck received FDA 510(k) clearance; EsaGuard earned FDA breakthrough device designation and guideline inclusion.
open_questions: Can BAD be integrated into routine surveillance to replace random biopsies?
Will methylated CCNA1 reliably predict recurrence across larger post‑ablation cohorts?
How does EsaCheck performance compare head‑to‑head with Cytosponge in short‑segment Barrett's?

cited_papers: Markowitz et al. 2023 Science Translational Medicine

key_findings: Pillar Zero achieves 82‑90% average accuracy across >100 radiology findings, outperforming major commercial vision models.
Image‑only Mirai model surpasses Tyrer‑Cuzick questionnaire for 5‑year breast cancer risk prediction.
CT‑based AI outperforms smoking‑history questionnaires for lung cancer risk.
BRIDGE statistical framework shows >90% overlap of top 5% high‑risk patients across successive AI model versions, enabling adaptive trial reuse.
open_questions: How to ensure equitable performance of foundation models across diverse demographic and scanner variations?
What regulatory pathways will support adaptive AI‑driven trial designs like BRIDGE?
Can synthetic imaging data effectively mitigate distributional bias without compromising clinical validity?

key_findings: Overexpression of DAM2 R404W in patient‑derived GBM stem‑like cells increased tumor sphere size relative to wild‑type and GFP controls.
Orthotopic xenografts of R404W‑overexpressing cells showed larger bioluminescent tumor burden and higher Ki‑67 proliferation than controls.
DAM2 R404W knock‑in mice displayed increased Sox9⁺/BrdU⁺ glial progenitors and decreased double‑cortin⁺ neuronal progenitors in the subventricular zone.
In vitro cultured neural stem cells from R404W mice recapitulated the increased glial progenitor phenotype, indicating a cell‑intrinsic effect.
Low‑grade glioma models generated via rCas9‑tVA with PDGF‑β showed higher proliferation (OLIG2⁺) and histologic features of malignant transformation in R404W mice.
Preliminary survival analysis suggests reduced overall survival in R404W mice bearing low‑grade glioma.
open_questions: What downstream pathways mediate the R404W‑driven glial progenitor expansion—canonical Wnt activation or alternative signaling?
Can pharmacologic inhibition of the identified pathways mitigate the tumor‑promoting effects of DAM2 R404W?

key_findings: Aged (22 mo) mice injected with lentiviral PIK3CA H1047R develop palpable tumors earlier and with higher incidence than young (2 mo) mice.
Mid‑aged mice show non‑palpable micro‑lesions with high Ki‑67, indicating early oncogenic activation.
Whole‑mount analysis reveals focal lesions in young mice versus diffuse ductal proliferation in aged mice.
Tumor growth rate is slower in aged mice despite earlier onset, mirroring clinical observations of less aggressive tumors in older patients.
ERα expression is higher in tumor‑adjacent glands, suggesting hormonal priming in the aged niche.
Flow cytometry shows increased PIK3CA‑positive cells in mid‑aged and aged glands, localized at the basal‑luminal boundary.
open_questions: Does estrogen signaling cooperate with mutant PIK3CA to drive tumor initiation in aged mammary tissue?
How do multiple pregnancies or ovarian hormone depletion affect the susceptibility of aged mammary epithelium to PIK3CA‑driven transformation?

key_findings: PIK3CA H1047R bladder organoids show increased sensitivity to alpelisib and pirtobrutinib (piptilicide) compared with WT organoids in vitro.
Both hotspot and WT organoids are resistant to growth in immunocompetent mice unless co‑implanted with CAFs.
Co‑implantation with CAFs enables tumor formation in flank; alpelisib treatment reduces tumor size and Ki‑67 proliferation in both genotypes.
Co‑culture reveals CAF‑derived IL‑6 and organoid‑derived GM‑CSF; GM‑CSF knockout does not consistently affect tumor formation.
open_questions: What immune cell subsets mediate the rejection of luciferase‑expressing organoids in immunocompetent hosts?
Does IL‑6/STAT3 signaling contribute to CAF‑driven engraftment, and can JAK inhibition enhance alpelisib efficacy?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Alpelisib efficacy in vivo is not genotype‑specific, suggesting microenvironment‑driven sensitivity.

key_findings: Organoids recapitulate tumor‑type specific transcriptomic signatures (adenocarcinoma vs squamous) observed in spatial profiling.
Responder patients (no event at 2 yr) show enrichment of inflammatory pathways in organoids, whereas non‑responders do not.
Co‑culture with pre‑activated allogeneic immune cells shows significantly higher CD45⁺ infiltration in non‑responder organoids.
Infiltrating CD8⁺ T cells in non‑responder organoids display an exhausted phenotype (e.g., PD‑1⁺, TIM‑3⁺) both at baseline and after cisplatin exposure.
PD‑L1 CPS and mutation status did not predict organoid responder classification.
open_questions: Can modulation of the exhausted CD8⁺ phenotype (e.g., checkpoint blockade) restore cytotoxicity in non‑responder organoids?
What pathways absent in organoids (e.g., Notch signaling) contribute to the discordance between spatial tissue and organoid data?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Exhausted CD8⁺ phenotype in non‑responders suggests intrinsic immune resistance despite higher infiltration.

key_findings: Aged bone marrow CD34⁺ cells transduced with APOBEC3C show a ~10‑fold increase in GFP‑reporter exon‑skipping versus cord blood controls.
RNA‑seq of aged APOBEC3C‑overexpressing HSPCs reveals up‑regulation of spliceosome genes (SRSSFs, SF3Bs) and increased exon‑skipping events.
Live imaging in the nanobioreactor demonstrates migration of transduced HSPCs toward the SurgiFoam niche and a shift from RFP (exon inclusion) to GFP (exon skipping) over 72 h.
FACS analysis confirms a significant increase in GFP⁺ cells in APOBEC3C‑overexpressing samples compared with empty vector.
open_questions: Does nuclear localization of APOBEC3C enhance its splicing impact, and can relocalization mitigate exon skipping?
Which specific splicing events driven by APOBEC3C contribute to myeloid bias or leukemic transformation?

key_findings: Ex vivo microtumor responses to carboplatin/paclitaxel correlate with clinical C125 biomarker and predict progression‑free survival.
Mirvetuximab soravtansine efficacy varies widely among 25 ovarian patient samples, matching FRα expression heterogeneity.
ADC response correlates with paclitaxel sensitivity, reflecting shared microtubule inhibition.
Combination of mirvetuximab with olaparib yields synergistic killing in a subset of samples, while others are driven mainly by olaparib alone.
Target antigen profiling reveals intra‑patient FRα heterogeneity, influencing ADC efficacy.
open_questions: Can ex vivo microtumor profiling predict long‑term clinical outcomes for ADC‑based regimens across cancer types?
What molecular features define the subset that benefits from ADC‑PARP inhibitor synergy?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Patients with low FRα expression exhibit resistance to the ADC despite high drug exposure.

key_findings: A nine‑cytokine eLive index predicts ICI response with 93% accuracy in a validation cohort.
Unsupervised clustering of cytokine responses defines four immune phenotypes, each with distinct cytokine patterns (e.g., IFN‑γ, CXCL9, CCL22, IL‑10, VEGF).
Subcluster 1 (TH1‑inflamed) shows CD8⁺ T‑cell activation (CD69⁺) and immune triads in NSCLC samples.
Subcluster 3 (cytotoxic) displays granzyme A/B up‑regulation and VEGF, indicating combined cytotoxic and angiogenic remodeling.
Multiplex IF confirms spatial co‑localization of T cells, B cells, and macrophages in responder biopsies.
open_questions: Do the identified immune subclusters correlate with duration of response or overall survival?
Can adding VEGF or myeloid‑targeted agents convert non‑responder phenotypes into responder phenotypes?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Non‑responder cluster shows minimal cytokine induction despite ICI exposure, indicating intrinsic immune suppression.

key_findings: Nascent and mature rRNA levels are elevated in primary AML blasts versus healthy hematopoietic cells.
HOXA9 activation drives Pol I expression and rRNA synthesis; HOXA9 inactivation reduces rRNA production before cell cycle changes.
Targeted degradation of POLR1A with dTAG decreases rRNA synthesis, induces G1 arrest, differentiation, and reduces viability.
Pol I degradation synergizes with venetoclax (Z-score >10) to enhance AML cell killing, independent of TP53 mutation.
open_questions: What is the therapeutic window for Pol I inhibition in vivo?
Can Pol I degradation overcome venetoclax resistance in patient-derived xenografts?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Pol I inhibition may have a therapeutic window due to AML addiction to rRNA synthesis.

key_findings: CYP4A22-AS1 is upregulated in cervical adenocarcinoma and predicts poor survival.
Knockdown of CYP4A22-AS1 increases radiation-induced apoptosis and DNA damage markers.
CYP4A22-AS1 regulates glycolysis via upregulation of PK1 through YBX1 interaction.
PK1 depletion reverses glycolytic enhancement and radiosensitizes CYP4A22-AS1 overexpressing cells.
In vivo, CYP4A22-AS1 overexpression accelerates tumor growth in mouse models.
open_questions: Does the CYP4A22-AS1/YBX1/PK1 axis operate in other tumor types?
Can pharmacologic inhibition of PK1 sensitize tumors to radiotherapy?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: CYP4A22-AS1 mediates resistance to radiation by metabolic reprogramming.

key_findings: Nanoassembly size ~6.3 nm enables renal filtration and accumulation in tumor kidney.
Both miR‑196b antagomir and CIA1 independently down‑regulate CAF activation (α‑SMA) and ECM markers (collagen I, LOX).
Conditioned media from treated CAFs reduces RCC cell apoptosis resistance, EMT markers, and migration.
In orthotopic RENCA mice, combined nanoassembly markedly reduces tumor volume and weight without systemic toxicity.
Treatment increases intratumoral CD8⁺ T cells, dendritic cells, and NK cells while decreasing Tregs and suppressive myeloid cells.
open_questions: Can targeting PDGFRβ improve nanoassembly tumor specificity?
What is the optimal dosing schedule for sustained CAF reprogramming?

key_findings: Mitochondrial SNPs in tRNA^Arg D‑loop differ among mouse strains and associate with metastatic burden.
Northern blots reveal 40‑50 nt tRNA^Arg fragments whose abundance varies with mitochondrial genotype.
Enzymatic end‑repair and demethylation enable detection of these fragments by small‑RNA‑seq.
MINX mice with mismatched mitochondria show altered primary tumor latency and number of lung metastases.
Fragment production is higher in strains with higher metastatic propensity, implicating a functional role.
open_questions: What endonuclease generates the mt‑tRNA^Arg fragments?
Do the fragments act in stromal cells or tumor cells to promote metastasis?

key_findings: Urinary EV isolation increases miRNA read proportion fivefold.
A 11‑miRNA feature set yields AUC 0.94 for cancer detection; performance holds in age‑matched subset.
Three‑miRNA prognostic panel (selected from 11) predicts recurrence‑free survival with HR 8.3 and 3‑year AUC 0.80.
Age and other clinical covariates do not confound the detection score.
open_questions: Will the miRNA panel retain performance in broader, multi‑ethnic cohorts?
Can longitudinal urine sampling monitor treatment response?

key_findings: Modified miR‑15a reduces viability of ovarian cancer cells at low nanomolar concentrations without delivery vehicle.
The construct retains potency in olaparib‑resistant cells, showing similar IC50 values.
RNA‑seq reveals up‑regulation of DNA damage pathways and down‑regulation of WNT, mTOR, AMPK signaling.
Western blots confirm down‑regulation of CHEK1 and E1, and activation of CDK1/CDC25A.
Bliss analysis demonstrates strong synergy between the modified miR‑15a and olaparib.
In vivo, treatment (3.75 mg/kg) markedly suppresses metastatic tumor growth in both parental and resistant models with no observable toxicity.
open_questions: What is the pharmacokinetic profile of the modified miR‑15a in vivo?
Can the approach be translated to other PARP‑resistant tumor types?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Modified miR‑15a overcomes olaparib resistance regardless of BRCA or TP53 status.

key_findings: Doxorubicin or fractionated irradiation induces dose‑dependent senescence in TNBC xenografts (X‑gal staining, beta‑gal activity).
Co‑injection of senescent cells with parental 231 cells does not affect primary tumor size but increases lung metastases (p<0.01).
Senescent cells accelerate early dissemination: 3‑day tail‑vein experiments show higher lung luciferase signal versus parental cells alone.
3D imaging reveals larger tumor cell clusters and extravasation of senescent cells themselves in the lung.
RNA‑seq identifies up‑regulation of adhesion pathways; JUP (plakoglobin) is highly expressed in senescent cells.
JUP knockout abolishes senescent‑cell‑mediated adhesion, cluster formation, and early dissemination (p<0.001).
In immunocompetent mice, senescent cells further enhance metastatic outgrowth beyond early dissemination, suggesting an immune‑modulatory role.
open_questions: Which immune cell subsets mediate the enhanced metastatic outgrowth observed in immunocompetent mice?
Does the JUP‑dependent clustering mechanism operate in metastatic sites other than lung?

key_findings: Normal breast tissue stiffness ~100‑200 Pa; invasive tumors reach 5‑6 kPa (30‑fold increase).
TAK2 knockdown or pharmacologic inhibition in 3D hydrogel (≤150 Pa) increases cell invasion and mesenchymal marker expression (vimentin, N‑cadherin).
TAK2 phosphorylation is high at low stiffness and drops sharply with increased matrix rigidity.
TAK2 inhibition (Tucabasertib) phenocopies knockdown, enhancing EMT and lung dissemination in orthotopic mouse models.
TAK2 interacts with IFN‑α1 and EPHA2 at low stiffness; high stiffness disrupts these interactions, activating Nyn‑mediated Twist1 phosphorylation.
Patient‑derived organoids recapitulate stiffness‑dependent invasion; TAK2 inhibition drives EMT markers and Twist1 nuclear localization.
open_questions: What upstream signals regulate IFN‑α1 expression in the tumor microenvironment?
Can pharmacologic activation of TYK2 counteract stiffness‑driven EMT in vivo?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: TAK2 activity is selectively lost in high‑stiffness environments, suggesting a context‑dependent therapeutic window.

key_findings: SPP1‑high macrophages are present in >80 % of CRC brain metastasis samples and co‑localize with tumor cells and fibroblasts.
Spatial neighborhood analysis identifies two macrophage‑enriched niches; one directly contacts tumor cells, the other contacts stromal cells.
SPP1 knockout in macrophages reduces expression of lipid‑metabolism genes (e.g., SQLE) and diminishes tumor cell invasion in co‑culture.
Macrophage SPP1 loss decreases tumor cell expression of metastasis‑related genes (e.g., S100 family, VIM).
Organ‑on‑a‑chip assays show a ~40 % reduction in macrophage migration speed when SPP1 is deleted.
Analysis of paired primary CRC and brain mets shows higher predicted SPP1‑integrin/CD44 interactions in brain lesions (p<0.01).
open_questions: Do SPP1‑positive macrophages also modulate the blood‑CSF barrier and facilitate tumor cell entry?
Is there a therapeutic window for targeting SPP1 without impairing normal bone‑marrow macrophage function?

key_findings: Low KPC1 expression correlates with high ZEB1 and CDH2 (N‑cadherin) in metastatic melanoma samples (p<0.001).
KPC1 knockout in melanoma cells increases ZEB1 protein levels without changing mRNA, indicating post‑translational regulation.
Cycloheximide chase shows prolonged ZEB1 half‑life in KPC1‑deficient cells.
Co‑IP demonstrates direct binding of KPC1 to ZEB1.
High KPC1 / low ZEB1 cohort exhibits significantly better overall survival (HR 0.45, 95% CI 0.30‑0.68).
MicroRNA‑155 mediates KPC1 down‑regulation in melanoma.
open_questions: Can pharmacologic activation of KPC1 be achieved in patients?
Does KPC1 loss affect immune checkpoint therapy response in melanoma?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: KPC1 loss does not affect p65 NF‑κB subunit, indicating selective impact on the p50 pathway.

key_findings: Jagged1‑positive breast cancer cells show >3‑fold increase in lymphovascular invasion compared with Jagged1‑negative controls (p<0.001).
Jagged1 overexpression leads to larger lymph node tumor burden (RFP‑PanCK area) and earlier colonization.
Coating lymphatic endothelial cells with Jagged1 protein disrupts VE‑cadherin junctions and creates intercellular gaps.
Notch4 neutralizing antibody blocks Jagged1‑induced endothelial gap formation and reduces transendothelial migration (≈45 % reduction).
VEGF‑R3 soluble trap reduces lymph node metastasis but does not affect primary tumor growth.
High Jagged1 expression in lymph node metastases predicts shorter relapse‑free survival (HR 2.1).
open_questions: Does Jagged1 also modulate immune cell recruitment within the lymph node microenvironment?
Can combined Notch4 and VEGF‑R3 blockade prevent distant organ metastasis originating from lymph nodes?
readouts: In vivo lymph node imaging (RFP, dextran)
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Jagged1‑driven effects are gamma‑secretase‑independent, indicating resistance to canonical Notch inhibitors.

key_findings: Allogeneic CD19 CAR‑T in 19 high‑risk pediatric B‑ALL patients achieved 100% MRD‑negative CR with a 3‑year PFS of 42% and no grade 3‑4 CRS/ICANS.
Only two cases of acute GvHD occurred (both grade 2, resolved with steroids/JAK1/2 inhibitor) despite use of unmanipulated donor cells.
CD7 CAR‑T with a protein‑expression blocker induced complete MRD‑negative remissions in two pediatric patients, one remaining disease‑free at 2 years post‑allograft.
GD2 CAR‑T in neuroblastoma (n=35) yielded >50% 5‑year EFS in low‑burden disease, with better outcomes when cells were collected at diagnosis.
Pre‑clinical data showed that knocking down TCR/HLA and CD52 together markedly improves expansion and persistence of allogeneic CAR‑T cells.
open_questions: What is the optimal lymphodepletion regimen to balance safety and CAR‑T expansion in allogeneic settings?
Can broader antigen targeting (e.g., dual CARs) further reduce relapse due to antigen loss?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Two patients relapsed with CD19‑negative blasts, highlighting antigen‑loss escape.
CD7 CAR‑T efficacy limited by low CD3+ cell counts or high blast contamination preventing product generation.

key_findings: Cord‑blood derived CD70 CAR‑NK cells from optimal units (frozen ≤24 h, nucleated RBC ≈ 80 M) yielded 70% 1‑year PFS and 95% 1‑year OS, whereas delayed‑freeze units performed poorly.
In a 42‑patient Hodgkin lymphoma study combining AFM13 with CAR‑NK, overall response rate exceeded 90% with two‑thirds achieving CR, despite lack of bridging therapy.
CAR‑NK cells persisted up to 6 months in peripheral blood, with early clonal expansion (clone 0) followed by emergence of a memory‑like clone (clone 4) linked to long‑term persistence.
CD5 CAR‑NK therapy in T‑PLL achieved CR in 3 of 4 heavily pre‑treated patients, with donor NK cells tracking to disease clearance.
Manufacturing from a single cord‑blood unit can produce 250 patient doses at <$600 per dose, enabling off‑the‑shelf scalability.
open_questions: How does the source of NK cells (cord blood vs peripheral blood vs iPSC) affect long‑term persistence and anti‑tumor immunity?
Can IL‑21 armoring further improve NK‑cell metabolism and durability compared with IL‑15?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Patients with cord‑blood units frozen after 24 h showed markedly inferior outcomes, indicating product quality as a critical variable.
Limited NK‑cell lifespan (1‑2 weeks) without cytokine support may restrict durability in non‑engineered NK approaches.

key_findings: In the MRD‑guided ALO‑501A trial, 7 of 8 patients cleared MRD after a single dose of allogeneic CD19 CAR‑T with standard flu‑cyclophosphamide lymphodepletion, without CRS/ICANS.
CD70‑targeted allogeneic CAR‑T (LO316) achieved a 31% ORR in CD70‑high RCC, with durable responses >12 months in most responders.
Gene‑editing approaches (TCR knockout, CD52 knockout, HLA‑E insertion) enable allogeneic CAR‑T expansion comparable to autologous products despite HLA‑agnostic lymphodepletion.
Selective depletion of alloreactive host T cells via CD70 targeting (the “dagger” approach) enhances CAR‑T persistence and reduces rejection.
open_questions: Will dual CD19/CD70 CAR‑T maintain expansion and safety comparable to single‑antigen CARs?
What is the optimal lymphodepletion intensity for MRD‑only settings to balance safety and efficacy?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: CD70 expression on activated host T cells can cause fratricide; a cis‑masking antibody strategy is used to mitigate this.
Patients receiving anti‑CD52 lymphodepletion showed longer CAR‑T persistence than those without.

key_findings: Classical SCC shows focal 3q amplification of SOX2 and a selective dependency on SOX2 for proliferation.
SOX2 knockdown reduces chromatin accessibility at thousands of sites and downregulates the classical SCC gene signature.
SOX2 overexpression restores accessibility and upregulates ferroptosis suppressor genes (GPX2, GSR, AKR1C3, SLC25A10).
SOX2‑deficient classical SCC cells exhibit increased lipid peroxidation and apoptosis upon ferroptosis inducer ML162 treatment.
open_questions: What upstream signals drive SOX2 amplification in the classical subtype?
Can pharmacologic inhibition of SOX2 or its downstream ferroptosis suppressors sensitize tumors to ferroptosis inducers?

key_findings: FOXP2B is highly up‑regulated in transformed small‑cell samples compared with de novo small‑cell.
FOXP2B overexpression reduces total and phospho‑EGFR levels and induces neuroendocrine markers (ASCL1, synaptophysin, chromogranin) in p53/Rb‑deficient LUAD cells.
Combined FOXP2B overexpression and REST inhibition further enhances neuroendocrine marker expression.
FOXP2B directly binds the EGFR locus, suggesting transcriptional repression of EGFR.
open_questions: What upstream signals induce FOXP2B expression during transformation?
Can FOXP2B inhibition prevent or reverse neuroendocrine transdifferentiation in vivo?

key_findings: CRISPR screen identified MBD4 as a top gene whose loss rescues growth suppression caused by AR‑ARE activation.
MBD4 knockout in LNCaP cells expands FOXA1‑motif enhancer accessibility and increases AR and H3K27ac signals at these sites.
Overexpression of MBD4 reduces FOXA1 enhancer sites, while knockout in normal prostate organoids drives luminal differentiation (CK8/18 up, CHOP2 down).
MBD4 interacts with HDAC1/2, suggesting a deacetylase‑mediated mechanism restricting FOXA1 activity.
open_questions: Does pharmacologic inhibition of MBD4 phenocopy the genetic knockout in prostate cancer models?
How does the MBD4‑HDAC interaction mechanistically suppress FOXA1 pioneer function?

key_findings: DPX8743 dissolves MYC condensates in MYC‑high tumor cells but not in normal cells with basal MYC levels.
Condensate dissolution correlates with G1 arrest, reduced MYC target expression, and tumor regression in MYC‑amplified CDX/PDX models.
Compound activity is potentiated by higher MYC protein levels and MYC genetic dependency; MYC knockdown desensitizes cells.
Seven‑day rat toxicology shows no weight loss or major organ toxicity except reversible thymus atrophy, indicating a therapeutic index >4×.
open_questions: What are the precise upstream protein targets of DPX8743 that mediate condensate dissolution?
Can DPX8743 be combined with standard MYC‑dependent therapies to enhance efficacy?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Selectivity achieved by phenotypic condensate screening; pan‑transcription inhibitors lack this specificity.

key_findings: NSD3 interacts with BRD4‑NUT and deposits H3K36me2 at mega‑domains.
NSD3 knockdown reduces H3K36me2, diminishes BRD4‑NUT chromatin binding, and lowers condensate intensity while increasing condensate number.
Hi‑C reveals ~2‑fold loss of long‑range contacts between mega‑domains upon NSD3 depletion.
Genes within mega‑domains, especially MYC targets, are down‑regulated, leading to modest growth inhibition and differentiation markers up‑regulation.
open_questions: Will pharmacologic NSD3 inhibition recapitulate genetic knockdown effects in vivo?
Are other NSD family members compensatory in NUT carcinoma?

key_findings: ecDNA exhibits the highest DNA and RNA fusion frequencies across cancers.
PVT1‑MYC is the most prevalent fusion on ecDNA, with >98% of fusions placing PVT1 at the 5′ end.
PVT1‑MYC transcripts show greater RNA stability and drive six‑fold stronger MYC‑target activation than canonical MYC.
In MYC‑depleted cells, PVT1‑MYC rescues viability more efficiently than canonical MYC.
open_questions: Can PVT1‑MYC fusion peptides serve as neo‑antigens for immunotherapy?
What mechanisms regulate the initial formation of ecDNA‑driven fusions?
readouts: TCGA and CCLE whole‑genome & RNA‑seq analysis

key_findings: VNTR2‑1 antisense transcript is expressed and contains multiple DRACH motifs for METTL3‑dependent m6A modification.
M6A‑intact reporter shows higher luciferase activity; METTL3 inhibition reduces this activity.
Flag‑tagged VNTR2‑1AS construct produces protein, confirming translational competence.
Overexpression of VNTR2‑1AS up‑regulates DNA replication and cell‑cycle pathways; knockout reduces these pathways and slows proliferation.
Translation‑deficient start‑codon mutant fails to enhance proliferation, indicating translation‑dependent function.
open_questions: Does VNTR2‑1AS affect TERT expression or telomere biology?
Can targeting METTL3 or the VNTR2‑1AS peptide provide therapeutic benefit in VNTR‑expanded cancers?

key_findings: The GLITZ Clinical Trial IND application was approved by the US FDA and Health Canada to assess multi-biomarker informed treatment in gastroesophageal cancer.
Cancer mortality has decreased by nearly 35% since the peak in the 1990s.
The number of cancer survivors in the US has increased by approximately 6.6 million over the last 15 years.
Over 20 new anticancer therapeutics were FDA approved between July 2024 and June 2025.
Targeting programmed cell death pathways is an effective strategy for treating chronic lymphocytic leukemia and acute myelogenous leukemia.
Venetoclax was successfully translated from laboratory research into a standard of care for AML patients.
RB loss combined with PTEN or TP53 loss drives adenocarcinoma-to‑neuroendocrine transition in mouse prostate models.
Matrix withdrawal or β1‑integrin deletion induces ASCL1 expression within 7 days in organoids.
LATS inhibition restores YAP activity and blocks ASCL1 up‑regulation, demonstrating reversibility of lineage transition.
Combined TEAD and Notch inhibition drives >90% of organoid cells to a neuroendocrine state.
FOXA1 relocalization to TEAD‑bound enhancers is required for transition; FOXA1 knockout prevents neuroendocrine differentiation.
Neuroendocrine cells become dependent on L‑MYC/TIP60 partnership, revealing a potential therapeutic vulnerability.
open_questions: Can pharmacologic reversal of neuroendocrine state improve response to AR‑targeted therapies?
What are the optimal timing and sequencing of TEAD/Notch inhibition with immunotherapies such as DLL3‑CAR T cells?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Lineage plasticity creates resistance to androgen‑targeted therapy by bypassing AR dependence.
Neuroendocrine transition may render tumors resistant to AR‑directed agents but creates new antigenic targets (e.g., DLL3).

key_findings: IL‑18‑armored CAR T cells achieved 75% complete response in CAR‑refractory lymphoma with no increase in CRS.
Dual‑target EGFRvIII/IL‑13Rα2 CAR T delivered via Ommaya achieved 2 PRs and ~70% disease control in 18 glioblastoma patients.
Higher intratumoral NK cell levels predicted longer PFS, whereas higher Treg levels predicted resistance in glioblastoma CAR T trials.
Sequential anti‑FAP followed by anti‑mesothelin CAR T in KPC mice markedly improved survival compared with either monotherapy.
Lipid‑nanoparticle‑delivered anti‑FAP CAR RNA achieved superior tumor control versus retroviral CAR T in pancreatic cancer models.
open_questions: What are the optimal biomarkers to predict CAR T persistence in solid tumors?
Can transient stromal depletion combined with CAR T lead to durable responses in patients?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: CAR T cells show limited infiltration and rapid exhaustion in dense pancreatic stroma.
Neuroendocrine lineage plasticity in prostate cancer creates heterogeneous antigen expression, reducing efficacy of DLL3‑CAR T.

cited_papers: Rork et al. 2023 J Clin Oncol

key_findings: Identified UBE2M as a global regulator of >200 E3 ligases, enabling phenotypic discovery of molecular glues.
Discovered DHTC3, a molecular glue that recruits FBXO3 to degrade BET4 via a chemically derived exit vector.
Revealed IBG‑1 acts via intermolecular bivalent gluing, bridging two RAD4 bromodomains and recruiting DCAF16 despite low affinity.
Showed that many kinase inhibitors cause “supercharging” of native degradation, leading to target destabilization without a dedicated E3 ligase.
Demonstrated that fulvestrant induces SUMOylation of ERα, which is required for transcriptional repression, while degradation by RNF4/RNF111 is dispensable.
open_questions: Can SUMOylation‑inducing small molecules be generalized to other oncogenic transcription factors?
What determines the selectivity of inhibitor‑induced supercharging across the kinome?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Molecular glues can target previously undruggable proteins by reshaping ligase surfaces.
Kinase inhibitor‑induced degradation may be context‑dependent, limiting broad applicability.

key_findings: SPARK predicts 40 molecular programs from routine pathology slides with AUC ~0.90 and Pearson ~0.74.
Adding program-level information to image features improves prediction of disease‑free survival and treatment response across multiple cancer types.
Mirai mammography model achieves a 5‑year c‑index of 0.80, outperforming density (c‑index 0.50) and questionnaire‑based risk models (c‑index 0.63).
High‑risk patients identified by Mirai correspond to risk levels exceeding those of BRCA1 carriers.
Prospective trials (UMass, UCSF, Israel, MiPEBS) are underway to evaluate AI‑driven risk‑adapted screening.
open_questions: How can AI‑derived molecular program maps be prospectively validated as predictive biomarkers for therapy selection?
What regulatory frameworks are needed to integrate AI risk models into standard screening guidelines?

key_findings: Both CTLA-4 and PD-1 colitis show expansion of resident memory CD8 T cells and Th1/Th17 CD4 effector cells.
Regulatory T cells are broadly expanded rather than depleted in human colitis biopsies.
CTLA-4 colitis uniquely expands S1PR1+ Treg populations not seen in PD-1 colitis.
Clonotypic expansion is observed in effector cells, with resident memory clones dominating in healthy controls and effector clones dominating in colitis.
open_questions: What is the functional role of the expanded S1PR1+ Treg population in CTLA-4 colitis?
Can peripheral blood TCR signatures predict imminent colitis before tissue symptoms appear?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: No depletion of Tregs observed with CTLA-4 blockade in human colitis, contrary to mouse models.
S1PR1+ Tregs may represent a compensatory but insufficient regulatory response.

key_findings: Wild‑derived microbiota, but not standard SPF microbiota, enables severe colitis after anti‑CTLA‑4 treatment.
Colitis is CD4‑Th1 dependent; depletion of CD4 T cells or neutralization of IFN‑γ abolishes disease.
Peripheral Treg depletion (Helios‑negative FoxP3+ cells) occurs with CTLA‑4 antibody; thymic Tregs remain.
Fc‑null CTLA‑4 antibody (H11 extender) retains anti‑tumor activity while eliminating colitis, demonstrating Fc‑dependence of toxicity.
Clonotypic analysis reveals oligoclonal expansion of Th1 cells recognizing microbial antigens in colitic mice.
open_questions: Which specific microbial antigens are recognized by the oligoclonal Th1 repertoire?
Can the Fc‑null strategy be translated to human CTLA‑4 antibodies without loss of efficacy in diverse tumor types?
What is the role of the residual peripheral Tregs in tumor control versus toxicity?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Fc‑mediated depletion of peripheral Tregs drives colitis; Fc‑null antibodies avoid this effect.
Microbiota composition dictates susceptibility to checkpoint‑induced colitis.

cited_papers: Nunez et al. 2024 Immune checkpoint blockade induce colitis is microbiota dependent

key_findings: TAZ-CAMTA1 fusion activates MAPK pathway; MEK inhibitor trametinib shows IC50 <10 nM in colony assays.
Phase 2 trial of trametinib in unresectable/metastatic EHE yielded 20 responders among 24 patients but did not meet primary endpoint for FDA approval.
Genetically engineered TAZ-CAMTA1 homozygous mice develop histologically identical EHE tumors, providing a faithful preclinical model.
CDK9 inhibitors (dinaciclib, CGP) induce apoptosis in EHE cell lines and dramatically reduce lung tumor burden in xenograft models.
Combination of MEK inhibition with TEAD inhibition (MGH CP1) shows synergistic growth suppression in vitro.
NMR‑based fragment screening identified small‑molecule hits targeting TEAD interface pockets, achieving sub‑micromolar affinity after optimization.
open_questions: What is the precise functional contribution of the CAMTA1 portion of the fusion to oncogenesis?
Can TEAD inhibitors be optimized for clinical use in EHE patients?
What mechanisms underlie trametinib resistance in EHE?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Trametinib toxicity limited treatment duration in some patients.
CDK9 inhibition appears selective for EHE cells due to dependence on transcriptional elongation complex.

cited_papers: Rubin et al. 2024 Clinical Cancer Research

key_findings: Received 525 research proposals in the past cycle.
Allocated $15 M to 34 projects across 150 investigators.
Engaged 20 industry partners in the adaptive trial platform.
Goal to increase 5‑year metastatic CRC survival from 13% to 35% within five years.
Advocate pool composition: 83% female, 17% male.
Processed 86 matching requests with 250 advocate responses.
Reviewed 328 pilot grants with participation of 36 individual advocates.
Implemented systematic evaluation surveys with >90% positive scores on respect and impact.
70+ patient advocates contributed to 21 preclinical immunotherapy teams.
Advocate involvement increased trainee awareness of patient relevance from 0% to ~50% in surveys.
Co‑created lay summaries, glossaries, and videos improved communication of complex TCR science.
Advocates reported enhanced understanding of basic research, while trainees noted better non‑scientist communication.
Assembled a cohort of >60 supratentorial ependymoma samples covering all molecular subclusters.
YAP1‑fusion tumors project to later developmental stages and consist almost exclusively of differentiated ependymal‑like cells.
CEFTA/RELA‑fusion tumors contain a mixture of neuroepithelial‑like stem cells, embryonic‑like cells, and differentiated ependymal/neuronal states.
Spatial transcriptomics identified two global tumor architectures (organized vs disorganized) driven by the presence of a mesenchymal‑hypoxia cell state.
In vitro cultures grown as PDX or neuron/astrocyte co‑cultures recapitulate the full differentiation hierarchy, whereas neurosphere‑only cultures enrich for stem‑like cells.

In vivo two‑photon imaging showed distinct morphologies and migration patterns: stem‑like cells are slow/proliferative, neuronal‑like cells display saltatory migration, and ependymal‑like cells are stationary with dynamic projections.
open_questions: What molecular mechanisms drive the transition from organized to disorganized spatial architecture over time?
Do specific cell states confer resistance to radiation or future targeted therapies?

key_findings: ZFTA/RELA fusion drives strong up‑regulation of ACOD1 and accumulation of itaconate in both mouse and human ependymoma cells.
shRNA knockdown of the fusion or ACOD1 reduces cell viability and ACOD1 expression.
ACOD1 whole‑body or tumor‑cell specific knockout in mice dramatically improves survival (median age 25 days → >50 % long‑term survivors).
Dimethyl itaconate treatment lowers fusion mRNA and protein levels in vitro and in vivo; rescue with exogenous itaconate restores fusion expression.
Itaconate inhibits KDM5 demethylases (IC50 ~470 µM), increasing H3K4me3; KDM5 inhibition phenocopies itaconate’s effect on fusion expression.
Glutamine antagonist GHU‑083 reduces itaconate production, lowers fusion levels, and extends survival in IOE mouse models.
Pharmacologic ACOD1 inhibition prevents spinal metastasis in treated mice (0/7 vs 7/7 in controls).
open_questions: Can selective ACOD1 inhibitors with better brain penetration be developed for clinical use?
What is the impact of ACOD1 inhibition on normal immune cells and macrophage function in patients?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Partial survival benefit in ACOD1 knockout mice suggests residual ACOD1 allele may sustain tumor in ~50 % of animals.

key_findings: CSF of tumor‑bearing mice contains high GM‑CSF levels, absent in tumor‑free controls.
GM‑CSF promotes expansion of CD34⁺MHC‑II⁺ hematopoietic stem cells in calvarial marrow, which migrate to dura and tumor.
These stem cells differentiate into immunosuppressive myeloid cells; CD4⁺ T cells skew toward FoxP3⁺ Tregs.
Intrathecal Lenzilumab lowers CSF GM‑CSF, reduces skull HSC proliferation, decreases tumor‑infiltrating myeloid cells, and increases CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration.
Tumor regression observed in ZFTA‑RELA ependymoma, choroid plexus carcinoma, and group 3 medulloblastoma models; effect replicated with intravenous dosing.
Combination of Lenzilumab with checkpoint inhibition prolongs remission beyond monotherapy.
open_questions: Will anti‑GM‑CSF therapy be effective in adult glioma patients with similar HSC expansion?
What are the specific antigens presented by the MHC‑II⁺ HSCs in the tumor context?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Tumors eventually relapse with CD8⁺ T‑cell exhaustion, suggesting need for checkpoint blockade.

key_findings: JQUAD1 selectively degrades EP300 with minimal effect on CBP in vitro.
AKT‑dysregulated osteosarcoma lines (PTEN loss or AKT amplification) are uniquely sensitive to JQUAD1.
Combining JQUAD1 with AKT inhibitors (MK‑2206 or capivasertib) yields synergistic cell death in ~10‑15% of 800 screened cell lines.
Synergy is linked to reduced translational capacity in sensitive lines, as shown by puromycin incorporation assays.
In orthotopic osteosarcoma xenografts, the JQUAD1 + MK‑2206 combination markedly suppresses tumor growth and prolongs survival compared to either agent alone.
open_questions: Can EP300 degradation be achieved safely in pediatric patients?
What biomarkers predict durable response beyond AKT activation?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Resistance associated with high basal translational rates and lack of AKT activation.
GPC2 downregulation not observed; resistance linked to MDSC infiltration in later studies (other talks).

key_findings: cfDNA quantity at enrollment predicts poorer survival independent of disease burden.
Relapsed neuroblastoma shows enrichment of ALK and RAS/MAPK pathway mutations, including FGFR1.
Longitudinal cfDNA dynamics correlate with treatment response: decrease during response, re‑increase at progression.
Clonal hematopoiesis events (e.g., JAK3) were detected in cfDNA, highlighting need for careful interpretation.
Predicted gene expression from cfDNA fragment patterns identifies activation of oncogenes (e.g., ALK, TERT) at relapse.
open_questions: Can cfDNA‑guided early intervention improve outcomes?
What is the functional impact of identified subclonal mutations?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Emergence of subclonal RAS/MAPK mutations during therapy suggests adaptive resistance.

key_findings: Gamma‑delta T cells are the most spatially privileged population, with ~45% of nearest neighbors being neural blast cells.
T cells in neural‑blast rich domains express exhaustion marker LAG3, whereas those in immune‑rich domains express activation markers CD4 and FOS.
Cross‑patient gamma‑delta clone 2 is detected in tumor, blood, and cfDNA across multiple patients and time points, often adjacent to tumor cells.
Alpha‑beta TCR pairing can be inferred by co‑detection of alpha and beta probes within the same cell, confirming clonotype identity in situ.
Predicted antigen specificity for clone 2 includes NY‑ESO‑1, present in ~23% of neuroblastoma tumors.
open_questions: Do gamma‑delta clones exert functional anti‑tumor activity or are they bystanders?
Can targeting NY‑ESO‑1 improve T‑cell mediated clearance in neuroblastoma?

key_findings: Bicistronic GPC2/B7H3 CAR T cells outperform single‑antigen CARs and co‑transduced mixtures in vitro and in vivo.
Dual CARs achieve complete tumor regressions and long‑term survival in neuroblastoma and medulloblastoma PDX models.
B7H3 expression remains stable under CAR pressure, while GPC2 is frequently down‑regulated, supporting the need for dual targeting.
Mice cured with dual CARs retain persisting memory T cells in bone marrow, conferring protection against rechallenge.
Relapse after dual CAR therapy is associated with increased MDSC infiltration.
open_questions: Will bicistronic CARs retain efficacy in immune‑competent models?
What mechanisms drive GPC2 down‑regulation under CAR pressure?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: GPC2 down‑regulation observed across all treatment groups.
MDSC infiltration linked to relapse in a subset of dual‑CAR treated mice.

cited_papers: Dotti et al. bicistronic CAR study

key_findings: LBR and TMPO are mislocalized to the cell surface specifically in MYC‑driven Group 3 medulloblastoma, not in normal neural cells.
LBR+ tumor cells display high proliferation signatures (G2/M enrichment).
LBR‑CAR and TMPO‑CAR T cells achieve potent killing in vitro at low E:T ratios.
Bispecific CAR combining LBR and TMPO binders yields superior tumor remission and durability in vivo.
Therapy‑adapted mouse models show enrichment of LBR expression after standard chemoradiotherapy, indicating a post‑treatment target.
open_questions: Can LBR/TMPO CARs be combined with checkpoint blockade to overcome T‑cell exhaustion?
Is the surface localization stable over long‑term treatment?
readouts: in vivo tumor clearance in mouse xenografts
RNA‑seq of LBR+ vs LBR‑ sorted cells
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Low antigen density of individual targets necessitates bispecific approach.

key_findings: Electron microscopy shows ~10% neuron‑to‑glioma synapses and glioma‑to‑glioma synapses in G34 xenografts.
Glioma cells exhibit evoked EPSCs and spontaneous activity, indicating functional integration.
Pharmacologic blockade of neuronal activity (TTX, NBQX) abolishes neuron‑induced proliferation boost.
Optogenetic activation of either glutamatergic or GABAergic neurons increases tumor proliferation in vivo.
Proteomics of activity‑stimulated conditioned media identifies N‑cadherin and neurofascin as upregulated secreted factors.
Recombinant N‑cadherin promotes proliferation; neurofascin enhances glioma migration.
open_questions: What receptors mediate N‑cadherin and neurofascin signaling on G34 cells?
Can targeting these adhesion molecules improve survival in vivo?

key_findings: REM422 induces rapid (2‑24 h) depletion of MIB protein in ALL PDX cells at nanomolar concentrations.
In vivo, daily oral REM422 (5 mg/kg) is well tolerated and extends EFS across diverse ALL subtypes.
T‑ALL PDXs show greater benefit (median +33 days, T/C = 3.6) than B‑ALL.
Seven of ten T‑ALL models achieve complete or maintained complete responses, including durable remissions beyond treatment cessation.
MIB expression alone does not fully predict response, indicating additional determinants of sensitivity.
open_questions: What biomarkers beyond MIB expression predict REM422 sensitivity?
Will combining REM422 with NOTCH inhibitors enhance efficacy?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Some T‑ALL PDXs with high MIB expression did not respond, suggesting alternative survival pathways.

key_findings: A monovalent HPV16 VLP trial showed 0 persistent infections in the vaccine arm versus 41 in placebo, demonstrating sterilizing immunity.
Single‑dose HPV vaccination achieved non‑inferior efficacy (97%–98%) compared with two doses in the ESCUDO trial, supporting dose de‑escalation.
Antibody titers after a single dose remain flat over 16 years, declining <2.5% per year, indicating long‑lived plasma cell maintenance.
Real‑world data from Denmark show ~90% protection against cervical cancer precursors in women vaccinated ≤16 y.
Global vaccine uptake has risen from 72% to 78% (≥1 dose) and 75% to 80% (up‑to‑date) among US adolescents, contributing to an estimated 1.4 million future deaths averted.
open_questions: What is the minimal antibody titer required for long‑term protection across diverse HPV genotypes?
Can single‑dose schedules be safely extended to older age groups or immunocompromised populations?

patent_or_ip_hints: NIH patents on HPV VLP technology

key_findings: HPV VLPs bind >90% of a 129‑cell‑line panel, with binding strongly correlated to EMT/TGF‑β transcriptional programs.
In a Phase I/II ocular melanoma trial, the therapeutic VLP‑IR700 regimen markedly prolonged time to standard‑of‑care referral compared with sub‑therapeutic dosing.
Therapeutic dosing halted tumor growth in ocular melanoma patients, suggesting disease‑modifying activity.
A bladder cancer window‑of‑opportunity study showed complete pathological response after intravesical VLP‑IR700 plus light, indicating potent local tumor ablation.
The VLP‑IR700 platform leverages dual specificity (tumor binding + light activation) to achieve on‑target cytotoxicity with minimal off‑target effects.
open_questions: What is the optimal light dose and delivery method for deep‑seated tumors?
Can the VLP‑IR700 platform be combined with checkpoint inhibition to amplify secondary T‑cell responses?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Binding is absent on hematopoietic cells lacking the specific HSPG modifications, providing intrinsic tumor selectivity.

patent_or_ip_hints: NIH patents on HPV VLP technology; IP on VLP‑IR700 conjugate with Ora Biosciences

key_findings: AI‑designed mini‑protein library yielded 45 binders (17% success) with highest affinity of 28 nM in just one month, a three‑fold speedup over traditional methods.

Reinvent AI tool accelerated small‑molecule lead optimization for a confidential target, reducing the design cycle from ~8 months to ~4 months while achieving target‑level potency, clearance, exposure, and tumor growth inhibition.

Computational pathology model identified membrane‑to‑cytoplasm optical density difference as a surrogate for internalization of the TROP2 ADC datupizumab duoxetecane, now entering prospective validation in a phase‑III trial.

A multimodal foundation model built with Tempus and Pathos integrates longitudinal EHR, labs, histology, and genomics to predict control‑arm performance and patient response, aiming to improve phase‑III success rates.
open_questions: How can AI‑driven computational pathology be scaled across diverse ADC platforms beyond TROP2?
What are the optimal data governance frameworks to share multimodal clinical data while preserving patient privacy?

key_findings: AI‑predicted SWIFT domain structures correctly identified three PU.1 TAD binding motifs, validated by pull‑down and HDX experiments.
Fitness correlation across >1,000 cancer cell lines highlighted SWIFT‑containing paralogs (SMARCD1‑3) as top codependencies, suggesting selective vulnerability.
Histone modification profiling showed that specific nucleosome acetylation patterns dramatically modulate BAF complex remodeling activity, revealing allele‑specific inhibition opportunities.
Synthetic‑lethal relationship between SMARCA2 and SMARCA4 mutations was confirmed, positioning SMARCA2 as a high‑value target in SMARCA4‑mutant lung cancer.
open_questions: Can AI‑designed small molecules achieve sufficient selectivity for SWIFT‑mediated PPIs without off‑target chromatin effects?
What is the therapeutic window for targeting intrinsically disordered regions of BAF subunits?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Paralog redundancy within BAF complexes may confer resistance; targeting SWIFT domain offers paralog‑specific selectivity.

key_findings: Design of antibodies against >50 diverse targets succeeded with ≤20 designs per target, yielding binders for ~50% of targets (≈10‑fold improvement over prior 0.1% rates).
Atomic‑resolution predictions matched cryo‑EM structures (global RMSD <2 Å, CDR loop RMSD <1 Å) for five test cases, confirming near‑perfect epitope modeling.
GPCR VHH agonist for CCR8 achieved functional signaling after testing only 10 designs, with 1 agonist hit, demonstrating feasibility of de novo agonist design.
Peptide‑MHC antibody selectively bound KRAS G12V peptide‑MHC complex while sparing WT KRAS and alternative MHCs, illustrating precise epitope discrimination.
Developability metrics (expression, stability, viscosity, polyreactivity) of AI‑generated antibodies matched or exceeded those of clinically approved mAbs on first‑pass designs.
open_questions: How can AI agents be further trained to predict and avoid immunogenic epitopes during antibody design?
What is the upper limit of design‑to‑experiment cycles before diminishing returns in hit rate?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Model failures traced to missing constraints (e.g., membrane or glycan clashes), highlighting need for explicit negative selection prompts.

key_findings: Adolescent high PHDI reduced overall invasive breast cancer risk by >30% for ER-negative tumors.
Association remained significant after adjustment for weight change since age 18.
Effect was strongest in premenopausal women and those with BMI <21 kg/m2 at age 18.
Whole fruits were protective; added saturated and trans fats increased risk.
open_questions: Would consistent adherence to the diet from adolescence through adulthood further reduce risk?
Can intermediate biomarkers (e.g., mammographic density) clarify the causal pathway?

key_findings: Cardiorespiratory multimorbidity (CRM) confers the highest lung cancer risk (HR 4.11) compared with single disease states.
22% of CRD patients progressed to CRM versus 4.9% of CVD patients.
CRM shows the shortest transition time to lung cancer among disease states.
Healthy lifestyle reduces progression from single disease to CRM by 34‑54% and from CRM to lung cancer by 57%.
open_questions: How to account for reverse causality between health status and lifestyle adoption?
What are optimal thresholds for lifestyle scores to maximize risk reduction?

key_findings: First‑generation Japanese immigrants have ~5× higher gastric cancer risk than NHW.
Risk declines across generations but remains ~2.5× higher in third generation.
Pattern is strongest for non‑cardia gastric cancer.
No effect modification by family history, education, BMI, smoking, or sodium intake.
open_questions: Would targeted gastric cancer screening be cost‑effective for high‑risk immigrant groups?
How does H. pylori prevalence across generations influence residual risk?

key_findings: PRIME achieved AUC 0.76 (24 mo) and 0.75 (36 mo) in US validation health systems.
Top 1% risk group has 0.61% 3‑year absolute PDAC risk (1 in 128) and captures 5.8% of incident cases.
Model performance modestly declines in UK Biobank (AUC 0.71) but remains well‑calibrated.
High‑risk individuals have similar prevalence of known PDAC pathogenic germline variants as the general population, indicating capture of sporadic risk.
open_questions: What absolute risk threshold optimally balances detection yield and resource use?
How will prospective implementation affect patient uptake and downstream imaging burden?

key_findings: Patients in the highest BMR quartile had 23% lower risk of overall death (HR 0.77).
Highest BMR quartile showed 36% lower risk of CRC‑specific death (HR 0.64).
Benefit was strongest in men under 50, with ~70% better survival.
BMR correlated positively with BMI and was higher in men than women.
open_questions: Can serial BMR measurements track cachexia development and guide interventions?
How does BMR integrate with imaging‑derived body composition metrics?

key_findings: 14.1% of older cancer patients used telehealth at least once in the first year post‑diagnosis.
Utilization peaked in 2020 (21.2%) then declined to 16.2% in 2021.
Black patients had the lowest utilization (11.2%); Asian/Pacific Islanders highest (17.9%).
Provider type (APPs, female clinicians) and academic facilities increased telehealth delivery.
open_questions: What specific barriers (digital literacy, broadband access) drive lower use in vulnerable groups?
How can provider‑level interventions improve sustained telehealth engagement?
readouts: E&M CPT codes with telehealth modifiers

key_findings: CONFLUENCE includes >2 M participants, tripling effective sample size of prior multi‑ancestry studies.
Identified 545 independent loci, of which 273 are novel.
A 544‑variant PRS improves AUC by 2‑3% across EUR, AFR, and AMR cohorts versus the 313‑variant PRS.
Resource will be publicly released with summary statistics and data access platform.
open_questions: How to calibrate PRS thresholds across ancestries for clinical risk stratification?
Can integration with lifestyle and clinical factors enhance predictive performance?

key_findings: Identified 18 proteins forming a PSPSE score that distinguishes current, former, and never smokers.
Higher PSPSE score significantly associated with increased lung cancer risk (HR ~1.5) in UK Biobank former smokers.
PSPSE score improves PLCOm2012 lung cancer risk prediction, especially in quitters >20 years.
Signature validated in an independent Asian cohort (Shanghai Men's Health Study) with consistent risk association.
open_questions: What are the functional roles of the 18 signature proteins in carcinogenesis?
Can the signature predict response to lung cancer screening or chemoprevention?

key_findings: Height PRS strongly associated with fatal prostate cancer (HR 1.30 per SD).
Residual height after accounting for PRS shows no association, indicating genetics drive the risk.
Androgen response pathway upregulated in tumors of taller men, linking height to prostate cancer biology.
open_questions: Can height PRS improve risk stratification beyond PSA screening?
What specific genetic variants within the PRS mediate androgen pathway activation?

key_findings: Identified three CNA‑based clusters: loss‑dominant (44%), CNA‑quiet (40%), gain‑dominant (16%).
CNA‑quiet tumors have significantly higher immune cell infiltration and improved overall survival.
Within the gain‑dominant cluster, Black women have a 60% higher hazard of death compared to White women.
open_questions: Do specific copy‑number events drive the immune‑cold phenotype in gain‑dominant tumors?
Can targeted therapies reverse the survival disadvantage in Black patients with gain‑dominant HSOC?

key_findings: Tumor‑dominant cytotoxic T‑cell enrichment predicts improved survival (HR 0.68).
Stroma‑dominant cytotoxic enrichment predicts worse survival.
Tumor TIM‑3+ exhaustion associated with better survival among tumors with ≥2% T cells.
open_questions: Would checkpoint blockade efficacy differ by the identified spatial immunotypes?
Can spatial profiling be integrated into routine pathology for risk stratification?

key_findings: DTC‑positive tumors enriched for mutations in Wnt, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, and NRF2 pathways.
Wnt‑mutated DTC‑positive tumors show increased EMT and decreased proliferation signatures.
PI3K‑mutated DTC‑positive tumors display upregulated proliferative pathways and reduced apoptosis.
APOBEC mutagenesis activity nearly doubled in DTC‑positive patients.
open_questions: Can targeting Wnt or PI3K pathways eradicate DTCs and prevent recurrence?
What is the temporal relationship between DTC emergence and pathway activation?

key_findings: PRS distribution unchanged across birth cohorts, but effect size increases in recent cohorts.
Stronger PRS‑CRC association observed in individuals <55 years, unscreened, without family history, and for distal colon/rectal cancers.
Innate immune system pathways enriched among SNPs showing birth‑cohort interaction.
open_questions: Which specific environmental factors (e.g., diet, obesity) drive the observed gene‑environment interaction?
Can integrating PRS with lifestyle scores improve early‑onset CRC screening?

key_findings: rs3742324 region shows allele‑specific enhancer activity and regulates STARD13 expression.
CRISPR deletion of the enhancer reduces STARD13 transcript levels.
STARD13 knockdown leads to greater downregulation of LATAS2 in BRCA2‑mutant cells.
RNA‑seq reveals upregulation of EMT and extracellular matrix genes (e.g., MMP9) when STARD13 is reduced in BRCA2‑mutant background.
open_questions: Does STARD13 modulation affect sensitivity to PARP inhibitors in BRCA2‑mutant tumors?
Are there therapeutic strategies to restore STARD13 activity?

key_findings: Implemented universal consent with >80% accrual across >50,000 patients.
Biorepository contains 1.3 million biospecimens, including 220,000 bone marrow/blood samples from heme malignancy patients.
Insight tool identified 523 AML patients with germline testing versus 1,195 without, revealing ancestry‑linked testing disparities.
open_questions: How will e‑consent impact consent rates across diverse populations?
What strategies will ensure equitable access to germline testing for under‑represented groups?

key_findings: Black AML patients have ~12‑year shorter median OS compared with White patients, especially pronounced in <30 y age group.
NPM1 mutation, usually favorable, predicts adverse outcome in African‑American patients (near‑universal relapse).
PHIP mutations occur in ~7% of African‑American AML and confer aggressive disease in mouse models.
Rho GTPase family mutations are present in 12% of African‑American/A Hispanic AML, a novel finding.
Clonal hematopoiesis is present in 15% of African‑American AML and associates with 80% relapse rate.
open_questions: What molecular mechanisms underlie the ancestry‑specific reversal of NPM1 prognostic impact?
Can targeting PHIP‑driven pathways improve outcomes in high‑risk ancestry groups?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: NPM1 mutation loses its favorable prognostic effect in African ancestry, suggesting ancestry‑specific resistance mechanisms.
CH in African‑American patients predicts high relapse despite being traditionally low‑risk.

key_findings: More than 50% of new pediatric oncology indications (2013‑2024) used pediatric extrapolation.
ICH E11A (2024) formalizes guidance, including allowance for safety extrapolation when supported by data.
Three‑step framework: concept development, plan creation, and plan execution with iterative updates.
Early FDA engagement (early advice meetings, pediatric study plans) is encouraged to reduce uncertainty.
MIDD methods (population PK, PBPK, QSP) can predict pediatric exposure and support dose selection without extensive pediatric trials.
Examples: gadolinium‑based contrast agents, RILACE, itolizumab, rituximab—all received pediatric indications down to neonates via MIDD.
Renal maturation modeling shows GFR normalizes after ~2 years, informing GBCA dosing in infants.
FDA recommends early, iterative MIDD discussions (type D, MIDD‑focused meetings) to reduce uncertainty.
Adult NETTER‑1 trial demonstrated PFS benefit (HR 0.21) and ORR 13% for Lutathera in SSTR‑positive GEP‑NETs.
NETTER‑P enrolled 9 adolescents; safety profile matched adults (lymphopenia, neutropenia).
Organ dosimetry (kidney, bone marrow) in adolescents was comparable to adults, though predicted high‑dose kidney probability exceeded 20% at the 95th percentile.
FDA concluded extrapolation appropriate despite limited pediatric efficacy data, issuing PMRs for long‑term renal and hematologic safety.
Lutathera received FDA approval for adolescents with SSTR‑positive GEP‑NETs in 2024, marking a successful pediatric extrapolation case.
Adult BLAST study showed 81% MRD‑negative conversion, providing a robust efficacy signal for extrapolation.
Pediatric dose‑finding study (MT103205) demonstrated tolerability and similar cytokine release syndrome rates to adults.

Meta‑analysis of three randomized trials (adult E1910, pediatric 201/20215, AALL 1331) plus BLIM‑FANT showed consistent survival benefit across ages, supporting extrapolation to pediatric consolidation therapy.
FDA granted age‑agnostic indications for blinatumomab in MRD‑positive B‑ALL and in consolidation, relying on adult efficacy and pediatric safety/PK data.
Post‑marketing requirements include long‑term safety follow‑up for neurotoxicity and cytokine release syndrome.
Phase 1 of TACA funded to generate 3,000 genomes from 1,500 African cancer patients across 7 countries.
Median sequencing coverage achieved 41X for germline and 121X for somatic samples, comparable to reference datasets.
Tumor mutational burden in African breast cancer cohort comparable to TCGA, suggesting eligibility for checkpoint blockade.
Enrichment of TP53 mutations and novel driver candidates (e.g., LEPR in TNBC, KRTAP10-6 in luminal) relative to European datasets.
Geographic subtype distribution observed: higher triple‑negative breast cancer prevalence in West Africa versus luminal B in East Africa.
Breast cancer proteomics (n=28) identified >2,000 proteins with a five‑fold decrease in CD36 compared to US cohorts.
Machine‑learning classifier achieved AUC 0.96 distinguishing tumor vs normal tissue using proteomic data.
Pancreatic cancer plasma proteomics showed ECM remodeling and inflammatory mediators; LGR1 achieved AUC 0.94 for cancer vs benign.
Prostate cancer tissue proteomics (n>150) uncovered a five‑protein panel linked to neurogenous metastasis.
Gallbladder cancer proteomics identified nine key proteins associated with ECM and smooth muscle contraction loss.
African ancestry patients showed lower CD8 T‑cell infiltration after adjusting for tumor purity and subtype.
MECOM short‑isoform focal amplifications were present in ~35% of African ancestry tumors versus ~10% in European ancestry, linked to poorer progression‑free survival in TCGA.
FBXW7 mutations enriched in African ancestry copy‑number‑high endometrial cancers.
Overall fewer clinically actionable mutations (OncoKB) in African ancestry tumors compared with European ancestry.
Ancestry‑specific expression of PLXNA3 and other genes correlated with admixture proportion.
open_questions: Functional impact of MECOM short‑isoform amplification on tumor biology and therapy response.
Mechanisms underlying reduced CD8 infiltration in high‑African‑ancestry tumors.

key_findings: Risk‑stratified HCC screening using the PLS risk signature improves cost‑effectiveness and predicts incident HCC in >2,000 US patients and a 1,300‑patient NIH cohort.
Low‑dose erlotinib (25‑75 mg) suppresses phospho‑EGFR in cirrhotic liver tissue, with risk‑signature improvement at ≥50 mg and no grade ≥3 toxicity.
Erlotinib reduces early HCC nodules in a rat fibrosis model in a dose‑dependent manner, but has minimal effect on larger established tumors due to poor tumor cell uptake.
Lipophilic statins (atorvastatin) and bariatric surgery improve the PLS risk signature, correlating with lower long‑term HCC incidence.
The EGFR‑driven myofibroblast signature can serve as a surrogate endpoint for future chemoprevention trials (ECHO‑B, CATCH‑B, TOSS).
open_questions: What molecular features determine why only a subset of patients achieve risk‑signature modulation with antiviral or statin therapy?
Can the PLS signature predict response to other targeted agents beyond EGFR inhibition?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Erlotinib fails to shrink larger HCC nodules because the drug is poorly taken up by tumor cells, limiting activity to early, myofibroblast‑driven stages.
Only ~80% of antiviral‑cured patients show risk‑signature reduction, indicating heterogeneity in chemoprevention response.

key_findings: High baseline gamma‑delta T cell levels in blood correlate with disease control and longer PFS/OS in atezo‑bev‑treated HCC.
Interferon‑γ is elevated at baseline in responders, supporting a Th1‑type immune milieu.
The HepatoSAJ CT‑AI model predicts liver decompensation risk (AUC ≈ 0.84) better than conventional clinical scores.
Portal hypertension identified by AI is a stronger predictor of mortality than tumor‑related factors in real‑world HCC cohorts.
Genomic profiling revealed targetable alterations in 65% of liver cancer patients; genotype‑matched therapy achieved disease control in 32% with a median PFS of 12 months.
open_questions: Does the gamma‑delta T cell signature reflect tumor‑infiltrating cells or systemic immunity, and can it be modulated therapeutically?
Can the HepatoSAJ model be integrated with longitudinal lab data to further improve decompensation prediction?
What are the mechanisms of resistance in patients with targetable alterations who still progress on matched therapy?

cited_papers: Zucman‑Rossi et al. Nat Rev Cancer 2023

key_findings: CHIP prevalence rises from 4.5% in cancer‑free individuals to 7.5% in treated cancer survivors (≈50% relative increase).
MCA prevalence rises from 3% to 4% in treated survivors (≈19% relative increase).
Therapy‑associated MCAs are distinct from those linked to secondary hematologic malignancy risk.
Presence of any autosomal MCA confers a hazard ratio of ~4.8 for secondary hematologic malignancy.
CHIP confers a hazard ratio of ~2.8 for secondary hematologic malignancy, with TP53 and PPM1D mutations linking therapy and malignancy risk.
open_questions: Will sex‑specific CH events further refine risk stratification?
How do ancestry and comorbidities modify therapy‑associated CH dynamics?

key_findings: APC mosaicism was identified in ~33% of tested unexplained polyposis patients.
Mosaic carriers presented at a younger median age (45 y) and had higher adenoma counts than non‑mosaic patients.
Colibactin‑associated mutational signatures were present in 40% of patients and often co‑occurred with APC mutations within the same lesion.
Blood detection of low‑frequency mosaic APC variants was possible in two cases, confirming systemic mosaicism.
Both mosaic APC and colibactin exposure represent distinct etiologic pathways for unexplained adenomatous polyposis.
open_questions: What is the relative contribution of bacterial colibactin versus APC mosaicism to cancer risk?
Can systemic screening for low‑frequency APC mosaicism improve early detection?

key_findings: Tumors from Black women show significantly increased collagen content compared with White women.
CD4 T‑cell infiltration is enriched and CD8 depleted in Black women’s tumors; poverty burden further raises CD4 dominance.
Black‑derived HR‑positive cell lines require collagen‑containing matrix for 3D growth, unlike White‑derived lines.
HCC1500 xenografts (Black origin) form palpable tumors with radial collagen alignment; MDA‑175 (White) do not.
In silico invasion modeling predicts collagen density boosts invasion only for Black‑derived cells.
open_questions: Does targeting collagen remodeling improve outcomes specifically in Black patients?
Can socioeconomic interventions modify the tumor immune microenvironment?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: White‑derived cell lines fail to thrive in collagen‑rich matrices, indicating selective microenvironmental dependence.

key_findings: Four microdysplastic signatures (absent, epithelial, stromal, mixed) were defined based on nuclear and stromal metrics.
Presence of any signature conferred >2‑fold increased breast cancer risk after multivariable adjustment.
Stromal signature strongly predicted ER‑negative cancers, especially in stroma‑rich tissue.
Signatures were predictive across age groups (<50 and ≥50) and in benign disease cohorts.
RNA‑seq of signature‑positive tissues showed immune and wound‑repair pathways activation.
open_questions: Can integration of mammographic density improve predictive performance?
Will prospective application of the signatures guide personalized surveillance?
readouts: nuclear size, perimeter, chromasia, density metrics

key_findings: Deep proteomics identified ~7,000 proteins per sample in both cancer and healthy cohorts.
Classifier achieved AUC 0.96, 86.2% sensitivity and 90.4% specificity overall.
In women with high breast density, sensitivity rose to 90.2% at fixed 90.4% specificity.
Stage‑0, I, II cancers detected with sensitivities of 84.6%, 88%, and 97% respectively.
Prospective pilot (n≈300) showed 89% sensitivity and 93% NPV, supporting clinical utility.
open_questions: Will assay performance be consistent across diverse racial/ethnic groups?
How will positive proteomic results impact downstream diagnostic work‑up and cost?

key_findings: Training set achieved 80.5% overall sensitivity and 97.5% specificity for pancreatic cancer detection.
Independent validation (n=1,445) confirmed 82.6% sensitivity and 97.5% specificity.
Performance remained consistent across three additional high‑risk validation cohorts.
Specificity loss across 11 non‑pancreatic cancers was negligible (<0.05%).
Pathway analysis of selected features recapitulated cancer hallmarks, confirming biological relevance.
open_questions: Can the assay detect pre‑diagnostic cancer in longitudinal samples?
What is performance in patients with IPMN or other premalignant pancreatic lesions?

key_findings: Risk‑based screening could improve breast cancer deaths averted while reducing false‑positive workups by up to 25% (CISNET analysis).
No consensus exists on a universal five‑year risk cut‑point for initiating annual screening; proposed cut points: >3% for annual + supplemental imaging, 1.67–3% for annual, <1.67% for biennial.
Implementation challenges include lack of consistent risk thresholds across trials, guideline variability, and need for model‑agnostic frameworks.
open_questions: How can a universally accepted absolute risk threshold be defined for clinical implementation?
What strategies will ensure equitable adoption of risk‑based screening across diverse populations?

cited_papers: JNCI systematic review on image‑based risk models

key_findings: From 3,000 screened proteins and 3,000 auto‑antibodies, 6 protein and 5 auto‑antibody markers met pre‑specified statistical criteria.
A four‑marker panel (including REG4 and JAK2) achieved 50% sensitivity at 95% specificity, exceeding the minimal performance needed to inform six‑month recall.
Validated markers in an independent CHS cohort (p<0.05 for 6 proteins, 5 auto‑antibodies).
Developed clinical‑grade MSD assays for top markers and plan prospective validation in the MD Anderson MERIT cohort (n≈250 cancers).
open_questions: Will the four‑marker blood panel retain performance in diverse racial/ethnic populations?
What is the optimal decision rule for combining blood markers with imaging and clinical data?

cited_papers: Pepe et al. 2008 J Natl Cancer Inst (PROBE design)

key_findings: High‑risk individuals (top risk score) reach the 10‑year CRC risk benchmark at age 44, suggesting screening 6 years earlier than standard age 50.
Low‑risk individuals (bottom risk score) reach the benchmark at age 56, indicating possible delay of screening by 6 years.
Negative colonoscopy confers sustained risk reduction for up to 20 years, but risk varies widely by underlying risk score, allowing interval extension up to 25 years for very low‑risk patients.
Only 64% of patients with high‑risk polyps receive recommended surveillance, and only 21% adhere to the guideline‑specified interval.
Polygenic risk scores add modest predictive value (AUC increase ~0.02) for post‑colonoscopy CRC and polyp recurrence.
Physician adenoma detection rate strongly predicts post‑colonoscopy CRC risk, with a three‑fold difference between lowest and highest ADR quartiles.
open_questions: How can risk models achieve higher discrimination (AUC >0.75) to be cost‑effective?
What is the optimal way to integrate PRS, lifestyle, and colonoscopy quality into a single actionable risk score?
How to ensure equitable access to precision colonoscopy recommendations across socioeconomic groups?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Current risk tools have modest AUC (~0.63), limiting cost‑effectiveness of risk‑based screening.
Implementation barriers include algorithm complexity, provider/patient acceptance, and potential to exacerbate disparities.

cited_papers: Lansdorp‑Vogelaar et al. cost‑effectiveness of risk‑based CRC screening 2023
CISNET breast cancer risk‑based screening analysis 2024

key_findings: Feasibility study (PREMERIDIAN) showed 100% blood sample capture in 17 patients and identified ctDNA lead times of 100–245 days before clinical recurrence.

In MERIDIAN, only 5/42 evaluable patients were ctDNA‑positive at early post‑treatment time points, and most of those already had macroscopic disease, highlighting the need for radiologic confirmation of MRD.
MRD‑negative patients (≈35) had excellent relapse‑free outcomes (30/35 alive without recurrence, median follow‑up >22 months).
The single patient randomized to revagostumab remained disease‑free for >22 months, whereas the observation patient progressed, providing proof‑of‑concept for MRD‑guided immunotherapy interception.
Longitudinal ctDNA sampling (multiple post‑treatment windows) increased detection sensitivity compared with single landmark testing.
Early ctDNA kinetics (day 8) after PD‑1 blockade in advanced disease correlated with later response, and decreasing ctDNA was associated with increased peripheral TCR diversity.
open_questions: What is the optimal timing and number of ctDNA sampling points to maximize MRD detection without over‑testing?
Can newer ultrasensitive assays increase the proportion of true MRD‑positive patients eligible for interception?
How generalizable are head‑and‑neck MRD kinetics and bispecific immunotherapy benefits to other tumor types?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: MRD detection sensitivity varied by assay type; tumor‑informed assays outperformed tumor‑agnostic panels.
Some ctDNA‑positive results coincided with overt radiologic disease, indicating false‑positive MRD if imaging is not integrated.
Limited assay sensitivity in head‑and‑neck cancer compared with other sites (e.g., colorectal) may restrict broader applicability.

cited_papers: Signatera assay validation studies (clinical cancer research)
Siu et al. 2022 Cancer Cell perspective on adaptive trial design

key_findings: Modeling predicts newborn cancer‑risk screening could reduce deaths before age 20 by 8% and by up to 54% in carriers of predisposition syndromes.

Retrospective analysis of 2,000 Michigan newborn spots found 6.8% carried pathogenic variants, with 5/5 RET carriers developing medullary thyroid cancer and RB1 carriers developing retinoblastoma or pinealoblastoma.
Estimated incidence of cancer among newborns with a positive screen is ~1 in 30,000, comparable to other rare screened conditions.
Prospective NCARE trial will randomize 10,000 mothers to focused vs. broad panels to assess feasibility, acceptability, and downstream clinical impact.
open_questions: What proportion of newborns with a positive genetic screen will never develop cancer (penetrance uncertainty)?
How to balance panel breadth with cost and false‑positive rates in a public health setting?

key_findings: CAP3 trial (1,547 participants) demonstrated the lowest cancer incidence in the 100 mg aspirin arm, with 30% of participants experiencing the fewest cancers after 8 years.
Serious adverse events were absent in the 100 mg group, indicating a favorable safety profile compared with higher doses.
Combined analysis of CAP2 and CAP3 yields HR 0.67 versus historic placebo, confirming a protective effect of aspirin across Lynch‑syndrome cancer sites.
