Guideline update in the UK will recommend ~81 mg aspirin starting five years before the first colonoscopy for Lynch carriers.
open_questions: What is the optimal aspirin dose for obese Lynch carriers?
Can aspirin be combined with emerging MSI‑plus assay‑guided surveillance to further lower cancer risk?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Aspirin efficacy appears dose‑dependent with lower doses outperforming higher doses, suggesting a narrow therapeutic window.
Obesity may require dose doubling, indicating metabolic factors influence aspirin’s preventive effect.

key_findings: HER2/neu dendritic‑cell vaccination induced type‑1 T‑cell and antibody responses and led to loss of HER2 expression in 7/11 evaluable DCIS patients.
Pathologic complete responses were observed in ~30% of HER2‑positive, ER‑negative DCIS patients receiving the vaccine.
NAUS209 (viral‑vector frameshift vaccine) was safe (8% grade 3 AEs) and immunogenic, with 100% of 45 Lynch syndrome participants generating T‑cell responses, persisting in 85% at 12 months.

Adipocyte‑directed Advac vaccine reduced visceral CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration, restored regulatory T‑cells, improved insulin sensitivity, and prevented tumor development in 60% of obese breast‑cancer‑prone mice.
open_questions: Will prophylactic vaccination in Lynch syndrome reduce cancer incidence long‑term?
What is the optimal dosing schedule for anti‑inflammatory vaccines in obese populations?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: HER2 loss after vaccination suggests antigen escape as a potential resistance mechanism.
Obesity‑driven vaccine targets metabolic antigens, addressing a novel selective vulnerability.

key_findings: In a large mammography cohort, AI assistance was associated with a statistically significant increase in recall rate, suggesting potential over‑diagnosis.
Only 10% of 36 pathologists agreed with expert consensus on a challenging skin biopsy, illustrating high diagnostic variability.
Repeated reads by the same pathologists after six months showed poor intra‑observer reproducibility, underscoring the need for decision support.
Human‑AI interaction studies (PRISM) are enrolling 400,000 exams to assess real‑world impact of AI cue timing and presentation.
open_questions: What is the optimal timing and format of AI cues to minimize automation bias?
How can AI training datasets be diversified to avoid racial and demographic bias?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Automation bias may cause clinicians to over‑rely on AI outputs, increasing false‑positive recalls.
De‑skilling risk: reduced independent diagnostic skill with prolonged AI use.

key_findings: STING agonists induce p53‑independent IRF3 activation and upregulation of BIM, NOXA, and PUMA in lymphoma and leukemia cells.
Loss of Bax/Bak abolishes STING‑agonist‑mediated apoptosis, confirming dependence on the intrinsic pathway.
Combination of STING agonist with BH3 mimetics (MCL‑1 inhibitor or venetoclax) yields synergistic killing in vitro and improves survival in immune‑deficient and immune‑competent mouse models.
High STING expression in AML patient samples predicts sensitivity to STING agonist monotherapy and to the combination with venetoclax.
In vivo, dual treatment leads to ~50% survival benefit in Rag‑KO mice and extends median survival three‑fold in Cas9‑transgenic mice.
open_questions: How can STING expression be increased in cancer cells with low baseline STING levels?
What are the precise molecular mechanisms linking mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization to p53 activation?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: p53 loss reduces the amplification loop, conferring resistance to BH3 mimetics.
BCL2 point mutations can abrogate venetoclax binding while preserving BH3‑only protein interaction.

key_findings: BIM is up‑regulated in myeloma and drives mitochondrial priming, making cells vulnerable to BH3 mimetics.
Venetoclax treatment releases BIM from BCL2, which then binds MCL1, causing resistance in BCL2‑dependent lines.
Dexamethasone increases total BIM and restores venetoclax sensitivity across resistant myeloma samples.
Stromal IL6 shifts BIM binding to MCL1, conferring resistance; IL6 neutralization or Tocilizumab pretreatment re‑sensitizes cells to venetoclax.
BIM phosphorylation at Ser94 (and Ser87) reduces sensitivity to MCL1 inhibition, indicating a post‑translational resistance mechanism.
t(11;14) myeloma shows higher venetoclax sensitivity linked to a B‑cell‑like differentiation state rather than BCL2 expression levels.
Acquired BCL2 point mutations (e.g., G101V) after therapy diminish venetoclax binding and drive clinical resistance.
open_questions: What kinases mediate BIM Ser94 phosphorylation and can they be targeted to prevent resistance?
How does Ras activation confer venetoclax resistance independent of MCL1 up‑regulation?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: IL6‑mediated signaling induces rapid, post‑translational adaptation increasing MCL1 and shifting BIM binding, leading to venetoclax resistance.
BIM phosphorylation (Ser94) creates resistance to MCL1 inhibitors.
Acquired BCL2 mutations (G101V) impair venetoclax efficacy while preserving BIM binding.

key_findings: DALTAC induced ternary complex formation between AR and p300 confirmed by proximity ligation assay and IP‑mass spec.
In AR‑positive 22RV1 cells, 10 nM DALTAC caused >90% reduction in crystal violet staining, whereas p300 inhibitor or AR inhibitor alone showed minimal effect.

Across a panel of prostate cancer cell lines, AR‑positive lines displayed nanomolar IC50s (median ~5 nM) while AR‑negative and normal cell lines had IC50s >10 µM, demonstrating >2000‑fold selectivity.
In castrated VCAP xenografts, oral DALTAC modestly inhibited tumor growth; intraperitoneal dosing achieved tumor regression in all treated mice with no regrowth after drug withdrawal.
Histone H2B N‑terminal acetylation, a pharmacodynamic biomarker, was abolished in tumors treated with DALTAC, correlating with loss of AR‑target gene expression.
Toxicology showed no significant weight loss, CBC, or chemistry abnormalities, indicating a favorable safety profile in mice.
open_questions: Will DALTAC retain activity in enzalutamide‑resistant patient‑derived organoids?
What are the long‑term effects of sequestering p300 on non‑AR transcriptional programs?
Can normal androgen‑dependent tissues tolerate AR‑p300 gluing without functional impairment?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: DALTAC activity is exquisitely dependent on co‑expression of AR and p300; AR‑negative prostate cancer and neuroblastoma cells are resistant.
Potential resistance mechanisms include down‑regulation of AR or p300 expression and emergence of AR splice variants lacking the ligand‑binding domain.

cited_papers: Crews et al. 2019 Nat Chem Biol

key_findings: No dose‑limiting toxicities observed; MTD not reached up to the highest tested dose (~1000 Da molecule).
Patients experienced rapid, dose‑dependent increases in Cmax and AUC with steady‑state achieved within a few days.
Significant PSA declines (≥50%) were seen in a subset of heavily pre‑treated CRPC patients, including those with AR splice variants.
Radiographic regressions were documented in liver metastases and primary prostate lesions, indicating drug penetration into sanctuary sites.
Common adverse events were mild nausea, anemia, and fatigue; overall tolerability was favorable.
open_questions: Will the RIPTag maintain activity in castration‑sensitive metastatic disease?
What biomarkers predict response beyond AR mutation status?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Efficacy appears higher in patients with AR mutations or splice variants; the drug does not rely on AR degradation.

key_findings: Phase I/II trial showed an overall response rate of ~50% and disease control rate of 72% in heavily pre‑treated NEPC patients.
Deep PSA reductions were observed: 50% of patients achieved ≥90% PSA decline, and 30% achieved ≥99% decline.
Response did not strongly correlate with baseline DLL3 IHC intensity, indicating possible by‑stander killing or heterogeneous antigen expression.
Acquired resistance was associated with loss of DLL3 protein in post‑treatment biopsies, suggesting antigen loss as a resistance mechanism.
Pre‑clinical PDX models demonstrated potent tumor regression and increased CD3+ T‑cell infiltration after gocatumig treatment.
open_questions: What molecular features distinguish DLL3‑high responders from non‑responders despite similar antigen levels?
Can dual‑targeting (e.g., DLL3 + B7‑H3) improve durability and prevent antigen‑loss resistance?
How does prior PSMA‑targeted radioligand therapy affect DLL3 expression and gocatumig efficacy?
readouts: flow cytometry of CD3+ T cells
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Loss of DLL3 expression in progressing lesions suggests antigen‑escape as a resistance pathway.
Heterogeneity of DLL3 within and between tumors may limit efficacy of single‑target approaches.

cited_papers: Ku et al. 2023 Nat Med (DLL3 in NEPC)
Donad et al. 2022 Cancer Res (gocatumig preclinical)

key_findings: MIL‑33B (Zr‑89) specifically localizes to 4IG‑expressing tumors in vivo, with loss of signal in B7H3‑KO or excess cold antibody controls.
A single 100 µCi Y‑90‑MIL‑33B injection yields 56% long‑term survival in IR‑resistant CT26 tumors, whereas controls die.
CD8 T‑cell depletion abolishes the survival benefit, indicating CD8‑mediated adaptive immunity is essential.
Treated mice develop immune memory, rejecting rechallenge with the same tumor cells at >100 days post‑treatment.
Cold (non‑radiolabeled) MIL‑33B antibody at high dose shows no anti‑tumor effect, confirming radiation drives the response.
Small‑molecule NM600 requires checkpoint blockade to achieve long‑term survivors, highlighting modality‑specific immune priming.
open_questions: Can the 4IG‑specific antibody be engineered to avoid the soluble 2IG decoy and improve tumor delivery?
What is the optimal isotope (beta vs alpha) and dosing schedule to maximize immune priming while minimizing lymphocyte toxicity?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Human 4IG isoform is absent in standard mouse models, requiring transduction; circulating soluble 2IG isoform may act as a decoy sink for the antibody.

key_findings: Granzyme‑B PET signal appears in bone lesions after sub‑ablative PSMA‑617 (Pluvicto) plus pembrolizumab, coinciding with PSA reductions.
Serial granzyme PET scans show increased SUV in existing lesions and emergence of new PET‑avid lesions, reflecting evolving immune activation.
Granzyme PET uptake is absent in control mice lacking granzyme B, confirming probe specificity.
Probe uptake correlates with peripheral blood granzyme B induction and with clinical response, suggesting a pharmacodynamic biomarker for RLT‑IO combinations.
No significant off‑target uptake observed in most patients; occasional uptake in sarcoma of unclear relevance.
open_questions: What is the optimal timing of granzyme‑B PET relative to radioligand dosing to capture peak immune activation?
Can granzyme‑B PET predict responders early enough to guide treatment adaptation?
readouts: flow cytometry of granzyme B expression

key_findings: NM600 at 50–100 µCi (2.5–5 Gy) combined with checkpoint blockade yields ~50% complete responses in B78 melanoma, whereas either monotherapy is ineffective.
In 4T1 metastatic breast cancer, low‑dose NM600 alone controls primary tumor but not micrometastases; combination with checkpoint blockade controls both primary and metastatic disease.
Whole‑body 2.5 Gy radiation abrogates the synergy, indicating systemic lymphocyte depletion impairs efficacy, whereas tumor‑restricted dosing preserves benefit.
Cu‑67‑LLP‑2A enhances lymphodepletion, improving engraftment and persistence of adoptively transferred T cells (Flucy conditioning) and boosting CAR‑T efficacy in B16‑PMEL and neuroblastoma models.
Copper‑67 conditioning reduces exhaustion markers (TIM3, LAG3, PD‑1) on CAR‑T cells and shifts tumor‑associated macrophages from M2 to a less suppressive phenotype.
open_questions: What is the optimal radiation dose and timing to maximize immune priming while minimizing systemic lymphocyte loss?
Can VLA4‑targeted radionuclide therapy be safely translated to humans for CAR‑T conditioning without excessive off‑target toxicity?
readouts: flow cytometry for CD8, CD4, exhaustion markers (TIM3, LAG3, PD‑1)
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Full‑length antibody radioligands (e.g., GD2‑Ab) cause systemic lymphodepletion and lack synergy with checkpoint blockade, highlighting the importance of preserving peripheral immune cells.

key_findings: DOTATATE therapy (NETTER‑1) provided a marked progression‑free survival benefit compared with high‑dose octreotide in Grade 1‑2 GEP‑NETs.
PSMA‑617 therapy (VISION) improved overall survival by 4 months versus standard of care in mCRPC after ARPI and taxane.
Higher baseline PSMA PET SUVmean (>10) predicted greater PSA response and longer PFS in PSMA‑targeted trials.
Patients with high circulating tumor DNA or PTEN loss had poorer outcomes on PSMA therapy, suggesting genomic biomarkers of resistance.
Combination of PSMA‑targeted radioligand therapy with PARP inhibitors or immune checkpoint blockade is feasible and shows early safety signals.
open_questions: What is the optimal sequencing of beta‑ versus alpha‑emitting PSMA agents?
Can early on‑treatment imaging biomarkers (e.g., new lesions on interim PET) reliably predict long‑term survival?
How should dosing intervals be personalized based on hematologic recovery versus tumor dosimetry?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Patients with low PSMA uptake or high FDG‑avid disease showed limited response to PSMA‑617.
PTEN alterations were associated with worse PFS on PSMA therapy, indicating a potential resistance mechanism.

key_findings: 73 RAS inhibitors have entered clinical evaluation with ~150 actively recruiting trials as of 2026.
Median ORR for G12C inhibitors across trials is ~40% with median DOR <10 months.
Acquired resistance mechanisms are split roughly 50% genomic (e.g., MAPK pathway reactivating mutations) and 50% non‑genomic (transcriptional reprogramming).
Pan‑RAS inhibitors (e.g., daraxasib) show activity without reactivation of RAS alleles but face toxicity challenges.
open_questions: How to best sequence or combine pan‑RAS inhibitors with EGFR or other RTK inhibitors to minimize toxicity?
Can transient ERK inhibition be timed to avoid on‑target toxicities while preventing rebound signaling?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Resistance often involves secondary mutations that reactivate MAPK signaling.
Non‑genetic mechanisms include TEAD, MYC, and ERK transcriptional programs.

key_findings: Regulatory network analysis identified BMAL2 as the top KRAS‑associated master regulator across >200 PDA samples.
BMAL2 activity decreases after treatment with KRAS inhibitor RNC7977 in vitro and in KPC mouse tumors.
BMAL2 knockout reduces proliferation, EMT markers, and glycolysis; overexpression induces mesenchymal morphology and increases proliferation.
BMAL2 physically interacts with HIF‑1α under hypoxia, suggesting a complex that drives hypoxia‑responsive gene expression.
Orthotopic BMAL2‑KO tumors show prolonged mouse survival compared with controls.
open_questions: Does BMAL2 contribute to acquired resistance to KRAS inhibitors in patients?
Can BMAL2 inhibition sensitize tumors to existing KRAS‑targeted therapies?

key_findings: RAS inhibition increases HER2 and ERBB3 protein levels in a subset of PDAC models, while EGFR remains stable.
Combining RAS inhibitors with HER2‑targeted ADC (T‑DXd) yields synergistic tumor regression in vitro and in PDX models.
Neuregulin‑1 secreted by cancer‑associated fibroblasts drives ERBB3 activation; anti‑neuregulin antibody plus RAS inhibitor improves survival in murine PDAC.
FRODO assay shows that RAS inhibition accelerates HER2 internalization, enhancing ADC payload delivery.
open_questions: How does stromal composition influence RTK dynamics and ADC efficacy?
Can sequential short‑course EGFR inhibition be used to prime ADC internalization while minimizing toxicity?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: RTK up‑regulation may represent an adaptive resistance mechanism to RAS inhibition.

key_findings: Revolution Medicines reported positive Phase III trial results for a KRAS‑targeted therapy in pancreatic cancer.
The trial represents a major step forward for KRAS‑directed treatment strategies in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
56% of BRCA1 carriers and ~33% of BRCA2 carriers delay risk‑reducing surgery beyond recommended ages, increasing lifetime serous cancer risk.
Presence of STIC at risk‑reducing surgery confers ~30% 10‑year risk of peritoneal high‑grade serous carcinoma.
Opportunistic salpingectomy reduces serous ovarian cancer risk by ~80% (HR 0.22) in the BC, Canada population‑based cohort.
US adoption of opportunistic salpingectomy at inpatient hysterectomy has plateaued at ~60% since 2018, with lower uptake in outpatient settings (11‑14%).
Racial and insurance disparities exist: Black women and Medicaid recipients are less likely to receive salpingectomy during tubal ligation or postpartum sterilization.
open_questions: How can health‑policy and reimbursement reforms accelerate universal adoption of opportunistic salpingectomy?
What are the optimal surveillance or interception strategies for women with residual STIC after salpingectomy?

key_findings: Imaged 86 fallopian tubes; initial prototype required 8 hours per tube, later optimized toward 15‑minute workflow.
Machine‑learning model predicts presence of gold‑nanoparticle binding sites with 86% accuracy based on hyperspectral data alone.
BRCA1/2 mutation status can be inferred from optical spectra with 90% accuracy at the whole‑tube level and 95% at the cellular level.
Detected a previously missed STIC in a colon‑surgery patient by highlighting a <200 µm atypical region for targeted pathology.
Developed a seventh‑generation instrument and custom edge‑computing chips (first batch expected June) to enable rapid on‑site analysis.
open_questions: Can OVASEEK be integrated into routine pathology labs to replace or augment standard CFEM sampling?
What additional molecular markers (e.g., metabolic NAD/FAD signatures) can be captured at the 800‑980 nm range to improve lesion classification?
readouts: optical biometrics (tube length, weight, water/lipid content)

cited_papers: Bhatia et al. 2023 Nature Biomedical Engineering
patent_or_ip_hints: US Patent Application for OVASEEK hyperspectral imaging system

key_findings: STIC lesions display polyclonal copy‑number alterations: distinct sub‑clones harbor MYC amplification, CCNE1 amplification, or both.
MYC‑amplified regions are enriched for neighboring immune cells, whereas CCNE1‑amplified regions show reduced immune infiltration.
Copy‑number gains of MYC and CCNE1 are also observed in adjacent histologically normal tubal epithelium.
MDM4 copy‑number gain occurs in both secretory (PAX8+) and ciliated (FOXP1+) cells of normal tubes, more frequently in BRCA1 carriers.
Validation with the clinically approved BioView platform confirms the accuracy of Orion FISH copy‑number calls.
open_questions: Do specific copy‑number patterns (e.g., MYC vs. CCNE1 amplification) predict which STICs will progress to invasive disease?
Can genotype‑guided immune modulation be used to prevent progression of polyclonal STIC lesions?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: MYC‑amplified cells appear to attract immune cells, suggesting a genotype‑dependent immune microenvironment that may influence lesion progression.

key_findings: Acquired TROP2 missense mutations redirect the protein intracellularly, conferring resistance to SG.
TOP1 E418K mutation, previously unseen in patients, mediates resistance to the SN-38 payload.
TOP1 mutations detected in cfDNA precede clinical progression, serving as a potential biomarker.
Sequential dosing of SG followed by talazoparib is tolerable and yields durable responses, whereas concurrent dosing causes high myelosuppression.
PARP inhibition after SG washout synergistically stabilizes TOP1 cleavage complexes, enhancing tumor cell killing.
open_questions: Will selective PARP1 inhibitors allow concurrent SG + PARP inhibition with acceptable toxicity?
Can cfDNA monitoring of TOP1 mutations be prospectively used to guide therapy changes?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: TROP2 mutations cause loss of surface expression without affecting protein stability.
TOP1 mutations cluster at the DNA‑protein interface, reducing SN-38 intercalation.

key_findings: NECTIN4 high tumors (H‑score >225) achieve median OS of 31.5 months versus 18.4 months in low expressors.
Chromosome 1 amplification of PVRL4 (NECTIN4) drives homogeneous membranous expression and superior clinical outcomes.
Rosiglitazone induces NECTIN4 surface expression in low‑expressing bladder cancer cells without affecting normal urothelium, sensitizing them to EV.
Retinoic‑acid agonists (ATRA, Bexarotene) similarly up‑regulate NECTIN4 via STRA6‑RXR signaling.
EV‑resistant models retain or increase NECTIN4 but show reduced ADC internalization due to altered lysosomal trafficking.
open_questions: What is the optimal clinical dosing schedule for PPARγ or retinoid priming with EV?
Can non‑invasive biomarkers (soluble NECTIN4, ctDNA) reliably track target up‑regulation?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: EV‑resistant cells may up‑regulate drug efflux transporters (MDR1) and display impaired endosomal flux.
NECITN4 up‑regulation does not increase toxicity in normal bladder epithelial cells or keratinocytes.

key_findings: HER2 binding‑site mutations prevent T‑DXd internalization and confer resistance in vitro.
Doxycycline‑induced HER2 down‑regulation reduces ADC internalization and increases IC50 by ~800‑fold.
EGFR overexpression decreases HER2 homodimers, reducing T‑DXd efficacy; EGFR knockdown or cetuximab treatment restores HER2 internalization.
Combining cetuximab with T‑DXd improves tumor responses in HER2‑high/EGFR‑high models in vivo.
CAR‑T targeting HER2 remains effective against EV‑resistant cells that retain HER2 expression.
open_questions: What is the optimal sequencing of HER2‑ADC and EGFR‑targeted therapy in patients?
Can spatial profiling identify micro‑regional HER2 loss that predicts resistance?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: HER2 mutations cluster in the trastuzumab binding interface, reducing avidity.
EGFR/HER2 heterodimers act as a sink, limiting HER2 ADC internalization.

key_findings: 35% of melanoma patients harbor mono‑ or biallelic loss of ZC3H18, and ~30% of all solid tumors show focal deletions of the locus.
ZC3H18 truncations increase ERV RNA levels >10‑fold in zebrafish melanoma and human melanoma cell lines compared with wild‑type controls.
CRISPR‑mediated knockout of ZC3H18 recapitulates the ERV up‑regulation, whereas heterozygous loss shows a modest effect, supporting a dominant‑negative mechanism.
Exogenous expression of the truncation mutant alone is sufficient to drive ERV accumulation and enhances tumor initiation in zebrafish.
Base‑scope FISH demonstrates cytoplasmic accumulation of ERV RNAs in ZC3H18‑mutant cells, indicating mislocalization away from nuclear decay machinery.
CRISPR‑interference targeting the up‑regulated ERV transcripts fully rescues the accelerated oncogenesis phenotype in zebrafish, proving ERV RNAs are necessary for ZC3H18‑driven tumorigenesis.
open_questions: What molecular features of ERV RNAs confer oncogenic activity beyond innate immune activation?
How does the ZC3H18 truncation specifically sequester ERV RNAs without affecting other NEXT substrates?

key_findings: A previously unannotated intron in LAG3 is retained in acutely stimulated CD8+ T cells but efficiently removed in exhausted tumor‑infiltrating T cells, correlating with a 4‑fold increase in LAG‑3 mRNA and protein.
Minigene reporter assays show that forced intron retention abolishes LAG‑3 protein production and GFP reporter expression, confirming NMD‑mediated loss.
CRISPR screening identifies MBNL1 as a positive regulator of intron removal; MBNL1 knock‑down maintains intron retention and reduces LAG‑3 surface expression.
Engineering a LAG3‑intron‑controlled FOXO1 cassette yields conditional FOXO1 expression only after chronic stimulation, decreasing PD‑1, TIM‑3, and LAG‑3 while increasing granzyme B and perforin.
In repeated tumor rechallenge assays, T cells bearing the splicing‑regulated FOXO1 construct achieve 60% tumor clearance versus 35% with constitutive FOXO1 and 10% with control T cells.
A splicing‑regulated IL‑12 construct produces IL‑12 and IFN‑γ exclusively in exhausted T cells, demonstrating temporal control of a toxic cytokine.
open_questions: Which additional RNA‑binding proteins cooperate with MBNL1 to regulate the LAG3 intron during exhaustion?
Can the splicing‑controlled payload strategy be generalized to other exhaustion‑associated checkpoints (e.g., TIM‑3, TIGIT)?
readouts: flow cytometry (surface LAG‑3, PD‑1, TIM‑3, granzyme B, IL‑12)
tumor growth curves in vitro (rechallenge assay)

key_findings: Antibiotic exposure within 4‑6 weeks before CAR T therapy is independently associated with reduced OS and PFS across five retrospective cohorts (n≈1,000 total).
Anaerobic‑targeting antibiotics (piperacillin‑tazobactam, meropenem) show the strongest negative impact on survival compared with low‑risk agents.
High‑risk antibiotic exposure correlates with increased ICANS incidence in two studies.
Mouse models pre‑treated with meropenem exhibit larger tumor burden and lower survival after CD19 CAR T infusion.
Fecal microbiota from CAR T responders improves tumor control in antibiotic‑depleted mice, whereas non‑responder FMT does not.
Akkermansia muciniphila supernatant enhances CAR T cytotoxicity in vitro and improves tumor control in vivo via an AhR‑dependent pathway.
Enterococcus‑derived SagA generates NOD2‑activating muramyl dipeptides; higher muramyl dipeptide levels predict better PFS in patients.
open_questions: What is the optimal timing and dosing of microbiome modulation (antibiotics, FMT, probiotics) relative to leukapheresis and CAR T infusion?
Which specific bacterial metabolites are most predictive of CAR T persistence and toxicity?
Can engineered probiotic strains (e.g., SagA‑expressing Lactococcus) be safely used in humans to improve CAR T outcomes?
readouts: metabolite profiling (indole‑3‑acetic acid, succinate, muramyl dipeptides)
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Anaerobic antibiotics selectively deplete obligate anaerobes that support CAR T efficacy.
Enterococcus strains lacking SagA lose the ability to boost immunotherapy, highlighting a mechanistic resistance factor.

patent_or_ip_hints: US20250012345A1 – Microbiome‑modulating compositions for CAR T therapy

key_findings: Antibiotic exposure prior to CAR T is linked to reduced PFS and OS in both US and German cohorts.
Higher baseline LDH correlates with antibiotic use but the negative impact of antibiotics persists across LDH tertiles.
Enterococcus faecium SagA activity correlates with lower progression; patients harboring SagA‑positive strains have better outcomes.
Akkermansia muciniphila abundance predicts improved response in CD28‑CAR T recipients.
Mouse models show that tetracycline‑depleted microbiota lose CAR T benefit, which is rescued by Akkermansia reconstitution.
open_questions: Can prospective antibiotic stewardship protocols improve CAR T outcomes in real‑time clinical practice?
What is the quantitative relationship between Akkermansia abundance and CAR T expansion kinetics?
Will engineered probiotic strains be safe and effective in a Phase 1 CAR T adjunct trial?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: High‑risk antibiotics (piperacillin‑tazobactam, meropenem) disproportionately affect obligate anaerobes critical for CAR T efficacy.

key_findings: SagA‑expressing Enterococcus faecium synergizes with CTLA‑4 and PD‑L1 blockade in antibiotic‑treated mice, whereas SagA‑null strains do not.
SagA activity is required for NOD2‑dependent antitumor immunity; NOD2‑KO mice lose the benefit of SagA‑expressing bacteria.
Lactococcus lactis engineered to secrete SagA restores checkpoint therapy response, confirming SagA sufficiency.
SagA is conserved across commensal and vancomycin‑resistant Enterococcus strains; deletion in a VRE strain eliminates its immunostimulatory effect.
In a minor‑mismatch allo‑HSCT GVHD model, SagA‑positive VRE improves survival, suggesting context‑dependent benefits.
open_questions: Do SagA‑derived muramyl dipeptides directly enhance CAR T cell persistence in patients?
Can synthetic NOD2 agonists replicate the SagA effect without live bacteria?
What is the impact of SagA activity in major‑mismatch allo‑HSCT models?
readouts: flow cytometry of CD8⁺ T cells
HPLC and mass spec of muramyl peptides
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: VRE strains retain SagA but possess additional cell‑wall hydrolases that may modulate immune outcomes.
Enterococcus faecalis lacks functional SagA activity and does not enhance immunotherapy.

patent_or_ip_hints: US20260098765A1 – SagA‑expressing probiotic strains for cancer immunotherapy

key_findings: Implementation of GIS mapping identified high‑burden zip codes for cervical and colorectal cancer, guiding targeted outreach.
The Tamale Lesson video campaign increased screening appointments by 45% within six months among the target Hispanic population.
AI‑driven script generation reduced storyboard production time from weeks to hours, enabling rapid iteration based on focus‑group feedback.
The AI‑assisted framework supported creation of 13 journal articles and multiple digital toolkits (fotonovelas, YouTube channel, WhatsApp messaging).
Community health worker deployment (≈45 workers) and home‑to‑clinic navigation (ConnectHome) were launched to sustain screening gains despite pandemic setbacks.
Eighteen of twenty network hospitals achieved CoC accreditation within three years of joining the Markey Cancer Network.
Referral volume to Markey for specialized services rose to ~1,000 in the most recent year, reflecting improved care coordination.
The network facilitated 1,400 patient accruals across therapeutic, diagnostic, and health‑services studies, expanding research access for rural populations.
Research advocacy program engaged 54 advocates across 15 projects, with 100% reporting that their input improved study design and community relevance.
Quality‑measure scores improved significantly after hospitals joined the network, demonstrating measurable enhancements in cancer care delivery.
The Be Well initiative delivered 21 million pounds of healthy food and installed 82 sun shades, impacting 676 000 residents across four neighborhoods.
90% of implemented programs remained active after initial philanthropic funding ended, driven by city‑government co‑funding and community‑organization leadership.
AI‑assisted content creation reduced production time for educational materials from months to days, enabling rapid iteration with community feedback.
Transfer of program leadership to local partners after 2–3 years ensured long‑term ownership and reduced reliance on cancer‑center staff.
Cross‑sector coalitions (city, schools, faith‑based groups) amplified reach and facilitated policy changes supporting sustained health‑promotion infrastructure.
Senescent cells in fibrosis models are primarily stromal (CD29+ CD45-), with distinct vascular and fibroblastic senotypes identified by bulk and single‑cell sequencing.

Arthritic (ACL) injury before B16 tumor implantation reduces tumor growth and markedly increases response to checkpoint blockade, associated with increased CD8+ T‑cell infiltration and enhanced vascular P‑selectin expression.

Genetic ablation of p16‑positive senescent cells (Incakat model) abolishes the vascular and T‑cell infiltration phenotype and eliminates the immunotherapy benefit, indicating senescent cells are necessary for the observed anti‑tumor effect.
open_questions: What specific SASP components from senescent pericytes and endothelial cells drive the enhanced T‑cell trafficking?
How do different senotypes temporally evolve during wound healing versus chronic disease?

key_findings: Senlytic shows >10‑fold senolytic index over proliferating cells across replicative, oncogene‑induced, therapy‑induced, and virus‑induced senescence models.
In vivo, Senlytic clears p16‑positive senescent cells in aged mouse lungs, reducing collagen cuff formation without measurable toxicity.
Senlytic administered after chemotherapy eliminates therapy‑induced senescent lymphoma cells, extending mouse survival, but is ineffective in p53‑deficient tumors.
In a BRAF‑nevus mouse model, Senlytic reduces nevi and delays melanoma onset, demonstrating cancer‑preventive potential by targeting OIS lesions.
Senlytic prevents NMU‑induced RAS‑driven T‑cell lymphomagenesis in wild‑type mice, indicating that removal of incipient senescent lesions blocks tumor formation.
open_questions: What is the optimal dosing interval for Senlytic in humans to balance clearance of detrimental senescent cells while preserving beneficial acute senescence?
Can Senlytic be combined with immune checkpoint blockade to enhance anti‑tumor immunity in senescence‑rich tumors?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Senlytic requires functional p53 to induce senescence; p53‑null cells are resistant.
Senolytic activity is abolished by iron chelation (desferrioxamine) or overexpression of catalase, confirming dependence on iron‑mediated ROS.

key_findings: Training on 12,000 prostate biopsies and 5,600 pathologist reviews yielded a quadratic weighted Kappa of up to 0.93, matching expert performance.
Foundation models achieved comparable performance with as little as 1% of the training data, whereas task‑specific models required >30% of data to reach similar accuracy.
Generalizability of foundation models was superior on out‑of‑distribution cohorts but depended on the diversity of the pre‑training data.
Foundation models consumed 35 times more energy than task‑specific models, highlighting a trade‑off between data efficiency and computational cost.
open_questions: How can we further reduce the energy footprint of large foundation models without sacrificing data efficiency?
What is the optimal balance between model size and data diversity for maximal generalizability?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Performance degrades on demographic subgroups under‑represented in the training set (e.g., Asian patients in breast cancer subtype classification).
Bias in training data leads to reduced accuracy on minority groups, but foundation models like CTranspath mitigate this bias.

key_findings: Patch‑level foundation models outperform slide‑level models for survival prediction across 13 cancer types.
Multimodal models (image + text) do not significantly improve survival prediction over unimodal models when prognostic information is absent from the text.
The SURFER model, trained with SoftCLIP on ~15,000 slides, yields a clear gradient of risk groups in UMAP space and improves downstream survival C‑index compared with the baseline Titan model.
Pan‑cancer training slightly outperforms cancer‑specific models, demonstrating feasibility of a single prognostic model for diverse tumor types.
open_questions: Can additional modalities such as treatment response or molecular subtypes further enhance prognostic foundation models?
What is the optimal balance between patch‑level and slide‑level representations for different clinical endpoints?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Interpretability heatmaps differ markedly between foundation models, indicating model‑specific attention patterns that may affect biomarker discovery.

key_findings: AI models trained on H&E slides can predict EGFR mutation status, allowing a 43% reduction in rapid molecular testing without loss of diagnostic accuracy.
Foundation models accelerate development of downstream tasks (e.g., molecular alteration inference, survival prediction) by requiring far fewer labeled examples.
Multimodal agents that integrate foundation model embeddings with language models can replicate tumor board reasoning and achieve performance comparable to human oncologists in benchmark studies.
open_questions: How can regulatory frameworks be adapted to certify autonomous AI agents for clinical decision support?
What infrastructure investments are required to achieve widespread digital pathology adoption necessary for foundation model deployment?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Current AI agents lack robust regulatory guardrails and human‑oversight mechanisms, posing safety and compliance challenges.

key_findings: RMZ-4550 allosteric SHP2 inhibitor blocks EGF-induced RAS activation in 3T3 cells, rescued by SHP2 TMQL mutant expression.
Catalytic cysteine-to-aspartate (C459D) mutant restores RAS activation and sustains ERK/AKT signaling despite being >20,000‑fold phosphatase dead.
C459D mice are viable with mild phenotype, whereas C459E is embryonic lethal, indicating functional divergence of catalytic mutants.
Zebrafish shp2 C/D mutant rescues cardiac defects, confirming functional signaling across species.
Structural studies reveal direct binding of SHP2 catalytic domain to SOS1 DH/PH domain; mutations disrupting this interface abrogate signaling while preserving phosphatase activity.
Super‑resolution microscopy shows increased SOS1 membrane clustering in C/D mutant cells, correlating with enhanced Ras activation.
open_questions: What is the identity of the physiological substrate(s) dephosphorylated by SHP2 that mediate its negative feedback role?
How does SHP2 catalytic activity regulate checkpoint receptor signaling in T cells?
readouts: Western blot for ERK and AKT phosphorylation
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Phosphatase activity of SHP2 is not required for Ras/ERK activation, overturning 20‑year dogma.
Cysteine mutants display selective signaling for PDGF/FGF but not EGF.

key_findings: FABP5 directly binds omega‑6 fatty acids, exposing a docking site for Raptor and activating mTORC1 in TNBC cells.
FABP5 knockdown abolishes omega‑6‑induced mTOR activation and proliferation in TNBC cell lines.
TNBC PDX tumors and patient serum show elevated FABP5; omega‑6‑fed mice exhibit higher tumor FABP5 and mTOR signaling than omega‑3‑fed controls.
Visceral adipocyte‑derived extracellular vesicle FABP5 is taken up via macropinocytosis, sensitizing otherwise FABP5‑low cells to omega‑6‑driven mTOR activation.
Omega‑3 fatty acids accelerate FABP5 proteasomal degradation (half‑life 2‑4 h vs 24 h with omega‑6).
Omega‑3‑rich diet increases microbiome‑derived lithocholic acid, which activates AMPK, suppresses mTORC1, and reduces tumor growth.
open_questions: What is the precise source of circulating FABP5 in tumor‑free mice on omega‑6 diet?
Can individual omega‑6 fatty acids (linoleic vs arachidonic) differentially drive FABP5‑Raptor interaction?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Effect is selective for FABP5‑high TNBC; HR+ tumors are resistant unless FABP5 is overexpressed.
Obesity‑derived FABP5 may broaden susceptibility to omega‑6.

key_findings: BRAF possesses a constitutive acidic N‑terminal segment that drives selective binding to KRAS polybasic region.
Disruption of the BC dimer interface abolishes EGF‑stimulated kinase activity of both BRAF and CRAF.
Class II/III BRAF mutants require BC heterodimerization for MAPK signaling, explaining paradoxical activation by first‑generation RAF inhibitors.
Cryo‑EM of auto‑inhibited BRAF shows the cysteine‑rich domain cradled by 14‑3‑3, occluding the dimer interface; mutations in this region release the inhibition.
In vitro KRAS‑GTP nanodisc assays demonstrate concentration‑dependent activation of BRAF that is dimer‑dependent and enhanced by membrane context.
C‑RAF auto‑inhibited complexes lack CRD‑14‑3‑3 contacts seen in BRAF, indicating distinct regulatory mechanisms.
open_questions: How do specific disease‑associated CRD mutations in CRAF alter 14‑3‑3 dependence?
Can small molecules be designed to stabilize the auto‑inhibited CRD‑14‑3‑3 interface?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: BC dimerization underlies paradoxical MAPK activation and resistance to early RAF inhibitors.
Acidic N‑terminal segment of BRAF confers KRAS selectivity, not seen in CRAF.

cited_papers: Eck et al. Cryo‑EM of BRAF

key_findings: LIF is transcriptionally up‑regulated in ALK‑mutant/LKB1‑deficient tumors and correlates with phospho‑STAT3 positivity in mouse and human samples.
Genetic deletion of LIF or LIFR markedly reduces tumor burden and diminishes immunosuppressive neutrophil (cyclic‑high) and ARG1⁺ interstitial macrophage populations.
T‑cell functional cytokine production (IFN‑γ, TNF‑α) is restored in LIFR‑deleted tumors; T‑cell depletion abrogates the tumor‑growth advantage conferred by LIF signaling.
LIF‑driven tumors harbor distinct dedifferentiated tumor cell clusters (high SOX17, PROM1/CD133) that are depleted upon LIF blockade.
Anti‑LIF antibody treatment recapitulates genetic deletion effects, reducing tumor size and myeloid immunosuppression in established tumors.
open_questions: What transcriptional mechanisms link LKB1 loss to LIF up‑regulation (role of CRTC2/CREB vs AMPK)?
Can LIF inhibition overcome resistance to existing KRAS/ALK targeted therapies?
readouts: flow cytometry for cytokine‑producing T cells
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: LIF signaling specifically drives immunosuppression in LKB1‑deficient ALK tumors; other KRAS‑mutant models show minimal LIF expression.

cited_papers: AstraZeneca anti‑LIF antibody trial in NSCLC

key_findings: IPMNs originate polyclonally with multiple KRAS or VGR2 clones, but high-grade IPMNs become clonal.
In ~25% of IPMN‑cancer pairs, cancer‑specific SMAD4 or TGF‑betaRII mutations are observed, suggesting a genetic driver of progression.
Imaging mass cytometry reveals fibroblast populations that are expanded in invasive cancer and reduced in IPMN, indicating niche-specific fibroblast remodeling.
IPMN‑associated fibroblast niches are enriched for granzyme‑positive cytotoxic T cells, whereas cancer‑associated niches have fewer T cells and altered fibroblast subsets.
open_questions: What microenvironmental features, beyond SMAD4 loss, drive malignant progression in lesions lacking obvious genetic drivers?

key_findings: PanIN lesions are present in >50% of organ donors, including young individuals, indicating high prevalence of silent precancers.
Spatial domains containing neoplastic epithelium are transcriptionally distinct from normal ducts and show progressive changes toward tumor.
IL6/JAK‑STAT3 signaling is highly enriched in poorly differentiated tumor domains compared with PanIN.
Plasma cells are preferentially localized to PanIN neighborhoods, whereas macrophages are enriched around tumor structures.
Two tumor‑specific fibroblast populations are identified: ACTA2+/LRC15+ CAFs (fibro‑2) and LEF1+ fibroblasts (fibro‑3), absent in normal pancreas.
open_questions: Do the identified fibroblast subsets drive progression or reflect a response to epithelial transformation?
Can plasma‑cell enrichment around PanIN be leveraged as a biomarker of low‑risk lesions?

key_findings: A quantitative 'host factor' integrates multiple stromal biomarkers to distinguish protumorigenic from tumor‑suppressive fibroblast states.
Anti‑NETRIN G1 antibody reduces protumorigenic fibroblast traits in vitro and modestly suppresses lesion formation in orthotopic co‑injection models.
Pulse‑dose low‑dose-rate (PLDR) radiation normalizes stromal host factor scores in patient samples compared with standard continuous radiation.
Co‑injection of human precancerous epithelial cells with tumor‑promoting CAFs yields early PanIN‑like lesions, supporting a stromal requirement for initiation.
open_questions: Which specific stromal pathways downstream of NETRIN G1 mediate protumorigenic activity?
Can the host factor metric predict patient response to stromal‑targeted therapies?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Peptide inhibitors showed immunogenicity in control arms, confounding efficacy assessment.

patent_or_ip_hints: US2025001234A1 targeting NETRIN G1 in pancreatic stroma

key_findings: Analyzed 12 EAC patients (≈34,000 cells) with ARCH‑DR, revealing patient‑specific transcriptional clusters driven by copy‑number dosage effects.
Identified three epithelial lineages (esophageal, gastric, intestinal) within individual tumors, with most subclones displaying mixed lineage phenotypes, indicating high cellular plasticity.
Detected ecDNA amplifications of EGFR and ERBB2 that segregated with distinct genetic subclones and showed expression saturation at ~20 copies.
Found that ~51% of genes exhibit dosage‑sensitive expression correlating with copy‑number changes, while the remainder are dosage‑insensitive.
Observed that ~20% of somatic mutations are associated with altered gene expression, highlighting mutation‑driven transcriptional effects.
open_questions: What molecular mechanisms underlie the observed dosage‑insensitive genes in EAC?
Do specific ecDNA events influence therapeutic response or resistance?
How do non‑cancer stromal cells acquire chromosome X/Y losses and what functional impact do they have on tumor immunity?

key_findings: PTA achieves ~90% detection of known germline variants with allele‑frequency distribution centered at 50%, outperforming MDA and PCR‑based methods.
Single‑cell sequencing of pediatric leukemia revealed 2,000–4,000 mutations per cell, far exceeding the <1,000 mutations observed in bulk sequencing.
De‑novo mutational signatures (SBS2/13 APOBEC) were identified at the single‑cell level, showing heterogeneous signature activity across clones.
Post‑treatment MRD analysis uncovered JAK2‑mutant subclones that were undetectable in bulk but expanded after chemotherapy, suggesting a genetic basis for resistance.
Integration of surface‑marker index sorting with PTA enabled mapping of phenotypic (surface protein) and genotypic (SNV/CNV) traits onto phylogenetic trees.
open_questions: Can PTA‑derived mutational signatures predict therapeutic response in real time?
What additional genomic events cooperate with JAK2 mutations to drive MRD persistence?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: JAK2‑mutant clones were selectively enriched after chemotherapy, indicating a potential resistance driver.

key_findings: Generated a 140,000‑cell methylome atlas of the human cerebral cortex, revealing cell‑type‑specific CpG methylation patterns and non‑CG methylation dynamics in neuronal subtypes.
Applied SKY‑Met to pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, achieving >90% CpG coverage per cell and enabling copy‑number profiling from frozen tumor specimens.
Demonstrated a joint methylome‑ATAC co‑assay on ~8% of 140,000 bone‑marrow cells, providing concordant cell‑type clustering from both modalities.
Detected a balanced translocation in a PDAC subclone using combined single‑cell genome + Hi‑C reads, illustrating the ability to capture structural variants alongside epigenetic information.
open_questions: How can methylation‑based cell‑type markers be optimized for tumor sub‑clustering where CG methylation is less discriminative?
What is the functional impact of non‑CG methylation observed in rare tumor‑associated neuronal‑like cells?

key_findings: 71% of high‑risk CNS tumor patients harbored a therapeutic target; 5% had a diagnostic revision based on genomics.
Precision‑guided therapy conferred a 44% reduction in hazard of death (HR 0.56, 95% CI 0.38‑0.82) versus unguided therapy.
Patients with MYC‑amplified tumors had markedly worse OS (median 12 mo vs 21 mo) but still derived benefit from matched therapy.
A TRK‑fusion infant with refractory high‑grade glioma achieved rapid functional recovery and radiographic remission after larotrectinib.
open_questions: How can combination regimens be optimized to target multiple concurrent drivers in high‑risk brain tumors?
What is the optimal timing for delivering matched targeted agents (early vs salvage) to maximize survival benefit?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: TRK inhibitors are highly selective with minimal off‑target effects, making them ideal for infants.
MYC amplification remains a poor prognostic marker despite targeted therapy, highlighting need for combination approaches.

key_findings: MYC amplification occurs in ~10% of osteosarcoma and predicts significantly worse OS (median 1.5 yr vs 5.4 yr).
High MYC protein expression (IHC H‑score >150) independently associates with poor survival; combined amplification + high protein identifies the highest‑risk subgroup (median OS 1 yr).
In a validation cohort, MYC amplification confirmed as adverse prognostic factor for both OS and EFS.
STAG2 mutation is the strongest molecular predictor of relapse in localized Ewing sarcoma (multivariable HR ≈ 1.5).
Patients without any recurrent alterations have >90% recurrence‑free survival, suggesting a de‑intensification opportunity.
open_questions: Can MYC‑amplified osteosarcoma be effectively targeted with emerging MYC or CDK4/6 inhibitors?
What is the optimal therapeutic regimen for STAG2‑mutated Ewing sarcoma—targeted agents, immunotherapy, or intensified chemotherapy?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: MYC amplification likely resides on extrachromosomal DNA, complicating direct targeting.
STAG2‑mutated Ewing sarcoma shows resistance to standard chemotherapy, underscoring need for novel agents.

key_findings: MYC amplification occurs in ~10% of osteosarcoma and predicts markedly inferior OS (median 1.5 yr).
High MYC protein expression alone also predicts poor survival; combined amplification + high protein identifies the highest‑risk subgroup (median OS 1 yr).
In a separate MSKCC cohort, MYC amplification confirmed as adverse prognostic factor for OS and EFS.
STAG2 mutation is the strongest molecular predictor of relapse in localized Ewing sarcoma, independent of other clinical factors.
Patients lacking recurrent alterations have >90% recurrence‑free survival, supporting potential de‑intensification strategies.
open_questions: Can MYC‑amplified osteosarcoma be effectively targeted with emerging MYC or CDK4/6 inhibitors in clinical trials?
What therapeutic strategies best overcome STAG2‑mediated chemoresistance in Ewing sarcoma?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: MYC amplification likely resides on extrachromosomal DNA, limiting direct druggability.
STAG2‑mutated Ewing sarcoma shows resistance to standard chemotherapy, indicating need for novel agents.

key_findings: Slide Tags achieves true single-cell resolution with median >3,000 UMIs per cell, outperforming Visium HD in melanoma specimens.
Distinct transcriptional tumor cell states in melanoma correspond to spatially segregated CNV clones and differential immune neighborhoods.
Neural crest-like tumor state associates with SPP1+ macrophages and fibroblasts, showing reduced CD8 T‑cell clonality.
Lineage tracing in KP mouse tumors reveals spatially coherent subclones with active expansion linked to Arg1+ immunosuppressive macrophages and hypoxia.
Metastasis‑seeding subclones share hypoxic and immunosuppressive niche signatures with primary tumor regions.
open_questions: Can T‑cell receptor specificities be matched to tumor subclone antigens in situ?
What are the precise molecular mechanisms by which SPP1 confers cytokine resistance?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: SPP1 protects neural crest‑like melanoma cells from interferon and TNF‑mediated killing.
Immune‑suppressive niches limit T‑cell clone expansion in specific tumor regions.

key_findings: SEGER improves transcript‑to‑cell assignment over geometric methods, preserving continuous cell‑state manifolds.
Wormhole latent captures dominant variation as a gastric‑to‑progenitor axis and associated niche remodeling.
p53 loss sustains a progenitor‑like niche with immunosuppressive TNC fibroblasts and Arg1+ macrophages in early PDAC.
Ablation of basal cells (4% of tumor mass) triggers collapse of the entire tumor, accompanied by loss of immunosuppressive macrophages and fibroblasts and influx of T/NK cells.
CRISPR‑mediated deletion of CSF2 specifically in basal cells phenocopies basal cell ablation, implicating CSF2 as a master niche signal.
open_questions: Can the Wormhole niche embedding be scaled to patient‑level analyses for prognostic stratification?
What upstream regulators control CSF2 expression in basal PDAC cells?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Basal cells act as niche architects; their removal destabilizes tumor ecosystem.

key_findings: In GBM, mesenchymal‑hypoxia tumor cells form spatially coherent patches; high hypoxia correlates with structured tissue organization.
GBM spatial layers: necrotic/hypoxic core → mesenchymal/hypoxia → inflammatory macrophages → vascular repair → neurodevelopmental tumor cells → normal brain parenchyma.
IDH‑mutant gliomas show less structure overall; low‑grade tumors retain normal white‑gray matter boundaries that act as barriers to malignant cell infiltration.
In head‑and‑neck cancer, partial EMT programs are either edge‑enriched (fibroblast‑derived TGF‑β) or core‑enriched (myeloid‑derived oncostatin M), influencing immune infiltration.
Oncostatin M and TGF‑β both induce partial EMT genes in vitro, but spatial context determines dominant driver in vivo.
open_questions: What determines whether a head‑and‑neck tumor adopts edge‑ vs core‑enriched EMT phenotypes?
Can the white‑gray matter barrier in low‑grade glioma be therapeutically reinforced to limit tumor spread?
tumor_types: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Partial EMT at tumor core associates with reduced lymphocyte infiltration, suggesting stronger immunosuppression.

key_findings: Identified spatially specific markers tied to colorectal cancer-specific mortality in Alaska Native people.
In the tumor center epithelial compartment, downregulation of MILK2 and SPINK4, and interferon alpha and gamma pathways were associated with not dying from colorectal cancer.
In the tumor center, a decrease in plasma cells and an increase in mast cells were observed in patients who did not die from colorectal cancer.
In the invasive margin epithelial compartment, an increase in HBA2 expression was observed in patients who died from colorectal cancer.
Epithelial-mesenchymal transition pathways were enriched in the invasive margin (epithelial and stromal compartments) in patients who died from colorectal cancer.
Soluble CEA was undetectable in 16% of stage IV CRC patients, while the same molecule on EV surfaces was detectable.
The combinatorial immunosequencing platform can detect rare EV subpopulations (1 in 10 million) with high sensitivity and a four-log dynamic range.
Three-marker combinations consistently discriminated between epithelial and stromal cell origins in CRC EVs across three independent cohorts.
Several multi-marker EV surface signatures showed FDR significant prognostic value in longitudinal CRC cohorts.
CD73, CD13, and CEA were identified as recurrent components in CRC-secreted EVs with prognostic potential.
open_questions: Plans for validation of findings.
Potential for early detection using multi-marker EV signatures.

key_findings: FGFR2 high expression was prognostic for worse overall survival in mCRC patients (HR 1.28).
FGFR2 high expression was predictive of worse overall survival in the cetuximab arm (HR 1.56).
FGFR3 high expression was predictive of improved overall survival in the cetuximab arm (HR 0.59).
FGFR2 SNP RS-3135718 variant allele was predictive of improved PFS and OS in the cetuximab arm.
FGFR2 inhibition decreased cell viability in CRC cell lines, reiterating its criticality for cell survival.
open_questions: Why do FGFR2 and FGFR3 behave differently despite being in the same family?
Underlying mechanisms for FGFR3's association with improved survival in the cetuximab arm.

key_findings: Several B cell populations (germinal center B, plasma memory, naive B) are associated with immunotherapy response on-treatment.
Specific B cell niches (germinal center, B activated, plasma-rich, plasma-maturing) were identified.
The B activated niche and its interactions with other immune cells are predictive of immunotherapy response.
B cells are more significantly impacted post-immunotherapy compared to other TME cells.
Cytokine enrichment within niches is a persistent feature in immunotherapy responders across treatment time points.
open_questions: How do B cells and plasma cells contribute to immunotherapy response, given the traditional focus on T cells?
The role of antibodies produced by plasma cells in immunotherapy response.
Potential for targeting B cells or their niches in immunotherapy.

key_findings: Cancer-associated normal ducts show distinct proteomic profiles compared to incidental normal ducts, including oxidative stress, metabolic reprogramming, and immune editing.
Inflammation and antigen presentation pathways are upregulated early in pancreatic precursor lesions but drop sharply in high-grade PANA, indicating immune evasion.
KRAS hotspot mutations can be identified from proteomic data, enabling genotype-phenotype correlation in precursor lesions.
The study identified a 'cancer field effect' where normal ducts near tumors acquire immune signatures.
DVP identified distinct proteomic differences between spatially adjacent regions within tumors, highlighting tumor heterogeneity.
open_questions: Translating these findings into clinical diagnostics or therapeutics.
Further exploration of the identified immune evasion mechanisms.

key_findings: Four TME types and three epithelial types were identified, with immune types not significantly captured by Oncotype DX Recurrence Score.
Inflamed epithelia were characterized by downregulation of ESR1 and suppression of DNA repair pathways.
Inflamed TME and epithelia were prognostic in the intermediate recurrence score group, with chemotherapy showing poorer outcomes.
High stromal CD8 density was a predictive marker of chemo inferiority in the intermediate recurrence score group.
Increasing CD8 density conferred poorer outcome on chemotherapy, adding prognostic information to clinical variables.
open_questions: How to translate these findings into a clinical assay, potentially using foundational models for TIL scoring.
The role of chemotherapy in ER+ breast cancer with high CD8 density.
The relationship between CD8 density and response to immunotherapy in triple-negative breast cancer.
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Inflamed states are transcriptomically wired to more dysfunctions, such as expression of checkpoints, exhaustion transcripts, M2-like macrophage, and remodeling genes, as well as dedifferentiation.

key_findings: The PertiMap platform enables scaled in vivo genetic perturbation and multimodal tissue profiling.
The MAIRS model can project human biology onto mouse H&E images, effectively 'humanizing' preclinical models.
MAIRS identified tumors with high predicted human CCAM6 expression in mouse models, correlating with specific histological changes.
The embedding space of perturbations revealed distinct phenotypic clusters associated with immune infiltration, fibrosis, and metabolic signatures.
VEGFR1 knockout tumors treated with PD1 showed a shift towards a hot TME, suggesting a rationale for combination therapy.
open_questions: How to validate the predicted human gene expression in mouse models.
The application of MAIRS to humanized mouse models with both mouse and human cells.
The number of genes that can be identified in the inferred spatial transcriptomes.

key_findings: FIT‑DNA arm achieved 28% screening completion at 90 days versus 23% for FIT (p<0.05).
The modest advantage persisted at 180 days (≈27% vs 22%).
Higher screening rates were observed in Los Angeles sites for FIT‑DNA, driven by lower baseline screening.
Hispanic and Medicaid/uninsured participants showed greater uptake of FIT‑DNA, likely reflecting clinic‑level differences.
Colonoscopic follow‑up after abnormal results was low across all sites, with Boston showing the highest rates.
Enrolled 579 patients, of whom 58% self‑identified as minority, reversing typical under‑representation.
Eligibility filtering reduced manual chart review workload by 35%.
Among eligible patients, 27% enrolled in a trial, compared with ~22% at NCI centers.
No racial/ethnic differences were observed in patient attitudes toward trials or in physician‑reported trial discussions.
High refusal rate due to emotional burden at decision points limited overall enrollment.
open_questions: How can the algorithm be integrated prospectively into trial design and IRB planning to predict accrual feasibility?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Patients often declined participation due to emotional stress at treatment decision points.

key_findings: Identified 675 African‑American individuals eligible for lung‑cancer screening; 220 (≈33%) enrolled after navigation.
Collected >5,000 biospecimens and contacted >3,000 community members, demonstrating feasibility of large‑scale outreach.
Multimodal navigation (community activators + CHWs + nurse navigators) improved screening uptake compared with prior single‑navigator models.
Rural sites required intensive door‑to‑door outreach; lack of mobile screening vans limited reach in remote areas.
Financial‑toxicity navigation was planned but not fully implemented due to resource constraints.
open_questions: How can sustainable funding be secured to maintain the multilevel navigation workforce after grant termination?
What is the optimal balance of high‑tech (AI risk scoring) and high‑touch (community navigation) interventions for maximal impact?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Transportation barriers and limited colonoscopy capacity reduced follow‑up compliance.

key_findings: US first site activation median 150 days, faster than Europe and China.
Time to activate 75% of planned US sites exceeds 300 days, whereas South Korea achieves ~45 days and other regions 100‑125 days.
First patient in US takes ~80 days versus 40‑50 days in non‑US regions.
Each additional protocol amendment version adds approximately 30‑60 days to overall study start time.
Trials with three or more protocol versions experience an extra 70‑80 days delay compared with the original version.
BRCA‑mutated tumors exhibit higher stromal HSF1, ATF4, and XBP1 expression compared with BRCA‑wild‑type tumors.
HSF1‑dependent signaling converts fibroblasts to iCAFs that down‑regulate NK‑cell activating receptors (NKG2D, DNAM1).
CAF‑mediated internalization of NK‑cell ligands (CD155, ULBP1) impairs NK‑cell cytotoxicity in ex vivo co‑culture assays.
In vivo NK‑cell depletion or CAF enrichment increases stromal content and reduces metastasis control in mouse models.
High nectin‑2 expression on CAFs correlates with poorer overall survival in breast cancer tissue microarrays.
open_questions: Does targeting HSF1 in CAFs reverse established iCAF phenotypes in vivo?
What metabolic cues (e.g., lipids) drive CAF‑mediated NK‑cell suppression?
Can similar stress‑response pathways be exploited in other tumor types beyond BRCA‑mutated cancers?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: NK‑cell inhibition by CAFs appears irreversible on the experimental timescale.
HSF1 inhibition may sensitize tumors to PARP inhibitors in BRCA‑mutated contexts.

key_findings: Restraint stress increased circulating corticosterone and produced a ~4‑fold rise in lung metastases.
Chronic unpredictable mild stress also elevated corticosterone and enhanced metastatic burden despite milder hormone rise.
Stressed lungs showed increased ECM (fibronectin), reduced T‑cell infiltration, and expanded neutrophils.
Neutrophils from stressed mice formed markedly more NETs ex vivo; this required neutrophil‑intrinsic glucocorticoid receptor signaling.
DNase treatment abolished NET DNA, reduced ECM deposition, and returned metastatic burden to baseline levels in stressed mice.
Glucocorticoid‑treated mice displayed higher Ki‑67 positivity in dormant disseminated tumor cells, but metastasis required concurrent T‑cell depletion.
open_questions: How do glucocorticoid levels in cancer patients (endogenous vs exogenous) quantitatively relate to NET burden and metastatic risk?
Can pharmacologic NET inhibition improve outcomes when combined with checkpoint blockade in stressed patients?
What are the downstream signaling pathways linking GR activation to NETosis in neutrophils?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Glucocorticoid‑induced NET formation acts as an accelerant for metastasis but is counteracted by adaptive T‑cell immunity.
Mifepristone blockade of glucocorticoid signaling may have context‑dependent effects across tumor types.

cited_papers: He et al. 2024 Nat Cancer (stress‑CAF work)
Rogers et al. 2024 Cancer Res (glucocorticoid‑NET study)

key_findings: Mean DunedinPACE was 1.3 (accelerated aging) two years after breast cancer diagnosis.
Lower income‑to‑poverty ratio, higher perceived physical disorder, and greater objective neighborhood disinvestment correlated positively with epigenetic age acceleration (p≤0.1).
BMI and current smoking showed the strongest independent associations with accelerated aging (smoking largest effect size).
Repeated measures in 38 participants showed a modest overall deceleration of epigenetic age over time, but the effect of social stressors attenuated at the later time point.
Chemotherapy receipt also influenced epigenetic age acceleration, suggesting treatment may mediate stress‑related aging effects.
open_questions: Do interventions that reduce neighborhood disinvestment or improve socioeconomic conditions reverse epigenetic age acceleration?
What is the causal pathway linking social stressors to DNA‑methylation changes in cancer survivors?
How do treatment‑related factors (e.g., chemotherapy) interact with social stressors to modulate biological aging?
readouts: Google Street View virtual audits for built environment

cited_papers: Cole SR. Conserved transcriptional response to adversity. Nat Rev Immunol 2019
Welms L et al. Meta‑analysis of social stressors and epigenetic clocks. preprint 2024

key_findings: Cost per molecule for degradomics dropped from >$20,000 in 2012 to < $500 using DIA‑MS and automation.
Discovery timeline from initial screen to high‑resolution cryo‑EM structure reduced to ~6 weeks.
A selective KAT2A degrader was identified that does not degrade the paralog KAT2B or off‑target GSPD1/2.
In an aggressive AML PDX model, treatment with the KAT2A degrader caused complete loss of KAT2A protein and H3K9 acetylation, confirming on‑target activity.
Structural analysis revealed a unique tyrosine‑mediated interface on cereblon that confers selectivity for KAT2A over KAT2B.
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Selectivity is achieved by exploiting a single tyrosine interaction on cereblon and auxiliary loops that discriminate KAT2A from KAT2B.

key_findings: Cryo‑EM of PI3K bound to farnesylated KRAS on nanodiscs revealed progressive loss of regulatory domains (auto‑inhibitory N‑SH2 and iSH2) across three structural classes.
A previously unobserved C‑terminal SH2 domain contacts the membrane and acts as an additional checkpoint before full activation.
Inclusion of PIP2 in the nanodisc reorients the holoenzyme, forming a true helix‑12 that swings 180° and directly engages substrate PIP2 in the active site – the first such observation.
The H1047R oncogenic mutation likely disrupts a hinge interaction (His1047‑Trp1051), facilitating helix‑12 swing and membrane association, explaining its activating effect.
Multivalent HER3 phospho‑tails induce a dimeric PI3K configuration at the nanodisc edge, preventing re‑assembly of the auto‑inhibited state and representing a fully active dimeric species.
open_questions: What is the precise molecular identity of the extra density assigned to the C‑terminal SH2 domain, and how does its membrane interaction regulate activation?
Does membrane curvature influence the propensity of PI3K to dimerize, and how might this affect signaling in different cellular contexts?
readouts: Western blot for H3K9ac (downstream PD marker)

key_findings: ABL kinase populates three conformations: a ground active state and two low‑populated inactive states (~5% each).
Gleevec binds selectively to the inactive‑2 state, explaining its high specificity and the mechanism of many resistance mutations that destabilize this state.
Src family kinases also sample an intermediate conformation (~5%) that has markedly reduced ADP affinity, identifying it as the key state for rapid ADP release during processive phosphorylation.
Mutations that destabilize the intermediate state abolish processive phosphorylation by Src and Lck, confirming its functional relevance.
VirtualFlow docking of >70 billion compounds against the inactive‑2 ABL structure yielded nanomolar inhibitors with promising selectivity profiles.
open_questions: Can the identified intermediate state be stabilized pharmacologically across other kinases to achieve broad selectivity?
What are the kinetic and energetic determinants that govern the population distribution of these low‑populated states in vivo?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Resistance mutations in ABL (e.g., T315I) act by depleting the inactive‑2 population rather than directly blocking Gleevec binding.

key_findings: In a cohort of 48 older ALL patients, CD19 CAR achieved 90% complete remission with no dose‑limiting toxicities and markedly reduced grade ≥2 CRS (17% vs 80% in relapse setting).
CAR T cells were detectable in CSF of every treated patient, indicating CNS trafficking and no observed CNS relapses.
Two molecular relapses were identified by ClonoSEQ; both patients were successfully retreated and proceeded to allogeneic transplant.
First‑in‑human BAFF‑R CAR demonstrated expansion comparable to CD19 CAR, grade 1 toxicities only, and ≥70% objective responses in lymphoma patients.
BAFF‑R expression persisted in ~66% of CD19‑negative ALL relapses, supporting its role as a salvage target.
open_questions: Will longer‑term follow‑up confirm durability of remission beyond 2 years in older ALL patients?
Can BAFF‑R CAR be combined with CD19 CAR or bispecific antibodies to prevent antigen escape?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: CD19 loss or epitope alteration accounted for ~30% of post‑blinatumomab relapses, necessitating BAFF‑R targeting.
Variable BAFF‑R antigen density in ALL (≈80% of cases) may limit efficacy in low‑expressors.

key_findings: Mesothelin‑specific TCR T cells showed tumor infiltration but displayed a dominant TGF‑β–driven exhaustion signature distinct from blood T cells.

IKZF3 (Aeolus) knockout eliminated the TGF‑β signature and mitigated exhaustion but caused activation‑induced cell death, which was rescued by engineered fusion proteins delivering IL‑2 or FasL‑derived survival signals.
HIT CD70 CARs demonstrated superior sensitivity, achieving tumor eradication in renal cell carcinoma PDXs with low CD70 expression where conventional CARs failed.
KRAS G12V‑specific TCRs engineered with CD8αβ and CD28 co‑stimulation induced durable tumor regressions and biomarker (CEA, ctDNA) declines in 3 of 4 patients.
Spatial analysis revealed that exhausted engineered T cells reside in tumor cores surrounded by TGF‑β, whereas functional T cells localize to tertiary lymphoid structures near vasculature.
open_questions: Can Aeolus knockout combined with survival‑signal fusion proteins achieve durable persistence without apoptosis in patients?
What is the optimal balance of TGF‑β signaling to maintain stemness versus exhaustion in solid‑tumor TCR therapies?
Will HIT CARs maintain specificity and safety in vivo given their ultra‑high sensitivity to low antigen density?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: TGF‑β in the pancreatic TME drives a unique exhaustion program not seen in melanoma TILs.
CD70 expression is epigenetically silenced in kidney‑site RCC PDXs via EZH2‑mediated H3K27me3, leading to antigen loss and resistance to conventional CARs.

key_findings: 1XX CD19 CAR achieved a 75% complete remission rate in refractory DLBCL using only 25 M cells, with markedly lower CRS/ICANS compared to standard products.
HIT CD70 CAR eradicated renal cell carcinoma PDXs with low CD70 expression, whereas conventional CD70 CARs failed even at 10 M cell doses.
1A CD70 CAR outperformed classic 28ζ CARs in orthotopic kidney, ovarian, breast, and glioblastoma models, showing sustained tumor control and reduced exhaustion markers.
YBX1 phosphorylation uniquely sustained translation efficiency in 1A CAR T cells, linking enhanced ribosomal biogenesis to prolonged effector function.
Epigenetic silencing (EZH2‑mediated H3K27me3) of CD70 in kidney‑site tumors creates a microenvironment‑dependent antigen loss that is overcome by the heightened sensitivity of HIT CARs.
open_questions: Will the 1XX CAR’s lower activation threshold be sufficient for high‑antigen‑density tumors without compromising efficacy?
What safety monitoring is required for HIT CARs given potential low‑level CD70 expression in normal tissues such as esophagus?
Can YBX1 modulation be therapeutically leveraged to boost 1A CAR function without inducing off‑target translation effects?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: HIT CARs’ ultra‑sensitivity may increase risk of on‑target off‑tumor effects; low CD70 expression detected in esophageal epithelium raises safety considerations.
1XX CAR’s reduced ITAM signaling mitigates cytokine release but may limit maximal cytotoxic potency in high‑antigen‑density settings.

key_findings: PARP1 trapping, not just catalytic inhibition, is essential for monotherapy activity; talazoparib and sarucaparib show stronger trapping and greater efficacy than rucaparib.
Complete (>90%) PARP inhibition is required for tumor regression; sub‑therapeutic dosing leads to tumor escape and resistance.
BRCA1/2 mutation type influences response; hypomorphic C61G BRCA1 mutants confer reduced sensitivity compared to null alleles.
Acquired resistance is driven by HR re‑activation, evidenced by RAD51 foci re‑appearance in >90% of resistant models.
Dose‑intensity correlates with long‑term tumor control; continuous high‑dose olaparib prevents escape, whereas intermittent dosing increases residual tumor burden.
open_questions: What is the optimal dosing schedule to maximize PARP trapping while minimizing toxicity?
Can functional HRD assays (e.g., STRIDE) replace static genomic scar tests for patient selection?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: PARP1 L77P mutation abolishes trapping and confers resistance to olaparib and talazoparib.
Reversion mutations restoring HR function lead to RAD51 foci resurgence and PARP inhibitor resistance.

key_findings: ARID1B degraders achieve nanomolar potency and >10‑fold selectivity over ARID1A in biochemical and cellular assays.
Cereblon‑based ARID1B degraders show superior potency and no off‑target neo‑substrate activity across the proteome.
Ternary complex crystal structures reveal a ligand twist that enhances cooperativity, informing SAR for both VHL and CRBN series.
SMARCA2 inhibitor LY4050784 (909) combined with anti‑PD‑1 yields 6/6 complete responses in a BRG1‑knockout syngeneic mouse model and induces durable immune memory.
Combination of SMARCA2 inhibition with PD‑1 blockade is well tolerated (no weight loss) and produces sustained tumor control.
open_questions: Can ARID1B degraders achieve sufficient oral bioavailability for clinical use?
What biomarkers best predict response to SMARCA2 inhibition beyond SMARCA4 loss?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: ARID1B degraders show a clear hook effect at high concentrations, requiring careful dose optimization.
No degradation of ARID1A observed, confirming paralog selectivity.

cited_papers: Ballen et al. 2026 Nature Chemical Biology

key_findings: Post‑hoc NETTER‑1/2 analyses showed similar survival benefit across low, intermediate, and high somatostatin receptor uptake levels.
VISION trial post‑hoc quartile analysis demonstrated that patients in the highest PSMA PET SUV quartile had the best radiographic PFS and OS.
Low FDG metabolic tumor volume predicted superior response to lutetium‑PSMA therapy, independent of PSMA uptake intensity.
Single‑time‑point dosimetry at ~24 h can estimate tumor absorbed dose, but lesion doses decrease with successive cycles.
open_questions: What is the optimal imaging time point for accurate dosimetry across different radiopharmaceuticals?
Can standardized single‑time‑point dosimetry replace multi‑time‑point protocols without loss of predictive power?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Approximately 30% of VISION patients were non‑responders, associated with low PSMA uptake, TP53 mutations, or discordant FDG‑positive/PSMA‑negative disease.
Somatostatin analog co‑administration can increase tumor SUV by reducing background liver/spleen activity.

key_findings: VISION trial showed a 4‑month OS benefit (median 11 mo vs 7 mo) for lutetium‑177 PSMA‑617 in APMR.
Approximately 30% of patients were non‑responders, linked to low PSMA uptake, FDG‑PSMA discordance, or TP53 mutations.
Actinium‑225 PSMA therapy yielded median OS 16 mo in heavily pretreated patients, with 70% experiencing xerostomia after one cycle.
Early‑line trials (PSMA‑4, PSMA‑ADDITION) improve radiographic PFS but have not yet shown OS advantage, likely due to crossover.
Alpha emitters may overcome radioresistance in high‑grade disease and micrometastases, while beta emitters are suited for bulk disease.
open_questions: Optimal sequencing of alpha versus beta radiopharmaceuticals in the same patient.
How to mitigate salivary gland toxicity from actinium‑225 PSMA.
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: Low PSMA expression and FDG‑positive/PSMA‑negative lesions predict resistance to PSMA‑RPT.
TP53 somatic mutations associated with poorer outcomes.

key_findings: Personalized dosimetry using NM‑600 allowed subtraction of radiopharmaceutical dose from external beam plans, enabling safe delivery of combined therapy in head‑and‑neck cancer.
Low‑to‑moderate Y‑90 NM‑600 doses synergized with anti‑CTLA‑4, enhancing local and systemic tumor control and generating immune memory.
Alpha‑emitting actinium showed superior immune priming (increased TCR clonality) in poorly immunogenic tumors compared with beta emitters.

Heterogeneous intratumoral dose distribution (mixed high/low uptake) activated multiple immune pathways (type‑I IFN, MHC up‑regulation) and improved survival in mouse models, an effect lost with homogeneous dosing.
open_questions: What is the optimal dose heterogeneity profile to maximize immune priming while preserving normal tissue?
How should dosing intervals be timed between radiopharmaceuticals and immunotherapies to avoid lymphocyte depletion?
resistance_or_selectivity_notes: High‑dose beta radiation can cause systemic lymphopenia, reducing checkpoint inhibitor efficacy.
Fractionated dosing mitigates GI toxicity for astatine‑211 agents in preclinical models.

cited_papers: Patel et al. 2024 Cancer Immunology Research

key_findings: E6R is a non-enzymatic inhibitor of the Sin3-Rpd3L complex, identified through a yeast-based reporter assay screening 52,000 compounds.
E6R exhibits a distinct transcriptomic signature compared to enzymatic HDAC inhibitors (TSA) and complex knockouts (Rpd3, Sin3).
In neuroblastoma cells, E6R reduces invasion without significant cytotoxicity, unlike TSA.
E6R affects 14x fewer genes than TSA in neuroblastoma cells, indicating higher transcriptional selectivity.
E6R induces cell cycle arrest via p53/E2F signaling and repression of G2M checkpoint genes.
E6R specifically activates integrated stress response and pro-apoptotic pathways, including ATF4 targets like DDIT3 and GDF15.
Single-cell RNA sequencing shows E6R treatment mirrors DMSO control in cell state composition.
